title: Deadly bacteria detected as NYC orders emergency cleaning of cooling towers
summary: A health expert discusses why Legionnaires' disease outbreaks keep striking the South Bronx and other historically marginalized NYC areas.
story: Infectious diseases expert Dr. Tyler Evans explains the risks tied to Legionella found in Bronx cooling towers, which symptoms residents should watch for, and when exposure may require medical care.

Health officials ordered the immediate remediation of 10 rooftop cooling towers in the South Bronx after preliminary testing detected Legionella bacteria amid a growing Legionnaires’ disease cluster that has sickened nine people and left one dead.

The New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene issued orders to clean and disinfect the sites. Among the affected structures are cooling towers at major hubs, including Yankee Stadium and Lincoln Hospital.
As public health workers work to clean the equipment, experts note that recurring outbreaks in these neighborhoods highlight deeper systemic vulnerabilities.
NYC LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE OUTBREAK KILLS FOURTH VICTIM, 76 CASES REPORTED

"When we look at outbreaks of Legionnaires' disease, in New York City, we almost always see it in the Bronx or Harlem," Dr. Tyler Evans, CEO of the Wellness Equity Alliance and former first chief medical officer for New York City, told Fox News Digital.
"A lot of times, we see a risk of infections taking place in historically marginalized communities."

New York City health officials ordered the immediate remediation of 10 South Bronx cooling towers — including units at Yankee Stadium and Lincoln Hospital — after detecting Legionella DNA during a cluster investigation that has sickened nine people and caused one death. (New York Yankees/Getty Images)
The department identified the cluster following a surge in cases dating back to late August. Tests confirmed traces of Legionella in 10 of 24 sampled towers, according to city health officials.

PCR (polymerase chain reaction) tests return results quickly, but cannot distinguish between live and dead bacteria. Culture tests to confirm live bacteria can take up to two weeks, prompting city health officials to order immediate cleaning out of caution.
HEART ATTACKS AND STROKES RISING WITH EXTREME WEATHER EVENTS, RESEARCH SUGGESTS

Late-summer weather has compounded the issue. High temperatures create ideal breeding grounds for bacteria inside industrial air-conditioning systems, which add water to the surrounding air, Evans noted.
"Record-breaking temperatures lead to accelerating the risk of the bacteria basically cooking, getting out to become vaporized, and then producing exposure to other people," he said.

Preliminary PCR testing quickly confirmed bacterial DNA, but because it cannot distinguish between live and dead bacteria, officials mandated immediate cleanings while awaiting culture test results. (iStock)

Legionnaires' disease, a severe form of pneumonia, cannot be spread between people, nor is it contracted by drinking tap water, the expert noted. Most healthy individuals are not sickened by exposure, but high-risk populations can face severe health consequences.

"In terms of people ... to be concerned about, it's really older adults — typically 65 and older — or people living with comorbid conditions," Evans said, pointing to underlying factors like diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or compromised immune systems.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Health officials urge anyone who has lived in, worked in or visited ZIP codes 10451 and 10456 since late August to monitor their health.
Key symptoms to watch for include high fevers, severe shortness of breath, chest pain and coughing up bloody mucus.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Evans noted that early medical care is crucial, as the illness responds well to standard antibiotic treatments when caught early.

"Infections fall into different buckets — bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites," he said. "Bacteria are alive. Antibiotics are effective against bacteria because you can kill them, which makes it very treatable."

Legionnaires' disease is a non-contagious form of pneumonia spread through inhaled vapor — not drinking water — that poses the highest risk to adults over 65 and individuals with underlying conditions like diabetes or COPD. (iStock)
While city officials have taken quick action to inspect and clean the structures, Evans emphasized that long-term prevention requires sustained public investment.
"Could we test all cooling towers across New York City on a regular basis during times of risk when it's hotter? Yes," Evans said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"City health officials do an amazing job, but it costs money. When federal funds are removed from public health, it's very hard to do more when you have less."

In a statement provided to Fox News Digital, a Yankee Stadium representative said that "new, state-of-the-art, high-efficiency chiller towers" have been installed, which have undergone water quality and bacteriological indicator testing on a weekly basis over the last three years.
"When we look at outbreaks of Legionnaires' disease, in New York City, we almost always see it in the Bronx or Harlem."
"In accordance with New York City Department of Health regulations, Yankee Stadium provides these results to the NYC DOH on a monthly basis," the representative said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While Yankee Stadium did test positive for "trace amounts of Legionella bacteria" on Sept. 11, the representative said that "no current cases have been associated with Yankee Stadium."
"Additionally, the New York City Department of Health has not at any point this month asked us to postpone our games."
Fox News Digital reached out to Lincoln Hospital requesting comment.

title: Woman loses best friend to ovarian cancer, then receives same devastating diagnosis months later
summary: A Minnesota woman diagnosed with stage 3B ovarian cancer after her best friend died from the same disease urges women to advocate for themselves.
story: Brian M. Slomovitz, MD, director of gynecologic oncology at Mount Sinai Medical Center in Miami Beach, Florida, says ovarian cancer was once known as the "silent killer," meaning it was often undetected until it reached an advanced stage.
A Minnesota woman whose best friend died from ovarian cancer was stunned when she was diagnosed with the same disease less than a year later.

Becky Drexler was there to support her best friend, Connie Dahl, when she was diagnosed with stage 4 ovarian cancer in April 2015 at age 51. After a courageous battle, Dahl passed away in September 2017.
During her friend's cancer fight, Drexler began volunteering with the Minnesota Ovarian Cancer Alliance (MOCA).
CANCER SURVIVORS MAY SEE SURPRISING BENEFITS FROM ONE SPECIFIC EXERCISE, STUDY SAYS
After retiring in 2017, Drexler was making plans to travel, garden, volunteer and spend more time with family and friends – but those plans were interrupted by her own diagnosis in July 2018.
"I was diagnosed with stage 3B high-grade serous ovarian cancer," Drexler, now 65, told Fox News Digital.
Becky Drexler (right) was there to support her best friend, Connie Dahl (far left), when she was diagnosed with stage 4 ovarian cancer in April 2015 at age 51.  (Becky Drexler)
Like her best friend, Drexler dismissed her own symptoms – including frequent urination, constipation, bloating and hip pain – as common signs of aging. She put off seeing a doctor at first.

"By early summer, I felt I was getting signs from Connie to nudge me along," she wrote in an essay sent to Fox News Digital. "Dragonflies represent Connie to me since she passed, and I saw them everywhere. I recall one afternoon being on my patio thinking, ‘Should I go see the doctor?’ when a couple dragonflies in my flower garden just wouldn’t leave me alone. I said out loud, ‘OK, Connie, I’ll go in and talk to the doctor.’"
ALCOHOL TIED TO SURPRISING CANCER DEATH PATTERN IN ADULTS UNDER 55, RESEARCHERS FIND
On Drexler's 57th birthday, her doctor called to say a CT scan had detected masses on both ovaries. After meeting with an oncologist, she had surgery four days later.
Drexler underwent six chemotherapy treatments (carboplatin and taxol) from September 2018 to January 2019.

"Those months were difficult but also filled with the support, love and laughter of family, friends, care team and MOCA," she said. "I knew Connie was part of my team as well – just in a different way."

After retiring in 2017, Drexler was making plans to travel, garden, volunteer and spend more time with family and friends – but those plans were interrupted by her own diagnosis in July 2018. (Becky Drexler)
Throughout Drexler’s cancer fight, she drew inspiration from her friend’s vow to "be positive, and to live, laugh and love to the fullest every day."

"This helped me greatly, as did attending MOCA support group meetings and talking to women who had or were experiencing the same things I was," she said. "There were times I wished Connie was still here so I could talk to her about what I was feeling physically and emotionally."
CURE FOR CERTAIN CANCERS IS ‘REALISTIC’ GOAL IN NEXT DECADE, PHARMA LEAD SAYS
In August 2020, Drexler’s cancer returned. She had surgery to remove the new tumor from her pelvic area.
"We discussed treatment options with my oncologist – she provided the pros and cons of standard chemotherapy, radiation, and no treatment, only monitoring," she shared.
"I was diagnosed with stage 3B high-grade serous ovarian cancer."

Ultimately, Drexler decided on targeted radiation, with chemotherapy as a backup option if radiation did not work or if there was another recurrence. After radiation was completed in January 2021, Drexler was again considered to have "no evidence of disease" (NED).
"I then began taking Lynparza, a PARP inhibitor maintenance treatment – something that was not even available for ovarian cancer patients when Connie was dealing with her cancer," she said.
From January 2021 until February 2026, while taking Lynparza, Drexler remained in NED status – "although there was always the concern in the back of my mind about when I would recur again."
VISION PROBLEM LEADS TO MAN'S STAGE 4 LUNG CANCER DIAGNOSIS, NEW DRUG EXTENDS SURVIVAL
In winter 2025, after experiencing gastric symptoms, Drexler underwent a PET scan. The scan revealed a tumor around her small intestine that had grown large enough to require surgery.

"Once the tumor was removed, it was confirmed to be a recurrence of my ovarian cancer," she said. "After recovering from surgery, I had another PET scan, which indicated a couple of spots were still present."
Becky Drexler (center) is pictured with other survivors presenting to medical students at Mayo Clinic in 2025. (Becky Drexler)
In May 2026, Drexler began an 18-week treatment cycle including carboplatin, taxol and avastin, which is expected to be completed at the end of September.
"I had a PET scan halfway through (late July), which indicated the treatment is working," she shared. "We were happy to learn that the spots were no longer visible and no new spots had appeared."
FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE

Depending on the results of her next PET scan, Drexler said her next treatment will likely be an antibody drug conjugate (ADC) maintenance plan, a recently-approved targeted cancer therapy that has shown "exceptional results."
Throughout her cancer journey, Drexler has continued volunteering with MOCA, serving on its board of directors, participating on committees and reviewing grants for ovarian cancer research.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"It does make me think back to when Connie was dealing with her cancer and the treatments that were not available to her but are now available for me and other women," Drexler said.
"I believe I am still here because of the advancements in treatments. Developing a reliable early detection test for ovarian cancer remains one of the most critical research goals."
Symptoms to watch for

Ovarian cancer was once known as the "silent killer," meaning that women would get it and not know anything until the disease was in advanced, more aggressive stages, according to Brian M. Slomovitz, M.D., director of gynecologic oncology at Mount Sinai Medical Center in Miami Beach, Florida.
About 75% of women are diagnosed with stage 3 or stage 4 disease, according to the doctor.
Dahl, Drexler, Drexler's husband and Dahl's husband (left to right) are pictured at the Drexlers' wedding in 2002. (Becky Drexler)
In recent years, researchers have identified that ovarian cancer actually does have symptoms, noted Slomovitz, who is also deputy director of the Braman Comprehensive Cancer Center.
"The problem is they are sort of non-specific symptoms, things that could occur in everyday life – stomach pains, abdominal bloating, things like that."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"There may be an increase in abdominal girth, meaning patients complain that their pants are too tight or they're noticing something different in the way their body's shaped," the doctor said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Those symptoms can also come with weight loss and decreased appetite, he noted: "They could oftentimes mimic gastroenteritis or eating a bad meal."
Any symptoms that persist or worsen over a period of one or two weeks should be checked out, the doctor advised.
‘Advocate for yourself’
To other women who may be experiencing worrisome symptoms, Drexler urges them to listen to their bodies.

"The early symptoms both Connie and I had were vague, like they are for most women," she said. "They seem like normal things that we can excuse away – we are aging, we are just stressed, we just need to eat better or lose weight."
"If something isn’t feeling right or a seemingly minor issue persists, and you think you might be concerned, see your doctor. Advocate for yourself."
"They seem like normal things that we can excuse away – we are aging, we are just stressed, we just need to eat better or lose weight."
For those who are diagnosed with ovarian cancer, Drexler emphasized that it’s important to see a gynecologic oncologist, as they have additional training in diagnosing and treating cancers.

Researchers have spent decades studying early detection and screening for ovarian cancer, Slomovitz said – "but unfortunately, no reliable method has been identified to diagnose women at an earlier stage."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

There is currently no recommended routine screening test for ovarian cancer in women at average risk, because available tests have not been shown to reliably detect the disease early enough to improve outcomes.
When ovarian cancer is detected at stage 1, the cure rate approaches 90%, Slomovitz said, underscoring the need for continued research into earlier detection.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Popular GLP-1 weight-loss drugs linked to potentially deadly brain disorder
summary: A study linked 15 cases of Wernicke encephalopathy to GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro, raising concerns about vitamin B1 deficiency risks.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel joins 'Fox & Friends' to discuss a recent University of California San Diego study regarding the effects of GLP-1 weight loss medication on the biological aging process. Siegel outlines the potential cardiovascular and neurological benefits of the drug while noting side effects related to digestion and thyroid function.
Researchers are warning about a rare but potentially life-threatening brain condition that may be linked to popular GLP-1 weight-loss medications.

A new study, published in Clinical Nutrition, identified 15 reported cases of Wernicke encephalopathy, a neurological disorder caused by severe vitamin B1 deficiency, in people taking GLP-1 receptor agonists.
Most of the reported cases involved semaglutide, sold under the brand names Ozempic and Wegovy, or tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound.
DOCTORS REVEAL HIDDEN DANGER FOR SOME OZEMPIC, WEGOVY USERS WITH BRAIN DISORDERS
Researchers found 15 cases through the FDA's Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), published medical literature and their own medical center.
Most patients reported gastrointestinal symptoms or nutritional issues, including weight loss, vomiting, loss of appetite or malnutrition, the study noted.
Researchers are warning about a rare but potentially life-threatening brain condition that may be linked to popular GLP-1 weight-loss medications. (iStock)

Reports of the disorder appeared more often among people taking GLP-1 medications than among those taking other drugs, the researchers found. They emphasized, however, that the study cannot prove the medications caused the condition.

Vitamin B1 plays an important role in brain function, the researchers said. Severe deficiencies can cause confusion, trouble walking, balance problems and vision changes. If left untreated, the condition can lead to permanent neurological damage or death.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Karthik Achari, a Chicago-based clinician and founder of PepMD who was not involved in the study, said the findings should be viewed in perspective.

"Researchers went through adverse event reports and the medical literature and found a small number of cases, 15, of Wernicke encephalopathy in people taking GLP-1 drugs," Achari told Fox News Digital. "That's out of millions of people on these medications. So this is rare."
Researchers identified 15 cases, finding that most patients experienced gastrointestinal symptoms or nutritional issues, including weight loss, vomiting, loss of appetite or malnutrition. (iStock)
"But it's real, it's serious, and the mechanism makes sense," he added.
GLP-1 medications can reduce appetite while also causing nausea and vomiting, making it easier for some people to become deficient in vitamin B1, Achari said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"The drug shrinks your appetite. It doesn't shrink your body's requirements," he said. "You can now eat very little without feeling it, which is the point of the medication, but your need for protein, vitamins, and fluids didn't go anywhere."

People with persistent nausea and vomiting, those losing weight very quickly while eating little, people with a history of bariatric surgery and those who use alcohol heavily may face a higher risk, Achari said.
The medications suppress appetite, experts say, but the body's requirements for nutrients and hydration remain the same. (iStock)
Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based nutritionist and author of "The Sleepdemic Solution," said proper nutrition and hydration should be considered part of treatment while taking GLP-1 medications.

"GLP-1 medications can dramatically reduce appetite, but that also means people may unintentionally under-eat the very things their bodies need most, especially protein, fiber and fluids," she told Fox News Digital.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Palinski-Wade said ongoing vomiting or diarrhea can increase the risk of dehydration and kidney problems. She urged patients to seek medical guidance if those symptoms continue for roughly 24 hours.
"Don't assume every side effect is just part of being on a GLP-1," Palinski-Wade said. "Severe or persistent symptoms deserve attention."

The researchers acknowledged that the study relied largely on reports submitted to the FDA and cannot prove GLP-1 medications caused the condition. They called for additional research, and experts said patients should not stop taking prescribed GLP-1 medications based on these findings alone.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to Novo Nordisk, Eli Lilly and the researchers for comment.
Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Food divorce’ trend among couples could drive them apart, experts warn
summary: The "food divorce" trend has some couples eating separately, but experts warn the growing trend erodes relationship quality and emotional well-being over time.
story: Regularly splitting apart for meals may contribute to isolation and disconnection, according to dietitian Tanya Freirich. Sharing flexible, modular meals can make it easier for people with different needs or schedules to eat together.

Between differing diet plans, food intolerances and conflicting work schedules, some couples are choosing "food divorce," a term circulating on social media for partners who intentionally cook, order and eat their meals separately.
While taking separate paths at mealtime might solve logistical headaches, experts warn that splitting up at the dinner table can come at a cost to the relationship.
Shared family meals can help people reconnect, build stronger emotional bonds and reduce stress, according to health institutions like Mayo Clinic.
‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT
For couples, experts say regularly eating apart could become a concern if it reflects broader emotional distance or reduces opportunities to spend meaningful time together.
Nutrition experts emphasize the issue is often less about the food itself and more about the lost opportunity for a built-in daily checkpoint.
"Food divorce" refers to the growing trend of couples intentionally cooking, ordering and eating meals separately due to conflicting schedules or specialized diets. (iStock)
"I think it reflects many people's very busy schedules," Tanya Freirich, a North Carolina-based registered dietitian nutritionist, told Fox News Digital.

"Mealtime can be a time to unite, to communicate, to build social relationships and foster a connection," she said. "If we're eating completely alone or at different times than important people in our lives, it may foster a little bit of disconnection."
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
Eating separately can contribute to a "roommate dynamic," experts note. Without regular time to reconnect and discuss the day, couples may have fewer opportunities for communication.
The practice can also contribute to isolation, according to Freirich.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Communities all around the world for thousands of years have come together around mealtimes," she said.
"If so many Americans are eating every meal alone for many days or most of their days, that certainly can't be great for mental health or well-being."

Eating alone can contribute to isolation, an expert warned. "If so many Americans are eating every meal alone for many days or most of their days, that certainly can't be great for our mental health or well-being." (iStock)
There can also be practical drawbacks because preparing separate meals or ordering from different restaurants may increase grocery costs, preparation time and kitchen cleanup.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Additionally, eating solo can affect individual dietary habits. Studies show people dining alone are more likely to eat quickly, mindlessly scroll on their phones or settle for heavily processed convenience foods compared to when they share meals with others.
"Communities all around the world for thousands of years have come together around mealtimes."
Couples can accommodate different dietary needs without preparing entirely separate meals.
For those navigating specific calorie targets, plant-based diets or medical restrictions, Freirich recommended building "modular" or "choose your own adventure" meals as a more efficient method.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Something like a deconstructed taco night, grain bowls, a pasta or noodle night or even a sheet pan meal where you're creating each food on its own," the expert said.
"So the protein, the carb, the veggies are being cooked separately. And then you get to decide your portions and make your own meal from those ingredients that can meet everyone's needs."
Research highlights that nearly one in four Americans eats every meal alone on any given day, increasing the risk of isolation. (iStock)
When conflicting schedules or caregiving duties make daily dinners impossible, experts recommend prioritizing quality over frequency.
Even sharing a quick weekend breakfast or setting aside one designated night a week can help maintain connection.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Be very intentional to connect when you can," Freirich suggested.
"Make that a really special meal. Be intentional with your connection. Put the phone away, and actually enjoy the other person's company."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Nighttime bathroom trips could reveal hidden health issues — here's when to worry
summary: Nocturia affects half of adults over 50, but experts say frequent nighttime urination could signal sleep apnea, diabetes or an enlarged prostate.
story: Dr. Wendy Troxel shares why getting the recommended amount of nightly shuteye doesn't always leave people refreshed, and outlines the most common reasons for poor sleep quality.
Getting out of bed once during the night to use the bathroom is common, but repeated trips could signal underlying issues, health experts warn.

Waking up more than once a night to urinate can meet the clinical definition of nocturia, which affects about half of adults over 50 and becomes more common with age, according to a recent StudyFinds report. The International Continence Society’s formal definition of nocturia includes even one nighttime trip, but frequency, disruption and a change from a person’s usual pattern all matter.

"Everyone has a baseline of what’s normal urinary frequency for them," Dr. Ali Dabaja, a urologist at Henry Ford Health in Michigan, told the outlet. "But if you wake at least twice to go to the bathroom during eight hours of sleep, that’s considered nocturia."
DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID
Nocturia isn't simply a bladder issue, according to Dr. Jeffrey Chester, a licensed physician and medical director of The Ohana Luxury Addiction Treatment Center in Hawaii.

"A change in nighttime urinary patterns is definitely worth mentioning to a physician or healthcare provider, especially when it begins suddenly, becomes more frequent, or disrupts a person's sleep," Chester told Fox News Digital.
Nighttime bathroom trips can disrupt sleep and may become more common with age. (iStock)
Alcohol and caffeine intake, the amount and timing of fluid consumption, and certain medications can all contribute, he added.
Waking up once isn't a cause for concern, agreed Catherine Darley, a naturopathic doctor and founder of Skilled Sleeper in Seattle.
JUST 10 MINUTES OF DAILY FLOOR EXERCISES MAY IMPROVE BALANCE AND AGILITY, STUDY FINDS
But more than once can be "concerning," she told Fox News Digital.

Experts note that it can raise the risk of falls, especially for those with mobility or balance challenges. Research shows two or more nightly trips to the bathroom are linked to a higher risk of fall-related injuries, StudyFinds reported.
Repeated nighttime wake-ups to use the bathroom can increase fall risks, research has found. (iStock)
Sleep disorders can also be a factor, Darley said, including obstructive sleep apnea, which can affect hormones involved in suppressing urine production overnight.
Restless legs syndrome could also contribute to nighttime urination and is more common with age, Darley added.
OLDER ADULTS TAKING 5 OR MORE PRESCRIPTION DRUGS FACE HIGHER RISK OF DEATH, STUDY FINDS
She advised starting with your primary care provider to look for an underlying cause, and checking in with doctors and pharmacists to see if medications could be involved in frequent bathroom trips.
In some cases, they could adjust the timing to prevent late-night wake-ups.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Other issues could be the cause, too, according to StudyFinds, including diabetes, an overactive bladder, an enlarged prostate and fluid buildup.
Experts say the timing and amount of fluids, caffeine, alcohol and some medications can contribute to nighttime urination. (iStock)
For some people, simple habits can help, including not drinking for roughly two hours before bedtime and stopping alcohol about three hours before bed, Darley said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

She also suggested keeping floors clear of rugs and clutter, using gentle amber lighting, sitting on the edge of the bed before standing to avoid getting dizzy — and installing grab bars for extra support.
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Political fights can rip couples apart — therapist shares 3 ways to save a relationship
summary: A marriage therapist reveals three strategies for couples navigating the political divide, from setting boundaries to finding compromise.
story: Dr. Anna Elton discusses why partisan disagreements can create tension between partners, and offers strategies for setting boundaries, staying curious and reconnecting after heated conversations.
More than one-third of Americans report having ended a relationship over political differences, according to recent research – and experts say those divisions may also be straining some marriages.

Some high-profile couples, including Democratic strategist James Carville and his wife, Republican political consultant Mary Matalin, have remained together despite their differing views – but experts say navigating those differences isn't always easy.
Anna Elton, Ph.D., a licensed marriage and family therapist and clinical sexologist in Massachusetts, said she has counseled couples on different sides of the political aisle.
'QUIET QUITTING' COULD SILENTLY DESTROY YOUR MARRIAGE – 4 WAYS TO BRING THE SPARK BACK
"A lot of couples come in and they want to work on communication, and politics can come up in our sessions," Elton, author of "The Formula of Desire," told Fox News Digital.
"I work with a number of couples who are in this place where they have a family, they have kids, but they can't talk about politics."
More than one-third of Americans report having ended a relationship over political differences, according to recent research. (iStock)
For many singles, Elton said, political compatibility is now something they consider early in the dating process.
WHY COUPLES SHOULD FLIRT WITH EACH OTHER EVERY DAY – PLUS THE 'RED FLAG' TO AVOID
She referenced a recent study that found younger adults tend to make assumptions about religion, gender roles, empathy and other characteristics based on political affiliation.
"So, before you get to know the person, you’ve already created this assumption of who this person is."
Younger daters are more likely to choose who they want to date based on political affiliation, experts say. (iStock)

"I've definitely been hearing from my younger clients who are saying, ‘I want to know which political party this person belongs to, and then I'll see if I want to even be going on a date and wasting my time with this person.’"
COMMON MARRIAGE HABIT COULD QUIETLY KILL YOUR SEX LIFE, EXPERT WARNS
For couples who have been married for decades, today's political divisions may present challenges that didn't exist when their relationships began, Elton noted.
The expert offered the following three tips for navigating politically charged conversations with a partner in a healthy way.
No. 1: Set boundaries ahead of time
Come up with rules for the conversation and set the tone before it starts, Elton suggested, noting that the first three minutes of a discussion typically predict the outcome.
Conversations that begin with a harsh tone or accusatory language are unlikely to be productive, she said. "So, before you talk, say, ‘OK, these are our boundaries for this conversation.’"
The first three minutes of a discussion can typically predict the outcome, according to the expert. (iStock)
Those boundaries can also extend to media habits, Elton said, including limiting how much political content couples consume, especially on social media.

"You read certain things and then all of a sudden, you keep scrolling on your social media and you see similar content coming up over and over and over again," Elton said. "And at this point, it creates an illusionary effect."
HOW OFTEN ARE MARRIED PEOPLE HAVING SEX? WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT THE INTIMACY STANDARD IN AMERICA

Hearing the same information repeatedly may lead people to gradually accept it as true, according to Elton. "Now think about two people who are in their echo chambers, and they're exposed to certain information that is contradicting each other."

As a general rule, Elton said couples should be mindful not to spend more time on their phones than they do engaging with each other. Excessive screen time can reduce face-to-face connection, leaving less room for eye contact, conversation and other shared experiences.
Set boundaries regarding how much political content you consume, especially when with your partner, the expert advised. (iStock)
Also, when someone is constantly consuming political content, it can become the primary topic they want to discuss, creating tension when partners hold different views, she cautioned.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

To help reduce conflict, Elton recommended limiting when political news or posts are consumed. She also suggested setting aside one phone-free date night each week to encourage face-to-face connection.
No. 2: Agree to disagree
While couples with differing political views are unlikely to agree on every issue, "agreeing to disagree" can help prevent hostility.
"We can still love each other," Elton said. "It's not going to affect our relationship."

"As soon as it gets to the point of seeing your partner through the lens of ‘if you believe this, this is who you are, and I can’t believe that I'm still in a relationship with you,’ that becomes a problem."
When political beliefs become the defining feature of a partner, relationships can suffer, according to the expert. (iStock)

Elton urged couples not to take political disagreements personally and instead approach them with curiosity. She also recommended looking at the same information together, allowing each partner to ask questions and draw their own conclusions rather than jumping into a heated debate.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The therapist also encouraged couples to focus on areas of common ground rather than viewing disagreements in black-and-white terms.
After a disagreement or failure to compromise, it’s important to always reconnect with your partner, she emphasized.
Never end a fight without re-connecting, the therapist advised. (iStock)
Sharing reassuring words like "I love you" and "You matter to me more than anything else" can be helpful, she said.
"I feel like you always need to say, ‘Hey, I hear what you're saying, but I'm not agreeing, and that's OK.’"
3. Consider the wider impact
When politics come into play in a relationship, it can have an impact on more than just the couple.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Elton encouraged partners to consider how sharing certain opinions can impact other loved ones, especially if one person confides in a family member or friend about the other's views.
"You can create this triangulation where you're connecting with someone against your partner, and you don't want that," she warned.

"Talk to your therapist, vent to your therapist… because if you start venting to your family and friends, then they start forming certain opinions about your partner, and it can affect how they talk to them, how they interact with them."
Before making any drastic decisions, such as ending a relationship over political discord, Elton suggested slowing down and returning to a more grounded state.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"We hear certain things and we fill in the gaps," she said. "When we hear someone's political affiliation, we often make assumptions about who they are without really hearing them out."
Rather than making assumptions based on the media or podcasts a partner consumes, for example, Elton encouraged couples to ask questions, stay curious and remain open-minded.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Unsealed FBI interviews reveal Obama, Emanuel discussions about Blagojevich Senate seat deal
summary: Newly unsealed FBI interviews reveal what Barack Obama and Rahm Emanuel told agents about Rod Blagojevich's plans for the Illinois Senate seat.
story: Former Illinois Governor Rod Blagojevich among 11 individuals granted clemency by President Trump.

Anyone who has a conversation with former Illinois Gov. Rod Blagojevich is likely to hear his claim that he was never going to sell the U.S. Senate seat vacated by former President Barack Obama in 2008, insisting his innocence in the high-profile case that led to him serving nearly eight years in federal prison. Blagojevich has repeated for years that he was closing in on a deal to appoint Lisa Madigan to the U.S. Senate.

Hers is a name that has largely dropped out of the public arena. At the time of the scandal, Madigan served as the Illinois Attorney General. More relevant to this case, she is the daughter of the very powerful and entrenched then-Speaker of the Illinois House Mike Madigan. The former Speaker has since gone to prison for a separate corruption case. (Welcome to Illinois.) Blagojevich claims he would have appointed Lisa to the Senate, in exchange for the father supporting his health care package and budget.

Shortly after the arrest of Governor Blagojevich in December 2009, both President-elect Obama and his incoming chief of staff Rahm Emanuel were interviewed by the FBI. Obama on December 18, 9 days after the Governor was arrested. Emanuel was interviewed on the 20. The records of those interviews were kept out of both criminal trials and away from the public, until now. Fox News has obtained the partially redacted FBI FD-302s of those interviews.

The Obama interview notes: "Obama was asked whether he was aware of Emanuel having a conversation with the Blagojevich administration regarding Lisa Madigan being considered for the Senate seat in exchange for legislation being passed."
RAHM EMANUEL WARNS DSA AGENDA DOESN'T PLAY WELL OUTSIDE 'UPPER WEST SIDE OF MANHATTAN'

Former Illinois Gov. Rod Blagojevich speaks to the press outside his home in Chicago on Feb. 10, 2025, after being pardoned by President Donald Trump. Blagojevich was convicted in 2011 on corruption charges and sentenced to 14 years in prison. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
"Emanuel would have been aware that Lisa Madigan was an acceptable candidate to Obama."
And "Emanuel had an open line of conversation with the Blagojevich administration."

The Emanuel interview notes that on December 8, 2008, "(David) Axelrod and Emanuel went to see (U.S. Senator Dick) Durbin, D-Ill. In this meeting they all agreed that Lisa Madigan would be a good candidate."
"As a result of this conversation, Emanuel contacted (Blagojevich Chief of staff, John) Harris and told him the merits of appointing Lisa Madigan as Senator."
The next morning, December 9, 2009, just after 6 a.m., Blagojevich was arrested at his home in Chicago.
RAHM EMANUEL WARNS ‘BERNIE BROS’ COULD SINK DEMOCRATS BY SADDLING MODERATES WITH SOCIALIST AGENDA

Then-U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois Patrick Fitzgerald said, "Governor Blagojevich was arrested in the middle of what we can only describe as a political corruption crime spree. We acted to stop that crime spree."

"That just proves the Madigan deal was very much front and center. It was something I was about to do," Blagojevich said in light of the newly unsealed information. "There never was a crime spree that Mr. Fitzgerald, the U.S. Attorney said he was stopping to justify arresting a sitting governor in his home."

Other interesting notes from the interviews: President Obama initially wanted Valerie Jarrett to succeed him the Senate. But he reversed his thinking early in the process deciding, "that he would like Jarrett to join him at the White House as a senior advisor."
However, "Emanuel was still interested in Jarrett taking the senate seat rather than working in the White House."

Rahm Emanuel speaks during the Inaugural Events Of The Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library on July 03, 2026, in Medora, North Dakota. (Bryan Bedder/Getty Images for Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library)
Because, according to the Emanuel interview, "the fact that she is the President-elect’s best friend, having her on the White House staff would be awkward."
"Rahm’s a crafty, political, crafty, cunning and very effective political operator," Blagojevich chimed in. "He was interested in being closer to the king."

Eventually, according to the Emanuel interview, Obama became resolute. "Obama told Emanuel he made a decision that Jarret was going to the White House and he was not going to reconsider this decision."

After that, a gaggle of familiar names entered the ring for consideration: Tammy Duckworth, and Reps. Jan Schakowsky, D-Ill., and Rep. Jesse Jackson Jr., D-Ill. (Who also went to prison for a separate case.)
MINNESOTA FRAUD SCANDAL WILL HAUNT FLANAGAN IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE RACE, TOP HOUSE REPUBLICAN WARNS
Then-Sen. Barack Obama, D-Ill. speaks at a Library of Congress rally. (Scott J. Ferrell/Congressional Quarterly/Getty Images)
Then Obama, busy with establishing a new administration, stated, "He did not want to put his thumb on the scale."

Still, he dispatched Emanuel to communicate with the Governor’s office that "Obama was interested in someone who he thought would be a good Senator for the people of Illinois and who could also hold the seat in the 2010 election."
Blagojevich ended up appointing Roland Burris to Obama’s vacated seat. Burris did not run for re-election.
Republican Mark Kirk won the seat in 2010 and was defeated by Tammy Duckworth in 2016.
Blagojevich served 7 years 11 months in prison until President Trump commuted his sentence in 2020. Blagojevich received a full pardon in 2025.

Fox News reached out to both former President Obama and Rahm Emanuel. They did not respond.

title: Trump declares victory in historic deal with Greenland as he secures 'permanent' US military rights
summary: President Donald Trump's Greenland deal bars China and Russia from the Arctic island and grants permanent U.S. military basing with no expiration.
story: President Donald Trump lashed out at NATO allies over their stance on Greenland and defense spending during a high-stakes summit in Ankara. American Military Project director Will Thibeau weighs in during 'Fox & Friends First.'
FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump struck a sweeping agreement with Denmark and Greenland this week granting the United States permanent military rights on the strategically placed Arctic island.

The U.S. will now have permanent access, basing and overflight rights in Greenland and the ability to establish additional military installations as needed, according to a senior U.S. official who outlined the deal exclusively to Fox News Digital.

The deal bars China, Russia and other non-NATO countries from establishing military bases or maintaining troops in Greenland. It also restricts adversaries from investing in sensitive sectors that could pose a threat to U.S. national security.

"This historic deal is a huge win for the United States and the American people," Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Fox News Digital. "Thanks to President Trump’s vision and leadership, this historic agreement permanently guarantees U.S. security interests in the Arctic at zero cost to the U.S. taxpayer.
DENMARK VOWS TO DEFEND GREENLAND AFTER TRUMP REITERATES US SHOULD CONTROL TERRITORY

President Donald Trump has struck a sweeping agreement with Denmark and Greenland granting the United States permanent military rights on the strategically vital Arctic island, Fox News Digital has learned. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci)

"Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area," Rubio said. "This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland.

The new agreement, which has no expiration date, stops short of transferring sovereignty over Greenland to the U.S. But administration officials still view its permanence as key to addressing the security concerns that drove Trump's push to acquire the territory in the first place.
"The difference here is we're not spending any money for the right" to expand the U.S. military presence, the senior official explained.
The deal is designed to remain in effect even if Greenland eventually becomes an independent country, they added.

"For over 100 years, Presidents have known the strategic importance of Greenland, but NONE of them were able to do anything about it. I am proud to be the President that permanently and conclusively addressed this very important situation. This is an "Infinite Life" Agreement, there is no end!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Friday.
Fox News Digital reached out to the governments of Greenland and Denmark for comment.

Trump had repeatedly argued that control of Greenland was necessary for U.S. national security, pointing to the island's strategic location in the Arctic as Russia and China expand their presence and capabilities in the region.

The deal significantly expands on the longstanding U.S. defense relationship with Greenland. The U.S. already operates Pituffik Space Base and has maintained military access to the island under a defense agreement dating back to 1951.
The Pituffik Space Base is pictured in northern Greenland Oct. 4, 2023. (Thomas Traasdahl/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP via Getty Images)

Under the new agreement, however, Denmark and Greenland would not have approval authority over additional U.S. military installations. The U.S. would consult with them but would have the right to build new installations when it determines they are necessary without needing their buy-in, the official said.
The administration believes an expanded U.S. military footprint in Greenland could eventually play a role in Trump's planned Golden Dome missile defense system.

"We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many. We will work with the people of Greenland in its development and construction," Trump added.
RUSSIA’S QUIETER NUCLEAR SUBMARINES THREATEN NATO, FORMER COMMANDER WARNS
The deal only allows the U.S. and its allies to make "sensitive investments" on the island, such as telecommunications infrastructure, undersea cables, ports and critical minerals.

The administration is seeking to prevent Greenland from becoming another version of what it sees as the strategic vulnerability that developed around the Panama Canal, where Chinese commercial interests have fueled U.S. concerns that ostensibly civilian infrastructure could have national security implications.
"We're never going to face that in Greenland as a result of this," the official told Fox News Digital.
Officials from both Greenland and Denmark, which holds sovereignty over the self-governing island territory, initially scoffed at Trump’s insistence that the U.S. must "own" Greenland.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen issued a defiant message against President Donald Trump's designs on Greenland at the 2026 NATO Leaders Summit Wednesday in Ankara, Turkey. (Serdar Ozsoy/Getty Images)

But months of negotiations between Rubio, White House advisor Stephen Miller and officials at the State Department and National Security Council led to a deal that satisfied all sides, a second official told Fox News Digital.

Representatives from all three countries went through "various rounds of quiet negotiations that never leaked and never got out there" starting in February, as Denmark and Greenland came to see the agreement as serving their own security interests.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"They recognize, at the end of the day, that they have a national security concern here as well," Rubio said. "Denmark and Greenland understand that they don't have the financial means necessary to defend Greenland if it were to come under attack or be threatened. The United States has the power to do that."

title: Foreign hackers breach two more US water utilities, threaten safety of Colorado residents
summary: Foreign hackers breached two Colorado water utilities, altering pumping cycles and disabling alarms before operators regained control of systems.
story: Former top Pentagon official and Heritage Foundation visiting fellow Steve Bucci joins 'Fox & Friends First' to analyze the surge of cyberattacks on U.S. water infrastructure.

Foreign actors hacked two Colorado water utilities' computer systems last month, changing pumping cycles, disabling alarms and altering equipment settings before operators regained control, state officials said Thursday.

The intrusions did not affect drinking water quality or treatment processes, according to Colorado Gov. Jared Polis' office. But the incidents add Colorado to a widening series of breaches in U.S. water and wastewater infrastructure.

High-profile cyberattacks have targeted more than 100 drinking water and wastewater systems across 12 states this year, according to the Environmental Protection Agency, expanding the footprint of a threat that federal authorities warned this summer was disrupting water operations across the country.
WATER CYBERATTACK HITS AT LEAST 7 STATES
Hackers targeted computerized controls at more than 30 Minnesota water systems, forcing some utilities to use manual operations and backup procedures. (Tony Webster/Wikimedia Commons)
Colorado officials have not identified the actors behind the intrusions of the two small systems or said whether they are connected to the broader activity reported elsewhere in the country.
"These were brief incidents, and the risks were quickly addressed by the providers themselves, who subsequently alerted the state," Polis spokeswoman Eric Maruyama said in a statement.
The hackers altered equipment settings, disabled remote access and alarms and changed pumping cycles, according to the governor's office.

The incidents demonstrate how hackers can reach beyond traditional computer networks and gain access to operational technology used to control physical equipment at water plants, including pumps, valves and other machinery.
The water utility systems that were impacted provide drinking water to approximately 400 people.
IRANIAN HACKERS ATTACKED OUR WATER SYSTEMS. HERE ARE 5 THINGS OUR LEADERS NEED TO DO NOW

Federal authorities warned in July that malicious cyber actors were targeting internet-connected operational technology at water and wastewater utilities. At the time, the FBI and EPA said utilities in at least seven states had reported incidents, some of which degraded water operations.

The agencies said attackers had remotely accessed internet-facing programmable logic controllers, or PLCs, and tampered with device configurations, in some cases causing utilities to lose monitoring or control capabilities. Reported operational effects included loss of water pressure and flooding.
The Colorado breaches follow a series of attacks on water systems across the country this summer, including cyber activity affecting more than 30 community water systems in Minnesota.
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis speaks to the National Governors Association at the Broadmoor Hotel in Colorado Springs, Colo., July 25, 2025. (AP)

Federal investigators have examined whether Iranian actors or hackers affiliated with Iran were responsible for the Minnesota attacks, though officials had not publicly attributed the activity at the time.
President Donald Trump disputed suggestions that Iran was behind the Minnesota attacks, saying during a Cabinet meeting, "They blame it on Iran. I don't think so."
He instead blamed Minnesota officials.
IRAN’S CYBERWAR TARGETS ORDINARY AMERICANS. WE NEED TO DISMANTLE THE HACKER NETWORK

The recent incidents have renewed attention to longstanding cybersecurity vulnerabilities within America's water infrastructure, particularly among small and rural utilities that can have limited cybersecurity staff and resources.

Many utilities use internet-connected industrial control systems to remotely monitor and operate pumps, valves, water pressure and other equipment. Federal officials have urged operators to remove programmable logic controllers from direct exposure to the internet and strengthen authentication and access controls.

The EPA, which serves as the federal government's sector risk management agency for water and wastewater systems, told Fox News Digital it is working with utilities, states and federal partners to identify vulnerabilities and strengthen cybersecurity.
The Environmental Protection Agency Headquarters Building in Washington, D.C. (Getty)
Since fiscal year 2025, the agency has identified more than 900 vulnerabilities in over 650 water systems and helped eliminate about 700 at more than 500 utilities.
The EPA has also conducted more than 710 cybersecurity risk assessments and provided direct technical assistance to approximately 15,900 utilities.

The FBI declined to comment when reached by Fox News Digital.

story: Fox News correspondent Brooke Taylor gets an exclusive ride-along with Homeland Security agents as they ramp up arrests of immigrants accused of participating in voter fraud. Helda Araceli Mendez-Merida, an illegal immigrant from Guatemala, allegedly voted in a federal election, the Department of Homeland Security said. (Getty Images; Department of Homeland Security)

She was arrested by a U.S. Border Patrol officer and released. An immigration judge issued a final order of removal for her in September 2019.

title: Judge says issues in Trump administration anti-weaponization case 'alive and kicking' despite DOJ push
summary: Judge Brinkema questioned whether the Trump administration's Anti-Weaponization Fund truly died or if the DOJ Judgment Fund serves as its equivalent.
story: Pro-life activist Paul Vaughn discusses his seven-figure settlement with the Department of Justice after his home was raided by the FBI after a protest at a Tennessee abortion center on 'Saturday In America.'

ALEXANDRIA, Va. — Department of Justice lawyers have asked U.S. District Court Judge Leonie Brinkema to dismiss a case connected to the Trump administration's $1.776 billion "Anti-Weaponization Fund," arguing that Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a formal recission order in August and has affirmed many times, including under oath before Congress, that the fund is dead.
However, Brinkema seemed skeptical Friday.
"The issues that underlie this case are still alive and kicking in my view," Brinkema said.

"The real concern that lurks ... is the concept of taxpayer money being used to promote particular political views," Brinkema said, pointing to pro-life activists convicted of violating the FACE Act and others who attempted an "insurrection" on Jan. 6 "to overthrow the legitimate election."
CLINTON JUDGE INDEFINITELY BLOCKS TRUMP'S $1.776B ANTI-WEAPONIZATION FUND

U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema questioned whether the issues surrounding the Trump administration’s now-rescinded $1.776 billion Anti-Weaponization Fund remain unresolved. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"That entity is gone," said Brinkema, referring to the Anti-Weaponization Fund and agreeing that Blanche has said under oath at his confirmation hearings that the fund is dead. "But is there a functional equivalent?" Brinkema said, referring to the DOJ's ordinary Judgment Fund authority.

The Judgment Fund is a permanent U.S. Treasury account managed by the Bureau of the Fiscal Service that pays court judgments and DOJ legal settlements against the federal government. Brinkema called that fund "a less transparent structure" and suggested that some defendants convicted of FACE Act crimes have already received large payouts from the DOJ's Judgment Fund.
JUDGE TEMPORARILY BLOCKS TRUMP DOJ'S NEARLY $2B 'ANTI-WEAPONIZATION' FUND

Justice Department lawyers asked a federal judge Friday to dismiss a lawsuit challenging the Anti-Weaponization Fund, arguing Attorney General Todd Blanche formally terminated it Aug. 2. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Here, Brinkema affirmed she was talking about the case of Paul Vaughn.

Vaugh, of Centerville, Tennessee, was convicted in January 2024 for his role in blockading an abortion clinic in Mount Juliet, Tennessee, in March 2021. Vaughn ultimately received a pardon and a taxpayer-funded payout from the DOJ's Judgment Fund that confirmed to Fox News is "seven figures."
BIDEN ADMIN USED ABORTION GROUP DOSSIERS, INCLUDING PHOTOS OF MINORS, TO TARGET CHRISTIANS, DOJ REPORT REVEALS

Judge Leonie Brinkema said the issues underlying a lawsuit over the Anti-Weaponization Fund remain "alive and kicking" despite the Justice Department’s insistence that the fund is dead. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
DOJ lawyer Andrew Block asked what remedy the plaintiff wants, given "the fund is dead."

Brinkema countered that although the case is nowhere near the remedy stage, "I think there are remedies." She brought up the possibility of requiring a "neutral" person to oversee a fund, "not someone from the DOJ, which I see unfortunately as coerced" in this matter.
"A proper, unbiased look. ... There's been too much talk from members of the administration, which undercut [DOJ's] position," Brinkema said. "They contradict themselves all the time."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Brinkema closed the hearing by telling both sides she intends to craft a new discovery order in the coming days, suggesting this case is far from over.
Jake Gibson is the Fox News Department of Justice and Federal Law Enforcement Producer.

title: Socialist Claire Valdez faces calls for federal probe after Mexico ‘fight’ pledge
summary: New York City socialist Claire Valdez faces Logan Act scrutiny after meeting Mexico's Morena party and vowing to carry independence fight to Congress.
story: New York's primary day serves as a litmus test for the Democratic Party as democratic socialists, including Zohran Mamdani, actively campaign for progressive challengers. Candidates Claire Valdez, Darieliza Avila Chevalier and Brad Lander advocate for policies such as Medicare-for-all and abolishing ICE.

A New York City socialist seeking to replace a retiring Democrat drew criticism Thursday after pledging to carry the "fight" inspired by Mexico’s struggle for independence into Congress. And critics pointed to her disclosure that she met with members of Mexico’s ruling left-wing party.

Claire Valdez, who is seeking Rep. Nydia Velázquez's seat in a district that includes Bushwick and Ridgewood, is facing calls for the State Department to investigate her under the Logan Act. It's a rarely enforced 1799 law that criminalizes certain unauthorized efforts by private citizens to influence foreign governments in disputes involving the U.S. Democrats have also invoked the law in connection with President Donald Trump.

In response to her post, immigration attorney and columnist Alicia Nieves tweeted at Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, a former ambassador to Mexico, calling for an investigation of Valdez after the candidate disclosed that she had met with members of Morena, Mexico’s ruling left-wing party.

"Given that she is currently a congressional nominee, not a member of Congress, and appears to have discussed facilitating support contrary to current U.S. policy as well as describing our country an ‘empire’ that has ‘stolen from us’ … I hope the administration will review whether these communications warrant investigation under the Logan Act."
COLORADO'S SOCIALIST CANDIDATE CALLS FOR 'MORE IMMIGRANTS INTO OFFICE' TO STOP AMERICA'S 'EXPLOITATIVE' NATURE
Claire Valdez protests against ICE. (Michael Santiago/Getty Images)

The act, enacted in 1799, came after the John Adams administration and congressional Federalists objected to Pennsylvania politician George Logan’s unauthorized trip to France, where he sought to ease tensions during what was called the "Quasi-War." Federalists feared private diplomacy could undermine the U.S. government’s foreign policy.
Adams and his Federalist allies also viewed Logan’s actions through the partisan tensions surrounding the 1800 presidential race against Thomas Jefferson.
In her tweet, Valdez wrote, "215 years ago, Mexicans fought an empire that demanded our land and our labor. And we won.
"I'll carry that fight with me to Congress as New York's first Mexican-American representative," Valdez pledged. "And I'm strengthened not just by Mexico's history but its present."

She said she met "comrades" in the Morena party who are "standing up to the empires and corporations that have always taken from us — and building a government for the working class. Viva la Independencia, Viva México!"
MAMDANI-BACKED SOCIALIST PREVAILS IN CROWDED PRIMARY TO REPLACE RETIRING REP

NYPD officers arrest New York City Council member Tiffany Caban and New York Assembly member Claire Valdez, right, along with protesters after they refused to leave the lobby of Sen. Chuck Schumer's office in Manhattan on Aug. 1, 2025. (Barry Williams/New York Daily News/Tribune News Service)
Fox News Digital reached out to Valdez and the Mexican government for comment. Morena could not immediately be reached.

Critics also pointed out that Valdez's father, Larry, is linked to a company that helped construct a Texas immigration center during the Obama administration. They contended that the connection conflicts with her opposition to immigration enforcement.
"This would be a great campaign for Congress in Mexico," added Christina Pushaw, a top communications official for Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.
Fox News Digital also reached out to community organizer Melvin Rivera, the Republican opponent facing Valdez, for comment.

Democrats cited the Logan Act in connection with Trump after he publicly remarked, "Russia, if you’re listening, I hope you’re able to find the 30,000 emails that are missing" in reference to his 2016 opponent Hillary Clinton.

Then-Senate Democratic Leader Harry Reid of Nevada suggested that Trump had violated the Logan Act. The law has also been invoked against other public figures, including former Sen. John Kerry, D-Mass., and the Rev. Jesse Jackson, but no prosecution under the statute has resulted in a conviction.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Two men faced proceedings under the Logan Act but were never convicted. A grand jury indicted Kentucky farmer Francis Flournoy in 1803 after he advocated a separate Western United States allied with France. Jonas P. Levy was arrested and held to bail under the law in 1853 after writing to Mexico’s president.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Valdez, the Democratic nominee for New York’s 7th Congressional District, will face  Rivera and other candidates in the November general election.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Dems abandon candidate who said MAGA is 'more destructive' than Nazis, but she’s stuck on the ballot
summary: North Carolina Democrat Shelly Headen called for an attack on U.S. soil targeting red states and compared Trump to Hitler in resurfaced posts.
story: Fox News senior correspondent Jonathan Serrie has the latest on North Carolina Democrat Shelly Headen's controversial social media posts on 'America Reports.'
A Democrat running for the state legislature in battleground North Carolina remains on the ballot despite her party publicly abandoning her after inflammatory social media posts she made resurfaced.

The North Carolina House Democratic Caucus and a county party group both condemned posts by Shelly Headen in which the legislative candidate called for an attack on U.S. soil targeting red states and compared President Donald Trump to Adolf Hitler.
But Headen remains a candidate because the filing deadline to drop out of the race was Aug. 20, and the general election ballots are finalized and were sent out to voters starting on Sept. 4.

Headen, who is challenging Republican state Rep. John Blust for the House District 62 seat in Greensboro-anchored Guilford County, posted a year ago, "I think our only hope is an attack on US Soil … preferably Alabama, Louisiana … where the stupid people live."
WATCH: HUGH HEWITT'S TAKE ON THE HEADEN CONTROVERSY
In separate posts, she argued that the damage done by Trump was "getting close to surpassing Hitler" and claimed the "MAGA cult may be more destructive and evil than the Nazis."

Breitbart reported that a Facebook post by Headen that pictured her at a memorial at the Nazis' Dachau concentration camp in Germany, where tens of thousands of people were murdered during World War II, with the words, "This is where Trump supporters belong."
Headen denied last week to the Greensboro News and Record that she posted the concentration camp image and said she believed the image was edited to include the words over a real photo.
Her old comments grabbed new national attention earlier this week when the White House Rapid Response account that supports Trump shared them on X and charged that Democrats "ARE SICK PEOPLE!"
DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

The Dachau concentration camp near Munich, Germany, was one of the first built by the Nazis. The Dachau Memorial Site archive has documented 32,000 deaths at the camp, but thousands more are undocumented. (Getty Images)

North Carolina Republican U.S. Senate nominee Michael Whatley posted on social media a photo of Headen and former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic Senate nominee, and argued, "Roy Cooper still stands with NC Dem who called for the genocide of Republicans. This is against everything America stands for."

"These remarks are reprehensible – Roy strongly condemns them and all forms of political violence and he believes it’s up to all of us to speak responsibly," Cooper's campaign emphasized in a statement.

title: How CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin's family foundation became a major funder of left-wing activist groups
summary: Arc of Justice, the family foundation tied to CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin, provided nearly $3.2 million to the protest group since 2009.
story: China expert Matthew Johnson, who is scheduled to testify before Congress on Tuesday, discusses Beijing's influence strategy, malign foreign influence and why the Chinese government seeks to shape debate inside the United States.

CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin's family foundation became a major financial backer of a network of left-wing activist organizations over more than two decades, providing nearly $3.2 million to CodePink while also bankrolling protest groups, legal advocacy organizations and progressive nonprofits, a Fox News Digital investigation found.

The foundation, Arc of Justice, is a $54.6 million private foundation formerly known as The Benjamin Fund. A review of its complete IRS filing history found it made nearly 1,500 grants totaling about $24.6 million to organizations involved in anti-war activism, progressive policy, legal advocacy and campaigns involving immigration enforcement, China, Cuba and the Israel-Hamas war.

Among its largest recipients were CodePink, Global Exchange, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Grassroots International and Social Good Fund, alongside grants to dozens of other organizations involved in anti-war activism, progressive policy, legal advocacy and progressive media.

Arc of Justice provided CodePink more than twice the approximately $1.33 million the group received from the funding network linked to Shanghai-based Marxist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham. A previous five-part Fox News Digital investigation found Singham's network directed at least $278 million into organizations that promoted pro-China messaging.
LAWMAKERS THROW OUT 'TROJAN HORSE' ACTIVISTS THEY SAY ARE ENGAGED IN AMERICAN SUBVERSION

CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin (left) and CodePink activists protest during a rally in Washington, D.C. (right). (Left: Mattie Neretin/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect; Right: Mostafa Bassim/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Arc of Justice has come under scrutiny after California revoked its charitable registration following years of financial compliance failures, though the foundation has been working to regain its standing with California regulators.

Benjamin, who co-founded CodePink with Singham’s wife Jodie Evans, has remained one of the group's most visible public faces, frequently leading protests and interrupting congressional hearings. On Tuesday, she was escorted from a House Foreign Affairs subcommittee hearing on alleged foreign malign influence after protesting during the proceedings.

The Fox News Digital investigation also found the foundation itself has undergone sweeping changes in recent months, with Benjamin stepping down from the board, new leadership taking over and the organization saying it intends to chart a different course for its charitable giving.

Arc of Justice began funding CodePink in 2009 and provided grants to the organization in 15 tax years through 2024, totaling $3,195,280.

According to the documents, CodePink was Arc of Justice's largest activist beneficiary. Since 2009, the foundation and its predecessor, The Benjamin Fund, also directed about $2.05 million to Global Exchange, the anti-war and social justice advocacy group Benjamin co-founded with her former husband, Kevin Danaher, which has long campaigned against U.S. military intervention and economic sanctions.

Arc of Justice also provided about $2.24 million to Grassroots International, which funds grassroots social movements around the world; $1.61 million to Social Good Fund, which provides nonprofit infrastructure and fundraising support for charitable projects; about $1.29 million to the Center for Constitutional Rights, a legal advocacy organization; and about $114,000 to Alliance for Global Justice (AFGJ), an activist nonprofit.

AFGJ has drawn scrutiny over its past fiscal sponsorship of Samidoun, a pro-Palestinian activist group later sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury. Benjamin said Arc's final grant to Alliance for Global Justice was $10,000 in 2022 and that the foundation "was not aware of any specific groups fiscally sponsored by AFGJ" when it made its grants.

Through attorney David Levitt, the foundation said both CodePink and Alliance for Global Justice were recognized by the IRS as tax-exempt public charities and that Arc was entitled to rely on that status when making its grants.

The grantmaking reached across a much broader activist network. Since 2009, IRS filings reviewed by Fox News Digital show Arc of Justice and its predecessor gave about $492,000 to World Beyond War, roughly $255,000 to the Institute for Policy Studies and about $124,000 to Jewish Voice for Peace. It also gave $110,000 to Grassroots Global Justice and about $90,000 to the Center for Popular Democracy.
IRS filings also show Arc of Justice and its predecessor provided about $65,500 to Democracy Now! since 2009, where Benjamin has frequently appeared as a guest over the years.

Founded in 2002 with the aim of preventing the Iraq War, CodePink has grown into one of the country's most visible anti-war protest groups, repeatedly disrupting congressional hearings and protests involving senior U.S. officials, including then-Secretaries of State John Kerry and Mike Pompeo. The group has also participated in nationwide No Kings protests, opposed ICE enforcement actions, organized anti-Israel rallies and campaigned against U.S. policy toward China, Cuba and Iran. Earlier this year, CodePink led a delegation to Cuba that included Twitch political streamer Hasan Piker.

Asked about Arc's long-term funding of CodePink and other activist organizations, Matthew Johnson, a senior fellow at the Jamestown Foundation, said sustained financial support can have an impact well beyond the dollar amounts involved.

"Small amounts of money can actually go a long way toward impacting the broader media ecosystem... from the perspective of political organization, they may be having an outsized impact on the kind of information that is available to Americans," Johnson told Fox News Digital.

Johnson, who testified before Congress Tuesday about how foreign adversaries may use nonprofits and other organizations to shape U.S. public opinion and policy, told lawmakers that CodePink launched its "China Is Not Our Enemy" campaign in 2020 following meetings in Beijing and has since pursued China-focused advocacy and organized travel. The campaign argued the United States should pursue cooperation with Beijing rather than confrontation. CodePink and Benjamin have denied taking direction from the Chinese government.
WATCH: Heritage Foundation senior fellow confronts CodePink's Medea Benjamin before House hearing
Benjamin told Fox News Digital the grants were intended to support CodePink's anti-war work.
"The foundation's donations to CodePink were made to support its anti-war work," she said in an email response.

At the House hearing on Tuesday, Benjamin also rejected suggestions that she or CodePink took direction from foreign governments. "I've been an anti-war activist from the days of Vietnam," Benjamin said. "I never had a foreign government tell me what to do."

Singham and the organizations he has funded, identified in the Fox News Digital report, have denied taking direction from the Chinese government, and neither Singham, Benjamin nor the organizations have been charged with wrongdoing.

Arc of Justice was formerly known as The Benjamin Fund, Inc., with California corporate records showing the foundation formally changed its name in November 2019.

Benjamin's father, Alvin Benjamin, a prominent Long Island real estate developer who founded The Benjamin Companies in the early 1960s, provided some of the foundation's earliest documented financial backing.
The Benjamin Fund's initial 2003 IRS return shows he contributed a partnership interest valued at $683,715 to the foundation, with Medea Susan Benjamin serving as president.

Much larger contributions followed. In 2010, the estate of Benjamin's mother, Rose Benjamin, contributed $10,863,060, according to the foundation's IRS filing. Five years later, the Estate of Alvin Benjamin contributed another $15 million, followed by another $8,603,450 in 2019.
Medea Benjamin — identified as Susan Benjamin on the filing — personally contributed $1 million to Arc of Justice in 2022, listing a Miami address.
Arc of Justice's wealth was largely tied to an investment portfolio that continued to grow while the foundation distributed millions of dollars in grants.

Federal tax returns reviewed by Fox News Digital show the foundation's assets grew from $39.63 million at the end of 2020 to $54.64 million in 2024, as it distributed millions of dollars annually in grants.

Arc of Justice generated much of its annual income from its investment portfolio, collecting dividends from stocks and mutual funds, interest on cash holdings and profits from investments that had increased in value.

In 2023, the foundation reported nearly $2 million in revenue, including $1.11 million in dividends and interest from securities, $166,421 in interest on savings and temporary cash investments and $686,919 in net gains from asset sales.

Its investment holdings also produced substantial gains as the portfolio increased in value. In 2020, Arc of Justice reported $12,344,501 in unrealized gains on securities, helping push its year-end assets to nearly $40 million.

Over more than two decades, IRS filings reviewed by Fox News Digital repeatedly reported no compensation for the foundation's officers and no highly paid employees, while the foundation directed millions of dollars to outside organizations.

After California revoked Arc of Justice's charitable registration, Fox News Digital reported that a new Florida nonprofit using the Arc of Justice name was incorporated at the Miami home of Benjamin's longtime partner, Tighe Barry, raising questions about the future of the foundation and whether its assets or operations were being moved out of California.

The address is a modest turquoise home largely obscured by trees — an unassuming setting for an organization tied to a private foundation with more than $50 million in assets. Benjamin and Barry have frequently appeared together at CodePink demonstrations over the years.

Levitt later told Fox News Digital the Florida corporation had been created as a "placeholder" while the foundation considered relocating its operations from California, but the move was never completed. He said the California corporation was never formally dissolved, no assets were transferred and the Florida entity "holds no assets and has conducted no business."

The foundation has been attempting to get its registration reinstated after recently filing five years of overdue reports covering 2020 through 2024 and paying $1,800 in filing fees and penalties as part of a petition for reinstatement, documents submitted to California regulators show.
$54M CODEPINK-LINKED FOUNDATION SHUT DOWN IN CALIFORNIA POPS UP AT RAMSHACKLE MIAMI HOME

The Miami property listed as the address of the newly incorporated Arc of Justice nonprofit features a weathered painted fence and sits behind dense tropical vegetation. (AJ Skuy for Fox News Digital)

In the reinstatement petition, Levitt attributed the missed filings to what he described as an administrative misunderstanding over whether the foundation had successfully relocated from California to Florida.

He wrote that, during the tenure of the foundation's "former president," who served through the end of 2025, foundation leaders believed Arc was no longer subject to California's charitable registration requirements because it had moved to Florida.

The petition says the foundation later appointed a "new president," who discovered the compliance problems in 2026 and began the process of bringing the organization back into compliance. The petition also states that the foundation's directors and officers personally paid the penalty portion of the overdue filing fees.
The filings identify Maya Danaher, Benjamin's daughter, as president of the California foundation. Danaher previously served as the foundation's treasurer before becoming president.
"As previously reported, I have resigned from the foundation's board, and its new management will set its own funding priorities going forward," Benjamin said.
LAWMAKERS SAY THEY ARE STANDING AT THE GATES AGAINST 'TROJAN HORSES' PROMOTING MALIGN FOREIGN INTERESTS

It is unclear why Benjamin resigned from the board, why the proposed move to Florida was ultimately abandoned or why the foundation's new leadership decided to shift its grantmaking priorities away from the causes it had supported for more than two decades.
Benjamin was not listed as an officer or director of the Florida corporation, where Barry was listed as secretary and registered agent.
Its stated goal is blunt: "WE ARE HERE TO SUPPORT SOCIAL JUSTICE NON PROFITS," according to the articles of incorporation.
