Scammers are choosing the best place to reach you

Different scams tend to favor different platforms. Malwarebytes found that job scams commonly arrive through email. Romance scams favor social media, where conversations with new people feel more natural. Meanwhile, tech support scams frequently start with a phone call. That makes sense when you think about how each scam works.

A fake recruiter can blend into a busy inbox. Someone starting a conversation on social media may seem harmless. A caller claiming your computer has a serious problem can immediately put you under pressure.
The channel becomes part of the trick. We've seen that with changing tech support scams. They can now begin with fake invoices, bogus security alerts or convincing support pages.
The web remains scammers' favorite doorway
You hear plenty about scam texts and suspicious DMs. However, the web remains the leading way scams reach people in Malwarebytes' data. Email came next, followed by SMS.
Malwarebytes says it blocks around 500,000 phishing websites every day. That number gives you an idea of how many fake pages criminals keep pushing online.

Some copy banks or popular retailers. Others imitate technology companies or government services. A link in a text can take you straight to one of these pages. The fake site may look polished enough to fool you at first glance.
So, when a message says something has gone wrong with an account, resist the urge to use the link it provides. Open the company's app yourself or type the website address directly into your browser.
Scam texts hit their peak around lunchtime

Here's the part that really caught my attention. Malwarebytes found that scam texts targeting Americans reached their highest volume around 12 p.m. ET. At noon, volume was about 874% higher than at 1 a.m. ET. Think about what your phone habits look like around lunchtime.

You could be leaving a meeting, grabbing something to eat or checking messages between errands. Your attention may already be split. Then a text arrives saying your package cannot be delivered. Another claims you owe a toll. Maybe a message warns that somebody accessed your account. That timing can work in a scammer's favor because you may react before giving the message a closer look.

Of course, a text arriving at noon does not automatically mean somebody is trying to scam you. The data shows when Malwarebytes observed the highest volume. Still, the pattern gives us another look at how organized scam campaigns have become.
IS THAT TRAFFIC TICKET TEXT A SCAM OR REAL?
A scam text can feel personal and believable even when it comes from an unknown number. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Fridays bring even more scam texts

The day of the week also appears to play a role. Malwarebytes saw its lowest scam text volume on Sunday. Activity then increased as the week went on. By Friday, people were receiving roughly 50% more fraudulent texts than at the beginning of the week.
The researchers cannot say exactly why Friday produced the highest volume. However, the pattern suggests scammers may be deliberately timing campaigns instead of sending messages at random.
Maybe you're finishing work and thinking about the weekend. You could also be juggling deliveries, travel plans or bills. Whatever the reason, criminals want you moving quickly.

That's something we've seen repeatedly with fake government messages. A DMV scam text can threaten fines or license problems while pushing you toward a payment page. The threat gets your attention. The deadline tries to stop you from thinking.
MrBeast is the most impersonated person in the data

Timing gets the message in front of you. Familiarity can make you trust it. Malwarebytes found that Jimmy Donaldson, better known as MrBeast, was the most impersonated person in its data. His likeness appeared in about 30% of impersonation scams observed by the company.

Elon Musk and Donald Trump followed him in the data. These scams can involve fake cryptocurrency giveaways or schemes that demand a fee before you supposedly receive money. The real person has nothing to do with the offer.

Scammers borrow a face you recognize because familiarity can lower your guard. That tactic has become even more troubling as AI-generated video and cloned voices improve. A face on your screen no longer proves the person actually made the video.
Google leads the list of impersonated brands
Scammers use the same strategy with companies you recognize. According to reports from Malwarebytes users, the five most impersonated brands were: Google, Microsoft, Apple, Roblox and Amazon.

Google's name appeared at least twice as often as Amazon's. That familiarity gives criminals a huge advantage. If you use Google every day, a fake security warning may look routine. An Apple customer may react quickly to a message about an account problem.
Amazon scams can land at exactly the right moment because so many of us regularly have packages on the way. So, treat the logo as decoration until you verify the message yourself.
Gaming scams are getting more attention
Gaming communities are also attracting scammers. Malwarebytes found Roblox, Steam, Discord and Minecraft among the most impersonated gaming platforms.
Roblox scam activity increased 15% between mid-June and mid-July. Steam saw a 19% increase during the same period. The potential losses can also get serious.

Malwarebytes says about half of the gaming scams it analyzed could lead to losses of $1,000 or more. That is particularly concerning when younger gamers may encounter fake offers through communities they already trust.
A message promising free in-game items or access to something exclusive can quickly lead to a fake login page. Once the victim enters a password, the scammer may take over the account.
AMAZON JOB SCAM TEXTS ARE SPREADING AGAIN WITH A NEW TWIST
Email scams often start with messages that look routine but hide urgent threats designed to trigger quick clicks. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to protect yourself from better-timed scams
Scammers can improve their timing, but you can make yourself a much harder target. The best defense starts with slowing down and verifying what you see.

Avoid links and phone numbers inside unsolicited emails, texts or social media messages. A link can take you to a copied website designed to steal your login or payment information. Likewise, the phone number in a fake security alert can connect you directly to the scammer. Instead, leave the message and contact the company another way.

Go directly to the company's official website or open its app. If the message claims you owe money, check your real account before paying anything. You can also contact the organization using a phone number you already trust. This breaks the scammer's control over the conversation.

Searching for a company's website can help, but pay close attention to what you click. Scammers can use sponsored search ads that lead to fake support pages or convincing copies of legitimate websites. Check the web address before entering sensitive information. When possible, use a saved bookmark or the company's official app.

Never give someone your password because they called or messaged you unexpectedly. The same goes for PINs, account recovery codes and one-time verification codes. A scammer may claim they need a code to verify your identity. In reality, that code may give them access to your account. If a caller asks for sensitive information, hang up and contact the organization yourself.

Be suspicious when an unexpected caller or message demands immediate payment. Before paying, confirm the charge through your actual account or by contacting the organization independently. Watch closely for payment requests involving gift cards, cryptocurrency or transfers that may be difficult to reverse. Urgency should make you more cautious, not less.

Strong antivirus software can help block known phishing sites and other malicious pages. Browser protection can also warn you before you enter information on a dangerous website. Keep your browser updated as well. Security updates help close weaknesses that criminals may try to exploit. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Your phone may already include tools that identify suspicious calls or messages. Turn on spam filtering when your device and messaging app support it. Mobile security software can provide another layer of protection by identifying scam texts and dangerous links. No filter catches everything, so continue checking unexpected messages yourself.

If something feels wrong, look into it before you reply. Search for the company's official contact information. Check your account directly. You can also use a reputable scam-checking service to examine a suspicious phone number, message or link. The goal is simple. Verify the claim somewhere outside the conversation the scammer started.

Once you know a message is fraudulent, block the sender and report it as spam. Most phones and email services include built-in reporting options. Reporting scams can also help providers identify campaigns and block similar messages for other users. Then delete the message so you do not accidentally interact with it later.
Act quickly if you already clicked or shared information
If you entered a password on a suspicious site, change it immediately using the real website or app.

Change that password anywhere else you reused it. Better yet, use a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords for each account so one stolen password cannot unlock several accounts.
If you gave away payment information, contact your bank or card issuer right away.
You should also review your accounts for unfamiliar activity.
If a scammer gained access to your device, disconnect it from the internet and run a trusted security scan.
Kurt's key takeaways

What grabs me about this research is how deliberate scam campaigns are becoming. Scammers are paying attention to where you spend your time. Now, the timing data suggests they may also be watching when you're more likely to respond. That changes how I think about those random-looking texts that pop up during a busy day. The message may feel like one more thing that needs your attention. That's exactly when you need to slow down. You cannot control when a scammer contacts you. You can control whether that person gets to set the pace. When something unexpected asks for money or account information, get out of the message. Find the real company on your own and check the claim there. That small pause can ruin a scammer's entire plan.
Have you noticed more scam texts arriving around lunchtime or toward the end of the week, and what kind of message almost fooled you into responding? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Thousands of hacked sites trick you into installing malware
summary: Over 5,400 legitimate websites now serve fake CAPTCHA scams that trick users into pasting malware commands into Windows Run via ClickFix attacks.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
You land on the real website of a local business and a CAPTCHA appears. It looks routine until the page tells you to open Windows Run and paste a command. That should stop you cold.
Security researchers say thousands of legitimate small-business websites have been compromised to spread this malware trap. Here's what to know before a familiar website catches you off guard.
NEW! Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Health Care With AI

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you take a more active role in your health care. You’ll learn how to organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare questions for your next doctor’s visit. No technical experience is needed.
Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com
FAKE PATIENT PORTAL SCAM CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN AND INFECT YOUR PC
A routine visit to a legitimate website can turn risky if a fake CAPTCHA tricks you into running commands on your computer. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
More than 5,400 websites have been compromised

This campaign is much bigger than a handful of infected pages. Netskope Threat Labs says it identified more than 5,400 compromised websites across more than 2,200 organizations worldwide over the past few months.
The sites have little in common beyond many belonging to small businesses. Researchers found clinics, plumbing companies, online stores and other businesses among the victims.
Where Netskope examined individual sites, they most often ran WordPress and sometimes PrestaShop. Researchers still do not know how attackers initially compromised them.
That is important because you could visit the legitimate website of a business you recognize and still encounter a malicious prompt.
Netskope says several hundred compromised sites can be active on a given day. It has recently seen more than 300 sites contacting the malicious infrastructure each weekday.
How the fake CAPTCHA malware trick works

The attack starts with malicious code hidden inside a compromised website. When you visit the site, that code can load another script. Then the page may blur and show what looks like an ordinary CAPTCHA.
Instead of simply asking you to prove you are human, the page tells you to open the Windows Run dialog and paste a command. That command can download and launch the attacker's malware.
Here is the warning sign I want you to remember: A legitimate CAPTCHA should never tell you to open Windows Run or paste a command into your computer.

We have seen fake CAPTCHA scams use this same trick before. The page looks familiar, so you may assume the instructions are part of a normal security check. They are not. The criminal is trying to get you to launch the attack yourself.
CLICKLOCK MAC MALWARE LOCKS APPS UNTIL YOU GIVE IN
Researchers found compromised websites using fake verification prompts that tell Windows users to open the Windows Run dialog and paste a command that can launch malware. (Netskope)
Why ClickFix can fool careful people
This technique is known as ClickFix. The clever part has less to do with some exotic computer hack and more to do with psychology.

You are already used to CAPTCHAs. Websites ask you to click a box or prove you are human all the time. So, when a convincing verification screen appears on a legitimate website, your guard may be down. Then the instructions make the dangerous action look like one more step in the verification process.

Cybercriminals have used similar ClickFix tricks with fake Windows update screens. The appearance changes, but the warning remains the same. A webpage should not be telling you to run computer commands.
Why hackers are hiding part of the attack on a blockchain
This is where the campaign gets more unusual. The attackers are using the BNB Smart Chain test network to store instructions used by the compromised websites.

You do not need to understand cryptocurrency to understand why criminals like this setup. Normally, attackers might keep malicious code on a regular web server. Once investigators find that server, a hosting provider may be able to shut it down.

A blockchain works differently. In this campaign, the attackers store code inside something called a smart contract. Think of it as a place where the hacked websites can check for their next set of instructions.
Netskope says the attackers are using the test version of BNB Smart Chain. Developers normally use this network to experiment without spending real cryptocurrency.
That gives the criminals inexpensive infrastructure that can also be harder to take down through traditional methods. There is another advantage.

The attacker can change what the smart contract delivers. The compromised websites can then pick up those new instructions without criminals having to modify every hacked site individually. That helps explain why this infrastructure is so useful to them.

Netskope researchers say attackers are also abusing WebRTC to create a direct connection from a victim’s browser to an attacker-controlled server and deliver additional malicious code. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
The campaign is already changing tactics

Netskope also found a newer version of the attack that skips the fake CAPTCHA. This version uses technology called WebRTC. Your browser normally uses WebRTC for things such as video calls and real-time communications. The attackers found another use for it.

Their code can create an encrypted data connection with the attacker and receive additional malicious code through the browser. Netskope says the code can then run without first being saved as a traditional file on the computer.
For you, the technical details are less important than the larger point. The criminals can change how the attack works while continuing to use the same network of compromised websites.
6 ways to protect yourself from fake CAPTCHA malware
A few simple habits can help you avoid handing control of your computer to an attacker.
If a website tells you to open Windows Run, PowerShell or Command Prompt, stop. Do not paste anything it gives you. Close the page instead.

A normal CAPTCHA may ask you to click a checkbox or identify pictures. It should not require you to change settings or run commands on your PC. If the instructions suddenly leave the browser, close the page.

Strong antivirus protection can help detect malicious scripts and malware if something slips past you. Keep it updated and enable real-time protection. If you accidentally follow suspicious instructions, run a full system scan. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Install security updates when they become available. However, update Windows through Windows Update. Update your browser through its built-in settings or official source. Do not trust an unexpected webpage that says you must download an update.

If you followed the instructions from a suspicious CAPTCHA, disconnect the computer from the internet. Run a full antivirus scan. Then use another trusted device to change passwords for sensitive accounts you accessed on that computer. Start with your main email account. Also review active login sessions and enable multifactor authentication wherever you can.

Website owners should take this campaign seriously too. Netskope recommends checking the integrity of your content management system files. Researchers found malicious code added to legitimate JavaScript files or hidden inside fake plugin directories. Keep WordPress, PrestaShop and any plugins you use updated. Remove plugins you no longer need. Keep in mind that Netskope has not identified how attackers initially broke into the websites in this campaign. Those steps are good security practices, but researchers have not tied a specific WordPress or PrestaShop vulnerability to these compromises.
Kurt's key takeaways

What gets me about this attack is how ordinary everything can look at first. You could be visiting the real website of a neighborhood business you have used before. Then a familiar CAPTCHA appears. That sense of trust is exactly what can make the next instruction dangerous. The blockchain technology behind the campaign makes life harder for security teams trying to shut it down. For the rest of us, though, the best defense is refreshingly simple. A website should never need you to open Windows Run or paste a command to prove you are human. If you see that request, close the page. That one warning sign could save you from installing malware yourself.

Would you recognize a fake CAPTCHA if it appeared on the website of a business you already trusted, or would the familiar site make you more likely to follow the instructions? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: AI robot for seniors can alert family after a call for help
summary: Tuya Smart's Doova AI home robot rolls to seniors who call for help and connects family via live video, but key privacy questions remain unanswered.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

If you have a parent or grandparent who wants to stay in their own home, you probably know the question that can sit quietly in the back of your mind: What happens if they fall and nobody realizes they need help? Tuya Smart thinks its small artificial intelligence robot could become part of the answer.

The company unveiled Doova at IFA 2026 in Berlin. This wheeled AI home companion is designed for seniors who live independently. It can move through the home, respond when someone calls for help and connect family members through live video when an emergency appears to be unfolding.

That gets my attention because Doova goes beyond sitting on a table waiting for someone to press a button or call out from across the room. It can actually come to you. And that raises a bigger question: How much could a robot like this really help someone live safely and independently at home?
THE BEST TIME TO TALK TO YOUR PARENTS ABOUT SENIOR CARE — BEFORE IT'S TOO LATE
NEW! Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Health Care With AI

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you take a more active role in your healthcare. You’ll learn how to organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare questions for your next doctor’s visit. No technical experience is needed.
Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com
Doova is an AI home companion designed to help seniors with safety, daily routines and staying connected with family. (Tuya Smart)
How Doova responds when a senior calls for help
Doova uses LDS LiDAR to navigate around the home. A four-microphone system helps it figure out where a voice is coming from. Meanwhile, AI vision analyzes a person's skeletal posture.

If someone falls or needs assistance, that person can say, "Hey Tuya, help." Doova then locates the person and rolls over to assess what is happening. Tuya says that if the user does not respond within 60 seconds, Doova starts an emergency response workflow. Family members receive an alert with a two-way live video call so they can see what is happening and arrange assistance.

For now, Tuya has not said that Doova automatically detects falls without the user first calling for help or that it directly contacts 911 or a professional monitoring service. So, I would treat it as an added layer of support rather than a replacement for a dedicated medical alert system.
Doova wants to be an AI companion too

Emergency help is only part of what Tuya has built into Doova. The robot uses a multimodal large language model so people can talk with it in a more natural way instead of memorizing rigid voice commands.

For someone spending long stretches at home alone, Doova can carry on a conversation or play entertainment. It can also help make sense of a confusing bill or letter. Another feature caught my eye. Tuya says Doova can identify potential scam risks.
YOUR SENIOR PARENTS ARE EASIER TO IMPERSONATE THAN YOU ARE

That could be useful for older adults who receive a suspicious message and want a second opinion before responding. However, I would never want someone relying solely on an AI robot to decide whether a bill, email or financial request is legitimate.

AI can make mistakes. If Doova flags something suspicious, the safest next move would still be to verify it independently or share it with someone you trust. We've seen how much personal information scammers can gather about older adults, particularly after major life changes such as moving into a retirement community.
A WHEELED ROBOT MAY BEAT HUMANOIDS INTO YOUR HOME
Attendees watch Doova in action at IFA 2026, where Tuya showed how the robot can move through the home and respond when someone needs help. (Tuya Smart)
It can help with everyday routines around the home

Doova can remind you to take medication, keep track of your schedule and give you weather updates. Tuya says it can also learn your preferences over time, which could make its suggestions feel more useful day to day.

The company plans to add a feature that helps find misplaced items around the house. If that works well, I can see the appeal. Plenty of us have spent far too long looking for glasses, keys or a remote that was nearby the whole time.
WOULD YOU PAY $8,000 FOR A ROBOT TO FOLD LAUNDRY?
Doova can patrol your home while you are away

Doova also doubles as a mobile home-monitoring device. Rather than continuously hugging the walls as some patrol robots do, Tuya says Doova travels to selected locations near the center of rooms. From there, it can perform a 360-degree scan.
The robot then creates a safety report that can be sent to the user's phone. When the battery runs low, Doova can return to its charging dock on its own.
AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU
That gives the robot another possible use when someone travels or spends part of the day away from home. However, this capability also leads straight into the biggest question I have about Doova.
What about privacy with Doova?

Doova has microphones, AI vision and live video inside the home. It can also learn a user's preferences over time. That can make the robot more helpful, but it also means giving it access to a lot of personal information.

We raised similar questions when we looked at another AI home robot that can recognize family members and build personalized memories. With Doova, I would want to know where video and audio are processed, what gets stored, who can see it and whether users can permanently delete what the robot has learned.

Tuya's launch announcement does not spell out those Doova-specific privacy controls. Until it does, that is something I would look closely at before bringing a camera-equipped AI robot into a loved one's home. You can also review our guide to limiting the information popular AI services collect about you.
Tuya showcased its connected-home technology at IFA 2026 in Berlin, including Doova, as part of its growing AI-powered smart home ecosystem. (Tuya Smart)
Doova can control your smart home

Tuya also designed Doova to work as a central smart home controller. A senior could use voice commands to adjust connected lights or curtains. Doova can also interact with compatible kitchen and bathroom devices.

I like the thinking here. Smart homes can become complicated very quickly, especially when every device has its own app. If Doova can put those controls into a simple conversation, that could make smart home technology far easier to use.
The robot has a 10.1-inch HD display with animated facial expressions. Its rounded design also looks more like a friendly household companion than an industrial machine.
What we still do not know about Doova

There are still some important blanks to fill in. Tuya has not announced a retail price or when consumers will actually be able to buy Doova. I also want to see how it handles a real home. Rugs, cords and tight spaces can trip up mobile robots. Stairs are another obvious challenge for something that moves around on wheels.

The bigger question is how dependable Doova would be during an actual emergency. Someone may be frightened, speaking softly or lying somewhere the robot cannot easily reach. That is where real world testing will tell us much more than a demonstration on the show floor.
We reached out to Tuya Smart with questions about Doova's emergency response, privacy protections, connectivity and availability but did not hear back before our deadline.
What this means to you

If you are helping a parent or loved one age in place, Doova gives us a pretty good look at where home technology is heading. Instead of relying only on stationary smart speakers or cameras, future AI assistants may move around the house and respond to what is happening nearby.

That could give families another way to stay connected while allowing older adults to maintain more independence. However, I would look closely at the emergency process before relying on any product like this. Find out who gets contacted and what happens when the internet fails. You should also understand exactly what the cameras and microphones collect.
Finally, think about the person who will actually use it. The best technology in the world offers little value if someone finds it confusing, intrusive or uncomfortable.
Kurt's key takeaways

What interests me most about Doova is the move from passive smart devices toward AI that can physically come to you. For an older adult who wants to remain independent, having a robot respond to a call for help and bring family into the situation quickly could offer real peace of mind.

Still, I would want much more information before trusting Doova with someone I love. Safety technology has to prove itself outside the controlled environment of a trade show. I want to know how reliably it reaches someone during an emergency and how much personal information it collects along the way.

The privacy side deserves just as much attention. A moving camera and microphone that learns your routines can become incredibly helpful. It can also become one of the most intimate connected devices in your home. Doova has an interesting idea at its core. Now Tuya needs to show the technology can earn the level of trust its role requires.

Would you put an AI robot with cameras and microphones in an aging parent's home if it could help family respond faster during an emergency, or would that feel like too much surveillance? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Man films himself taking down Flock cameras, gets arrested
summary: Jevon Martinez livestreamed himself removing 10 Flock Safety cameras in Bernalillo County, but authorities say eight belonged to neighborhood associations.
story: Flock Safety founder and CEO Garrett Langley joins host Kayleigh McEnany on 'Saturday in America' to address the growing backlash against AI license plate reader cameras. While critics like Senator Bernie Sanders raise mass surveillance and privacy concerns, Langley defends the technology by highlighting its role in solving over one million crimes and locating 10,000 missing persons across America.
You might expect someone taking down surveillance cameras to avoid being filmed. Jevon Martinez did the opposite.

The 44-year-old Rio Rancho, New Mexico, man recorded himself removing Flock Safety camera equipment around Bernalillo County on Sept. 2. He loaded the equipment into his pickup truck while explaining his reasoning to people watching online. The timing gave Martinez his opening.

Days earlier, Bernalillo County Sheriff John Allen had moved to end the department's three contracts with Flock Safety. Allen cited concerns about privacy, data sharing and his confidence in the company. However, he still supports automated license plate reader technology and plans to look at other vendors.

Martinez apparently saw the remaining cameras as unfinished business. What happened next shows how quickly a fight over surveillance can turn into a criminal case once someone starts removing hardware they do not own.

TEENS ACCUSED OF DESTROYING FLOCK CAMERA UNTIL BATTERY EXPLODED, IGNITING FIRE NEAR HOMES: REPORT
Jevon Martinez recorded himself removing Flock Safety license plate reader cameras around Bernalillo County, New Mexico, before deputies arrested him. (Jevon Martinez via Facebook)
Jevon Martinez explained everything on social media

Martinez made his position unusually easy to understand because he documented it himself. In a Sept. 2 social media post, Martinez said BCSO no longer subscribed to Flock. He wrote that he was taking down the equipment so he could return it.
He also insisted that he was neither destroying nor stealing the equipment. Martinez described it as property that had been left unattended.

His videos carried the same message. "Since BCSO is busy, I know BCSO is busy, everyone who works for BCSO, I know you guys are busy, so I went ahead and helped you out," Martinez says while driving his pickup.
The camera then shows what he means by "helped." His truck bed is filling up with Flock equipment.

This also was not Martinez's first encounter with law enforcement over license plate readers. Rio Rancho police had arrested him months earlier in a separate Sandoval County case involving the alleged removal and damage of three license plate reader systems. He faced nine felony charges in that case.
He turned the Flock camera removals into a challenge

Martinez does not come across in the videos as someone trying to keep a low profile. Quite the opposite. "We got a bunch of these bad boys," he says while showing off the equipment in the back of the truck.
Then comes the line that gives the videos an almost game-like quality. "Let's see how much I can get in one day. That's gonna be the challenge for everyone out there."

At another point, Martinez tells viewers, "Not in my city, not in my state." He also repeatedly calls the Flock cameras "tyranny trees," a nickname that says plenty about how he views automated vehicle surveillance. Reports of his livestream show him dismantling one of the systems while continuing to explain his position. Martinez creates his own record as he goes, with his face, voice and actions captured on camera.
Most of the cameras came from neighborhood systems
This is where Martinez's social media explanation runs into an important problem. Bernalillo County authorities say he removed 10 Flock camera systems with an estimated combined value of $16,500.
However, only two were associated with BCSO. Authorities say the other eight were managed by neighborhood associations. That changes the picture considerably.

Martinez repeatedly described what he was doing as returning equipment to the sheriff after BCSO ended its relationship with Flock. Yet most of the systems authorities recovered were connected to other organizations.

BCSO also says the equipment remained property that members of the public had no authorization to remove. So while Martinez's videos clearly explain what he believed he was doing, they do not settle the ownership question.
EX-INDIANA DEPUTY CHARGED WITH FELONY FOR ALLEGEDLY USING FLOCK CAMERAS TO STALK GIRLFRIEND
Martinez showed Flock Safety equipment piled in his pickup truck after dismantling camera systems he called "tyranny trees." (Jevon Martinez via Facebook)
Deputies stopped him outside the sheriff's office
Martinez said throughout his videos that he planned to return the equipment to BCSO. However, investigators give a somewhat different account of how that ended.
According to the criminal complaint, Martinez drove past BCSO headquarters three times while the equipment remained in his truck. Deputies eventually stopped him outside the sheriff's office.

Video of the arrest shows deputies surrounding his pickup with guns drawn before placing him in handcuffs. Martinez was unarmed, and the charges against him stem from the alleged removal of the equipment rather than a violent offense.

Court reporting differs slightly on the precise larceny charge. One account of the criminal complaint describes attempted larceny over $2,500, while BCSO reporting lists larceny over $2,500. He also faces an interference with communications charge.

Martinez appeared virtually in Bernalillo County Metropolitan Court on Sept. 4. Prosecutors did not file a pretrial detention motion, and Judge Claire McDaniel did not order him held in the Bernalillo County case.

That did not mean Martinez walked free. He remained in custody because of the separate Sandoval County case tied to the earlier alleged license plate reader removals. Reports say that Sandoval County held him over a violation of his release conditions and that a grand jury has since indicted him in that case. The cases remain unresolved, and the charges are allegations unless and until proven in court.
The sheriff also had serious concerns about Flock
There is another wrinkle here that makes this story more interesting. Sheriff Allen had already reached his own breaking point with Flock Safety.

BCSO had three contracts connected to the company. One covered five automatic license plate reader cameras. Another involved 16 speed cameras connected to the Flock network. A third covered gunshot detection technology.
Allen said he had lost confidence in Flock over privacy safeguards and data sharing. He also raised concerns about other law enforcement agencies gaining access to New Mexico plate data.

Still, Allen has defended the underlying technology as a useful law enforcement tool. His disagreement centers on the vendor and the safeguards surrounding the data. That puts BCSO and Martinez in an unusual position. Both expressed serious concerns about Flock. Their ideas about what should happen next could hardly be further apart.
Why Flock cameras raise privacy questions

Automatic license plate readers can create a detailed record of where vehicles appear. Flock's LPR systems collect license plate text along with the date, time and camera location. They can also record basic vehicle characteristics such as make, model and color. Flock says the system does not collect the driver's identity through the LPR camera.
Police can use that information to generate leads in investigations. The concern comes from what happens when millions of those observations become searchable.

We saw the risks firsthand in Colorado, where a woman faced a porch theft accusation after Flock cameras linked her truck to the area. Other location data eventually helped her show where she actually was.

Flock cameras have also moved into places you may visit every week. CyberGuy found license plate readers operating at some Home Depot and Lowe's parking lots in Connecticut. That means pulling into a store can create another record tied to your vehicle.

Then there are systems that can combine different types of signals. We recently looked at SignalTrace, technology that can correlate wireless device signals with license plate reader information and travel patterns.
All of this helps explain why a camera on a roadside can trigger such a strong reaction. It does not give someone permission to dismantle one.
What this means to you

You can question automatic license plate readers without ever touching a camera. Start by finding out which company operates the readers in your community and how long your local agency keeps the data.

Then ask who can search the system and how officials audit those searches. Private cameras deserve attention too. A homeowners association, shopping center or business may operate plate readers that connect with law enforcement.
Public records can help you understand how local agencies use the technology. Public meetings also give residents a way to challenge contracts before officials renew them.
If you want cameras removed, push the people who have the legal authority to make that decision. That keeps the debate focused on surveillance policy rather than turning it into a criminal case.
TENNESSEE OFFICIAL SAYS FLOCK CEO SHOULD BE HANGED 'PUBLICLY FOR TREASON’ AS CONTROVERSIAL CAMERAS FACE REVOLT
Authorities say Martinez removed 10 Flock camera systems worth an estimated $16,500, including eight managed by neighborhood associations. (Jevon Martinez via Facebook)
Kurt's key takeaways

I understand why these cameras make people uncomfortable. A system that quietly logs where vehicles appear deserves close scrutiny, especially when information can move between agencies. Bernalillo County's own sheriff had enough concerns about Flock to walk away from the company. Martinez clearly shares the privacy concern, but his videos show what can happen when someone decides to take the next step on his own.

The biggest factual problem with his argument is hard to overlook. Authorities say only two of the 10 systems he removed were associated with BCSO. The other eight were managed by neighborhood associations. Then there are the videos themselves. Martinez wanted people to see what he was doing. He explained his reasoning and showed the equipment piling up in his truck. Those posts may help him make a political argument online. They also give investigators a remarkably detailed record of what happened. For me, the useful questions are who gets to collect our movement data and what limits control access to it. Those are fights worth having in public.

If your local sheriff said it no longer trusted a surveillance company, would you want every camera removed immediately or would you accept a replacement system with stronger privacy safeguards? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

title: 153 million driver's license scans may be on the dark web
summary: A dark web service called Nexus claimed to hold over 153 million driver's license records, and the FBI confirms it is now looking into the incident.
story: Fox News national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin has the latest on the FBI's investigation into an alleged black market operation selling stolen driver's license records, examining the potential national security and identity theft risks, how millions of personal identification documents may have been compromised and what federal authorities are doing as the investigation unfolds on 'Special Report.'

Think about how often you hand someone your driver's license without giving it much thought. You rent a car, check into a business or go somewhere that needs to verify your age. Someone scans your ID, hands it back and you move on.

A dark web service called Nexus claimed to have collected more than 153 million driver's license records from people in the United States and Canada. It also claimed to have more than 10 million identification cards, over 3 million travel documents or international IDs and at least 579,000 medical cards. That's a staggering amount of identity information.

There is an important caveat, though. The 153 million figure comes from Nexus itself. It has not been confirmed as the number of unique people affected. Some records also contained multiple images of the same license. Still, researchers found enough real driver's licenses in the database to get the FBI's attention.

INSURANCE BREACH EXPOSES 7M DRIVER'S LICENSES
A dark web service called Nexus claimed to hold more than 153 million U.S. and Canadian driver’s license records, raising concerns about identity theft. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
What investigators found inside Nexus

KrebsOnSecurity reported that Nexus appeared on the Russian-language cybercrime forum Exploit on Aug. 31. The service advertised access to identity documents covering more than 170 million people in North America. Driver's licenses made up the biggest category.

Nexus claimed more than 153 million driver's license records. It also advertised millions of other identity documents and hundreds of thousands of medical cards. Krebs tested the service by running a blank search. That returned roughly 11.5 million pages of results with about 15 records per page.

That does not prove there were 153 million different people in the database. However, it does support the possibility that the collection was enormous. More concerning, the driver's license total increased by nearly 400,000 records in about 24 hours while Krebs was examining the service.
The people running Nexus claimed they had been continuously taking new data for more than a year. Investigators have not independently verified that claim.
The clues hidden inside the driver's license scans

The timestamps attached to some of the images helped researchers begin tracing where the records might have originated. Cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs discovered his own Virginia driver's license being offered as a free sample by the people promoting Nexus.

His record contained six image files. Those included images of the front and back of his license, along with infrared and ultraviolet versions. Krebs then asked friends and family members for permission to search for their licenses. Nine people whose licenses appeared in Nexus said the timestamps closely matched dates when they had traveled or presented identification. That led investigators away from the idea that airport security alone might explain the records.

For example, Krebs reported that he had used his passport at airport security during one trip. Later that day, he and his mother handed their driver's licenses to a Hertz rental car representative. Their driver's license scans in Nexus carried timestamps only seconds apart.

Security researcher Zach Edwards found his license in Nexus too. His timestamp lined up with a trip to Las Vegas. Edwards said he had presented his license in several places during the trip. However, he specifically remembered having it scanned at Planet 13, a marijuana dispensary.
IDScan.net acknowledges a security incident

The Planet 13 connection pointed researchers toward Louisiana-based identity verification company IDScan.net, which announced a partnership with the dispensary in 2022. Its scanners can capture IDs using ultraviolet, infrared and white light, similar to the additional scans found in some Nexus records.

IDScan.net has since acknowledged a security incident. The company says an unauthorized third party may have accessed or copied customer information stored in accounts on its cloud. That information may include full names and driver's license or other government-issued identification numbers.

IDScan.net says it is notifying potentially affected people and offering free credit monitoring. However, the company has not confirmed that the Nexus collection came from its systems or that the 153 million records represent 153 million unique people.
IDENTITY THEFT RARELY ANNOUNCES ITSELF: 6 SIGNS YOU MISSED

A dark web service called Nexus claimed to have collected more than 153 million driver's license records from people in the United States and Canada, along with millions of other identification documents. (iStock)
FBI confirms it is looking into the incident

The FBI has now confirmed that it is examining what happened. In a statement to Reuters on Sept. 2, the bureau said it was "looking into the incident" but could not provide more information because of the ongoing investigation.
Reuters reported that the breach, if confirmed at the reported scale, could rank among the largest exposures of government-issued identity documents in North America.

Shortly after KrebsOnSecurity published its investigation, the Nexus dark web site disappeared. Its login page was replaced with a message saying the service was no longer available. That does not mean the stolen records disappeared with it. Anyone who purchased or downloaded information before the site vanished could potentially retain copies.
Why a stolen driver's license scan can cause serious problems

Your driver's license holds information criminals can use to make impersonation attempts much more convincing. Depending on the state, it may include your full name, address, date of birth, license number, photograph and signature.

A high-quality image of the front and back can also give a criminal something physical to present during an identity check. That can become especially concerning when businesses use driver's licenses to verify customers remotely or in person.
A stolen card number can usually be canceled. Your name, photograph and other identity information are much harder to replace.
6 steps to protect yourself now
California driver's license. (iStock)
You cannot pull back a driver's license scan that may already have leaked, but you can make stolen identity information harder to use and watch for warning signs.

A credit freeze can make it much harder for someone to open a new credit account using your identity. The Federal Trade Commission says freezes are free. They also do not affect your credit score and remain in place until you lift them. To fully freeze your credit, contact Equifax, Experian and TransUnion separately .

A freeze primarily protects against new credit accounts. It will not stop someone from misusing an existing bank account or another service that does not check your credit. The FTC recommends credit freezes as one of the strongest protections against new-account identity theft.
Look through your credit reports for accounts, inquiries or personal information you do not recognize. An unfamiliar account can be an early sign that someone is using your identity.

Do not assume one clean check means you're finished. Stolen information can sit unused for months before a criminal tries it. The FTC recommends reviewing your credit reports regularly for accounts you do not recognize.

A credit freeze cannot stop every form of identity fraud. Turn on transaction alerts through your bank and credit card providers. Also watch for password changes, new devices and changes to your contact information. Check your statements instead of relying only on alerts.
Your primary email account can become a gateway to everything else. Use a strong, unique password, store it in a trusted password manager and enable multifactor authentication when available.

Protect your mobile account too. Ask your carrier whether you can add an account PIN or stronger protection against unauthorized number transfers. Also, treat unexpected calls differently when the caller already knows information about you.
Knowing your address or driver's license details does not prove someone is legitimate. That information could have come from stolen records.

Even with good security habits, identity theft can still happen. Your Social Security number, financial information or other personal data may already be exposed without you knowing it. An identity theft protection service can add another layer of monitoring.

Depending on the service and plan, protection may include credit and financial account monitoring, alerts when personal information appears in known breaches or risky online locations and access to specialists who can help with recovery if fraud occurs. Some services also offer reimbursement or coverage for eligible identity theft losses.
Look closely at what each service monitors, how quickly it sends alerts and what recovery help is included.
See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

If you discover someone using your identity, document what happened and start the recovery process quickly. The FTC recommends reporting identity theft through IdentityTheft.gov. The service creates a recovery plan based on the type of fraud involved.

If someone misuses your driver's license, contact your state motor vehicle agency as well. Procedures for replacing a compromised license or changing a license number vary by state. Keep copies of reports, case numbers and correspondence. You may need them later when disputing fraudulent activity.
STOLEN IDS SOLD FOR ‘HAPPY MEAL’ PRICES FUEL BILLIONS IN US BENEFIT FRAUD
Kurt's key takeaways

What jumps out at me here goes beyond the massive 153 million figure. We hand over our driver's licenses all the time, often without knowing who keeps the scan or how long they store it. If criminals get a copy, they may have another powerful piece of information to use for identity theft. While investigators work to determine where the Nexus records came from, protect what you can. Consider freezing your credit, keep an eye on your accounts and use identity theft monitoring if you want added protection. And the next time someone scans your license, ask what happens to that image after you leave.
After seeing how driver's license scans can potentially end up in criminal hands, will you think twice before letting a business scan yours? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Illegal immigrant rideshare driver charged with rape in Maryland had prior NYC sex abuse arrest
summary: Abdoulaye Dia, an Empower rideshare driver, had a prior New York sex abuse arrest before he allegedly raped a teen passenger in Silver Spring.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
An illegal immigrant rideshare driver accused of sexually assaulting a teenage female passenger in Maryland has a history of sex abuse in New York, federal authorities said.
Abdoulaye Dia, of Lanham, Maryland, was charged with first-degree rape, kidnapping, second-degree assault and third-degree sex offense, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said.
On Tuesday, Montgomery County Police officers were called to a hospital where an underage teen girl reported a rape. She told police she was raped by an Empower rideshare driver.
RIDESHARE DRIVER ARRESTED IN ALLEGED SCHEME TARGETING IVY LEAGUE STUDENTS FOR SEX: PROSECUTORS

Dia, a citizen of Guinea, took her to a parking lot in Silver Spring, where the alleged assault occurred.
Investigators identified Dia through information obtained from the rideshare app. He was arrested Wednesday.
TWICE-DEPORTED ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH RAPE AS DHS URGES FAIRFAX TO HONOR ICE DETAINER

Dia was previously arrested June 10 in New York City for sexual abuse by forcible compulsion, forcible touching of the sexual/intimate parts of another person, injuring a child less than 17 and sexual abuse without consent, a DHS spokesperson told Fox News.

title: Hasan Piker calls Bin Laden a ‘spoiled brat,’ labels 9/11 ‘blowback’ in Axios interview
summary: Hasan Piker called Osama bin Laden a "spoiled brat" and labeled 9/11 blowback for U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East and Afghanistan.
story: Fox News congressional correspondent Bill Melugin reports on backlash facing Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed after far-left streamer Hasan Piker claimed that America is worse than al Qaeda on ‘America Reports.’

Hasan Piker, the internet streamer and YouTube personality known for his progressive commentary, called Osama bin Laden a "spoiled brat" for his reasoning in orchestrating the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks, which he called "blowback" for U.S. actions in the Middle East in the preceding years.

Speaking with Axios, Piker discussed bin Laden's remarks about why he targeted the United States: U.S. support of Israel, American oil policies and U.S. bases in the Middle East. He noted that bin Laden was once a U.S. ally when the U.S. trained, funded and armed the mujahideen in Afghanistan during the Soviet-Afghan War.

"The action was so heinous and so violent that — and also … given his position as formerly an American ally — I think that he came across a little bit more as a spoiled brat that wasn't getting his way. With many backers in the Saudi kingdom as well and the royal family," Piker said.
CLINTON, BUSH RECEIVED MULTIPLE WARNINGS ON BIN LADEN HIJACK PLOTS BEFORE 9/11, DECLASSIFIED FILES SHOW

Twitch streamer Hasan Piker is facing renewed scrutiny for his remarks during an Axios interview. He said Osama bin Laden was a "spoiled brat" and remarked on the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks. (Sam Barnes/Web Summit via Sportsfile via Getty Images)
The left-wing streamer said he wants fewer actors like bin Laden to "exist in general."

"The other path of least resistance is to not interfere in these affairs in general and not continue to dominate and create an environment where people are going to seek out revenge and put us in a position of danger," he said.
RADICAL EL-SAYED ALLY DOUBLES DOWN ON ANTI-AMERICAN RHETORIC WITH STUNNING TERRORIST COMPARISON
The World Trade Center in New York City after being attacked by hijacked planes Sept. 11, 2001. (Newspix via Getty Images)
Piker called the Sept. 11 attacks a "horrifying tragedy" and called them blowback for U.S. actions in the Middle East.

"Blowback is not a justification. Blowback is just what it is," he said. "A justification offers either a moral condemnation or a moral acceptance of the act. I do not accept the act of 9/11 morally".
HASAN PIKER INSISTS MIDDLE EAST WOULD BE 'MORE STABLE' IF IRAN HAD NUCLEAR WEAPONS DURING AXIOS INTERVIEW

Piker has faced backlash for remarks in the same interview where he compared the United States to al Qaeda "pound for pound."

"Pound for pound as far as the number of deaths, yes," Piker said. "We have caused tremendous terror all around the world."

title: ICE officer accused of lying to FBI about Minneapolis shooting pleads not guilty
summary: Christian Castro pleaded not guilty to six federal charges in the shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis during a Minneapolis immigration operation.
story: Fox News correspondent Christina Coleman reports from Dallas on a federal judge blocking attempts by Minnesota to extradite ICE agent Christian Castro from Texas. Castro faces charges stemming from the January shooting of a Venezuelan migrant during Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott investigates whether the officer legally qualifies as a fugitive.

A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of lying to the FBI about a January shooting in Minneapolis pleaded not guilty Friday to six federal counts of making materially false statements.

Christian Castro appeared in a federal courtroom in St. Paul after prosecutors accused him of shooting 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg through the front door of a Minneapolis home during Operation Metro Surge.
Castro told investigators he was being attacked with a broom and shovel before opening fire, but prosecutors say surveillance footage contradicted his account.

During his court appearance Friday, Castro, 52, was wearing an ankle monitor and was instructed by a judge to travel only between Minnesota and South Texas. If he has any altercation with law enforcement, he is required to report it within 72 hours, the judge said. He was then released.
ICE OFFICER PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO LYING ABOUT MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING INVOLVING VENEZUELAN MAN

Christian Castro, right, an immigration officer accused of shooting a Venezuelan man during an immigration crackdown in Minneapolis earlier this year and lying to investigators, leaves with attorney Daniel Gerdts after a hearing at the Warren E. Burger Federal Building Friday in St. Paul, Minn. (AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt)

Castro was previously held in Texas custody for about 90 days before he was released. He was held for so long partly because Texas Gov. Greg Abbott refused to sign an extradition warrant to hand him over to Minnesota authorities.
Castro was booked in Minnesota last week following his release in Texas, his home state. Upon his release there, Castro was required to wear an ankle monitor and to surrender his passport and guns.
He faces federal and state charges related to the shooting.
ABBOTT TAUNTS FAR-LEFT AG WITH FIERY WARNING OVER ICE EXTRADITION FIGHT: 'SUCH BAD LAWYERS'
Christian Castro is charged with lying to investigators about a January 2026 shooting. (AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt)

Prosecutors said Castro lied about the circumstances of the shooting, which occurred during Operation Metro Surge, part of the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration. He said he was being attacked with a broom and shovel before he fired his weapon.
The law enforcement operation saw thousands of federal agents in Minnesota that resulted in sweeping arrests, as well as the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens.
‘UNPRECEDENTED’: JUDGES REVEAL BEHIND-THE-SCENES COORDINATION ON TRUMP IMMIGRATION CASES

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, left, and Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, right, battled on X over whether an ICE agent involved in a recent shooting in Minneapolis should be extradited to Minnesota. (Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Minnesota authorities have battled the Trump administration over who should handle any charges against Castro. The administration contends that only federal authorities have jurisdiction over the case.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Michael Rapaport rips NYC Mayor Mamdani during Jewish gathering outside Gracie Mansion
summary: Celebrity Michael Rapaport slammed New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during remarks at a Jewish gathering on Friday, calling him "Zohran the moron"
story: Celebrity Michael Rapaport slammed New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani at a Jewish schools-related demonstration outside of Gracie Mansion on Friday.
Outspoken actor and comedian Michael Rapaport excoriated New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a Jewish gathering outside of Gracie Mansion on Friday.
"Zohran the moron is the most divisive mayor in the history of this city by far," the celebrity asserted. "He's a two-bit con man."
"His wife is an antisemite. His wife is a racist" as well as ‘a homophobic,’" Rapaport said.
MICHAEL RAPAPORT CHEERS MACKLEMORE GETTING DROPPED FROM ED SHEERAN'S TOUR, SAYS 'f--- YOU'
Michael Rapaport visits the SiriusXM Studios on March 31, 2026, in New York City. (Noam Galai/Getty Images)
The mayor's office on Friday responded to Fox News Digital's comment request by referring to remarks Mamdani made when asked earlier this week about the planned gathering.
"I welcome them," the mayor said. "They can have a vigil, or I've heard some describe it even as a protest."
Mamdani said whatever the gathering "is intended to be, they have the room and space to do so outside of Gracie Mansion."
"I think that at the time that they are there I will probably be somewhere else across the city," he said.

Rapaport said he is "absolutely considering running for mayor," though he left the door open to backing another candidate if that person would have "a better chance of winning." The next Big Apple mayoral contest is in 2029.
MAMDANI MAKES EYEBROW-RAISING CLAIM ABOUT NETANYAHU PROTESTS AHEAD OF NYC VISIT

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during a news conference to announce a lawsuit challenging the federal government's new public charge rule, which could make it harder for immigrants to obtain green cards if they rely on public benefits, at City Hall in New York City on Sept. 14, 2026. (ANGELA WEISS / AFP via Getty Images)
Rabbi Binyamin Krauss, principal of SAR Academy, a Modern Orthodox school in New York City, explained the plans for the gathering in a piece published by The Times of Israel.

"On Friday morning, students from SAR, Ramaz, and a number of other schools will stand on East 88th Street and daven. They’ll sing. A few of them will speak. Then they’ll get back on the buses and return to class, two days before Yom Kippur," Krauss wrote.

"Here’s what we want students to learn in the three periods this costs: you belong in this city, and when Jews feel unsafe we gather, and we pray, out loud. We express both our vulnerability and our agency at the same time. Showing up is a civic act, one the Constitution protects and one they’ll need for the rest of their lives," he noted. "Our students love this city and they love Israel, and they don’t see a contradiction."
MAMDANI'S NEW $4M NYC PUBLIC BATHROOMS AUTO-OPEN DOORS AFTER 10 MINUTES

There were also individuals who appeared to be Jewish counter-protesters expressing anti-Israel sentiments near the gathering on Friday. They could be seen with a sign with the messages, "Mayor Mamdani A Friend of Jews While Opposing Israeli Crimes" and "Anti-Zionism Is NOT Anti-Semitism."

title: Judge Judy warns of 'danger' if prosecutors don't retry Lindsay Clancy after murder trial ends in mistrial
summary: Judge Judy Sheindlin says there's a "danger" in not retrying Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three children.
story: Criminal defense attorney Donna Rotunno weighs in on the Lindsay Clancy murder case following a mistrial. They discuss the potential for a plea deal on 'Fox & Friends Weekend'. They debate whether a second trial is likely or if a plea bargain will resolve the charges after the deaths of her three children.

Judge Judy Sheindlin weighed in Thursday on the closely watched Lindsay Clancy murder case following its mistrial, warning there could be a "danger" in prosecutors deciding not to retry the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three young children.
The 83-year-old judge and television personality was asked by TMZ whether Clancy should face another trial after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict earlier this month.
"I think there's a danger in that, in not retrying," Sheindlin responded.

Sheindlin, who launched the popular syndicated show "Judge Judy," which aired for 25 seasons, was also asked about her view on the outcome of the trial after the jury's deliberations ended in a reported 11-1 split in favor of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.
PATRICK CLANCY SPEAKS OUT AFTER HUNG JURY IN LINDSAY CLANCY CASE, ADDRESSES PROSPECT OF ANOTHER TRIAL
"I can't give you a two-minute answer on that," Sheindlin said.
She was then asked whether she believed Clancy should have been found guilty.
"There's no question, my dear, that she killed her children," Sheindlin said. "The only question is, is there an excuse for it? Make up your own mind on that one."
DR PHIL SAYS LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL A 'TEACHABLE MOMENT' ON POSTPARTUM PSYCHOSIS: 'THERE WAS A FAILURE HERE'

Kevin Reddington, defense attorney for Lindsay Clancy, and Lindsay Clancy look on as Judge William Sullivan (out of frame) instructs the jury to continue deliberating, during Lindsay Clancy's murder trial at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on September 4, 2026. ( )
TMZ also asked Sheindlin about Rep. Nancy Mace's public call for Clancy to be publicly executed.
"I think it's ridiculous," Sheindlin responded.
Clancy's defense does not dispute that the 36-year-old former delivery room nurse strangled her three children with exercise bands in January 2023.
Her defense has argued that she was not criminally responsible because of mental illness or defect.
LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR DENIES BIAS ALLEGATIONS, WANTS 'CONVERSATION STARTED' ABOUT WOMEN'S MENTAL HEALTH
Judge Judy Sheindlin warned there could be a "danger" in prosecutors deciding not to retry Lindsay Clancy following the Massachusetts mother's mistrial. (Unique Nicole/Getty Images)
Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial Sept. 4 after seven days of deliberations when jurors said they could not reach a unanimous verdict.
Several jurors later said 11 members of the panel favored finding Clancy not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, while one favored conviction.

Immediately after the mistrial was declared, Clancy's longtime defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, signaled that he would fight another attempt to put her on trial. The defense has indicated it plans to argue that the circumstances surrounding the mistrial should bar a second trial.

However, in a recent interview with Fox News' Bryan Llenas, Reddington said that if prosecutors reduced the top charge to second-degree murder, he would opt for a bench trial — one without a jury — in the hope that she would receive probation.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Clancy remains in custody at Tewksbury Hospital and is due back in court Sept. 29.
Fox News Digital's Michael Ruiz and Stepheny Price contributed to this report.
