Rodan-Benzaquen says of European Jews, "electorally, we don't weigh," so they have again become a political football. She says when left and far-left parties say, "Oh, we want to fight against antisemitism. The only reason why they're saying it is because it's a tool to attack the far-right."

Tyler Speicher is an American journalist living in Slovenia after spending 25 years covering stories ranging from the Little League World Series to hurricanes, 9/11 and its aftermath for New York City news outlets, including 20 years on the Fox News Channel assignment desk.

title: NATO jets shoot down drone in Lithuanian airspace as Russia grows 'increasingly reckless,' Rutte says
summary: Two Italian Eurofighter Typhoons scrambled under NATO command and downed a drone over Lithuania that officials say likely came from Belarus.
story: Two Italian Eurofighters scrambled under NATO command to intercept an explosive-laden drone over Lithuania, marking the nation's first operational air defense shootdown. (Lithuanian Army)

Two Italian Eurofighter Typhoons operating under NATO command scrambled overnight and shot down a drone over Lithuania, marking the first time a drone has been downed in the Baltic nation's airspace, officials said Tuesday.
The incident came less than a day after NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte warned that strikes close to alliance territory would drive the 32-nation bloc to increase its support for Ukraine.
The drone was destroyed near the village of Pratkūnai, about 60 miles northwest of the capital, Vilnius.
RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS

Lithuanian soldiers are securing the area where Italian fighter jets during NATO's Baltic Air Policing Mission shot down a drone early morning near Pratkunai village, Kaisiadorys district roughly 60 miles northwest of the capital Vilnius, Lithuania, Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026.

"Last night, two Italian Eurofighters deployed on NATO Air Defence mission at Siauliai, scrambled and shot down a drone over Lithuanian airspace," a NATO official told Fox News Digital. "The operation was coordinated through NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre in Uedem, Germany. Investigations are ongoing together with national authorities."
Lithuanian officials said the drone most likely entered from neighboring Belarus and remained in the country's airspace for about 30 minutes before it was intercepted.
Lithuanian soldiers are securing the area where Italian fighter jets during NATO's Baltic Air Policing Mission shot down a drone early this morning near Pratkunai village. (AP Photo)
Lithuanian Air Force Commander Antanas Matutis said the recovered drone was "likely" carrying explosives.
Authorities are examining the wreckage of the downed drone to determine its origin and purpose.
The incident comes amid heightened tensions along NATO's eastern flank.
RUSSIA EXPOSES NATO WEAPONS GAP AS TOP COMMANDER WARNS ‘THE MATH IS NOT IN FAVOR OF THE WEST’
Speaking in Brussels on Monday, Rutte said strikes "close to NATO territory" showed Russian President Vladimir Putin's "desperation and also his desire to sow fear and terror."
"Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine," Rutte said, while pledging to strengthen NATO defenses along its eastern flank.

Debris of what, according to the Lithuanian national crisis management centre, was a drone shot down by a NATO fighter jet, lies on the ground near Pratkunai village, Lithuania, September 15, 2026, in this screengrab from a handout video. (Lithuanian Army/Handout via Reuters)

In a separate incident Tuesday, Denmark said a Russian frigate fired flares toward a Danish military helicopter conducting routine surveillance over the Baltic Sea. Denmark summoned the Russian ambassador over the encounter.
Meanwhile, Russia continued drone strikes across Ukraine, killing three people in Kyiv, Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, according to Ukrainian officials.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv remained ready to support de-escalation if the U.S. could ensure Russia was prepared to stop its attacks. Ukrainian forces also struck an oil refinery in Syzran and targeted a drone production facility in Taganrog, he said.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Bradford Betz is a Fox News Digital breaking reporter covering crime, political issues, and much more.

title: UK breakup push escalates amid historic pact after Trump backs reunification of Ireland
summary: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland leaders signed a historic joint declaration in Cardiff, warning that Westminster's time is coming to an end.
story: President Donald Trump expressed support for Irish unification during a meeting in Dublin, just days after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham ruled out potential referendums in Northern Ireland and Scotland.

The leaders of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland called Monday for the British government to "prepare for, plan and facilitate" constitutional change that could lead to the breakup of the United Kingdom, with the remarks coming days after President Donald Trump said he would "love to see" Irish reunification.

"Westminster’s time is coming to an end," Scottish First Minister John Swinney, Welsh First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth and Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill said in a historic joint declaration issued in Cardiff.
The nationalist party leaders had met Monday to strengthen cooperation among Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland and advance what they described as "constitutional change."
KEIR STARMER REPORTEDLY CONSIDERING STEPPING DOWN AS PM AND COULD ANNOUNCE TIMETABLE FOR DEPARTURE
Scottish, Welsh, Northern Irish leaders say that Westminster is not working and are back self-determination. (Adrian DENNIS / AFP via Getty Images)
The declaration, signed during the summit in Cardiff, signals an unprecedented challenge to Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the U.K.’s constitutional settlement.
Trump spoke about the status of Northern Ireland over the weekend, saying Saturday during a visit to Dublin: "It’s going to happen eventually. It might as well happen now."
On Sunday, Trump repeated his support for a united Ireland, saying it made sense to merge the Republic of Ireland with Northern Ireland.
"It just seems to me that you have Northern Ireland and you have Ireland, and it would seem to me that one of the naturals of all time is put them together," Trump said in Doonbeg.
NIGEL FARAGE RESIGNING FROM UK PARLIAMENT
President Donald Trump reacts on the first tee during the final day of the Irish Open on Sept. 13, 2026, in Doonbeg, Ireland. (Charles McQuillan/Getty Images)
"You asked about Scotland. That one I won't talk about yet. I'll save that for another day," he added.
By Monday, the nationalist leaders had released a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to drive constitutional change.
They said no Westminster government has the right to block democratic decisions made by Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland.
"Each of our nations has the right to determine its own future, through democratic means and in accordance with the wishes of its people," the three leaders wrote.

"For the first time ever, people across these islands have First Ministers in Scotland, in Wales and in the North of Ireland who are all committed to independence from the United Kingdom. For people watching across these islands – for people watching around the world – there could be no clearer sign that Westminster’s time is coming to an end," the statement continued.
MEET 'COUNT BINFACE,' THE TRASH CAN-CLAD COMEDIAN CHALLENGING NIGEL FARAGE

Andy Burnham delivers his inaugural speech as UK's new Prime Minister on July 20, 2026 in London, England. The Member of Parliament for Makerfield becomes the UK's 59th Prime Minister, succeeding Sir Keir Starmer, who resigned as leader of the Labour Party and Prime Minister in June. (Photo by Dan Kitwood/Getty Images) (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)
"We call for the British Government to prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change in each jurisdiction," the memorandum said.
According to GB News, Burnham was told Monday that he could not stop the breakup of the U.K.
Sinn Féin, the largest party in the Northern Ireland Assembly, issued the warning after signing the memorandum with the SNP and Plaid Cymru.
O’Neill said the three nations shared a "common cause" because "Westminster does not and will never serve our people well."
She added during a news conference that Burnham would not be able to "hold back the tide" of nationalism.

"We’re certainly living in times of enormous change, change that is unstoppable, change that, no matter what is said by any British prime minister, will not be able to hold back the tide of what’s happening in front of our eyes right now.
"Our common cause here is the understanding that Westminster does not and will never serve our people well," she added.
KING CHARLES FOLLOWS QUEEN ELIZABETH'S PLAYBOOK WITH A TWIST DURING TRUMP STATE VISIT: EXPERT

President Donald Trump speaks with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin during a meeting in the Oval Office of the White House, on St. Patrick's Day, Tuesday, March 17, 2026, in Washington. (Alex Brandon/AP Photo)
The memorandum commits the parties to cooperation on economic policy, renewable energy and rebuilding ties with the European Union, among other areas.
It also calls for greater self-determination and states that the nations should work together as equals.
A spokesperson for Burnham said: "The Prime Minister is committed to delivering change across all four nations of the United Kingdom and believes strongly in the Union.

"The United Kingdom is at its best when people come together around our shared values and problem-solving, rather than division, and the Prime Minister will continue to ease pressures on household finances and delivering greater economic security, rather than engaging in constitutional debates or further referendums."
Fox News Digital has reached out to 10 Downing Street for comment.

title: Russia readies new 500-mile missile as weapon expert warns of 'terminal end game surprises'
summary: Russia plans to test a new 800-km ballistic missile by year's end, with an analyst warning its advanced maneuverability could strain Ukraine air defense.
story: Defense analyst warns Moscow’s new missile may come with maneuvering capabilities or "terminal end game surprises".

Moscow is preparing for a final test of a new ballistic missile capable of striking targets hundreds of miles away and potentially maneuvering in ways that could challenge Ukraine’s already strained air defenses, a defense analyst warned Monday.
The warning comes as Ukrainian military officials said that Russia could conduct the test in the coming months and potentially in live-fire strikes.

"According to our estimates, Russia plans to conduct final tests of a new type of ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 km by the end of this year," Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU), said at a meeting of the Ukraine-NATO Interparliamentary Council, according to Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda.

"If, for instance, this 800-kilometer missile has more advanced maneuverability, well then that's going to create greater problems for Ukraine in that they're going to need the more sophisticated interceptors to get them," Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Fox News Digital.
RUSSIA DEPLOYS NORTH KOREAN MISSILE UNIT TO UKRAINE; MOSCOW-PYONGYANG AXIS DEEPENS: REPORT
A Sarmat missile, also known as "Satan 2," is being fired from an undisclosed location in Russia. (East2West)
"This means terminal maneuvers that weave a little bit so that the defender doesn't quite know where it's going or what trajectory it will have," Karako said.
"Another possibility is that they just figured out a way to make some kind of 800-kilometer missile more cheaply or in large numbers," the expert said of the Russians.
Karako said developments in precision-guided munitions, along with a broader shift away from unguided weaponry, could offer clues about the type of missile Russia will launch.
NEXT-GENERATION MISSILE DEFENSE AT MISSION SPEED
Ukrainian firefighters work to extinguish a fire at a market following a Russian missile strike in Kyiv.  (AFP)

"Everyone is going for increased maneuverability," Karako explained. "Just about every gravity bomb that we have has some kind of terminal guidance for precision," he said, specifically of the U.S. arsenal.
"In a similar way, a moment's not too far in the future where you don't really have that many purely ballistic missiles."
"You have things that may be ballistic for a good part of their path, but are also equipped with maneuvering reentry vehicles or some kind of terminal end game surprises," he warned.

Meanwhile, according to Ukraine's DIU, Russian forces may try to strike targets in western Ukraine during the missile tests as a live-fire demonstration, which Karako said is standard practice in wartime.
"This is a business-as-usual arrangement where you might do lots of developmental testing and then formally field and then have your operational testing," the expert said.
RUSSIA UNLEASHES NEARLY 600 MISSILES AND DRONES ON KYIV IN DEADLIEST STRIKE SINCE MAY
Smoke rises over Kyiv following a Russian missile and drone attack that struck multiple districts of the Ukrainian capital. July 8, 2026. (East2West news)

"There are all kinds of norms being broken, though, because it is, after all, wartime, and so it may well be the case that some of this stuff is tested — maybe not the first time — but some of the early tests are done, frankly, in the field in Ukraine," he added.
The missile would, however, fall into a category once prohibited under the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, Karako warned.

Signed by President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev in 1987, the INF Treaty required the United States and the Soviet Union to eliminate ground-launched ballistic and cruise missiles with ranges between 500 and 5,500 kilometers (roughly 310 to 3,400 miles).
The United States withdrew from the treaty in 2019 amid alleged Russian violations.
"This range is one that was formerly prohibited by the INF Treaty that capped ballistic and cruise missiles at 500 kilometers in range," Karako said.
"To some extent, you see Russia filling that gap, which is understandable and reasonable. Of course, they were violating the INF Treaty, which was why the United States got out of it."
PENTAGON PLOTS NEW NUCLEAR OPTIONS FOR TRUMP AS AMERICA’S BIGGEST ADVERSARIES RAISE STAKES: REPORT
At the closing ceremony for the Geneva Summit, Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev and President Ronald Reagan sit near each other, on November 21, 1985. (Bettmann via Getty Images)

Missiles and artillery have been central to Russia's campaign against Ukraine since the start of the war in 2022. Ukrainska Pravda reported Aug. 10, citing Ukrainian military intelligence, that production of Russia's primary missile types had reached between 110% and 120% of monthly targets.
According to the Kyiv Independent, Russia fired at least 1,858 missiles of various types at Ukraine from the start of 2026 through Aug. 27.
"This is what's hitting Ukraine on a daily and weekly basis. And so it's in that broader context of that demand for standoffs of various kinds that you see new things pop up," Karako said.
RUSSIA THREATENS STRIKES ON UK MILITARY TARGETS, ‘CATASTROPHIC CONSEQUENCES’ OVER UKRAINE
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte (not seen) hold a joint press conference in Kyiv, Ukraine, on June 3, 2026. (Danylo Antoniuk/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy highlighted the growing strain on air defenses in an interview with Deutsche Welle at a Canadian military base in North Bay Sept. 12.

"I want to have 100-120 [interceptor missiles] for these difficult months, especially the cold months," Zelenskyy said. "We'll see how many months this winter lasts — that is, these cold months: one, two, three. We don't know. This is truly a major challenge."
"It is the case that Russia really is on a wartime footing, and they really have mobilized their defense industrial base to be cranking these (missiles) out like sausages," Karako said.
"There was a point in which everything was going to the front, everything was going to Ukraine."
"There have been other reports more recently that suggest that Russia may be keeping some in reserve," Karako added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"There are lots of worries. If you're in Poland, if you're in Romania, if you're in the Baltics, you're worried about the Russians."

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Iran’s proxy money machine: How the Houthis built a multibillion-dollar network despite US sanctions
summary: The Houthis' advance toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is fueled by a sprawling sanctions-evasion network spanning Iranian oil, crypto and Russia.
story: Adam Rousselle, founder of Between the Lines (BTL) Research, says Iran-backed Houthis have built a sprawling financial network spanning oil, ports, crypto, Russia and China — complicating U.S. efforts to choke off the money sustaining the group.

The Houthis’ rapid advance toward one of the world’s most important shipping chokepoints is putting fresh scrutiny on the sprawling financial network that has helped transform the Iran-backed group from a Yemeni insurgency into a heavily armed regional power capable of threatening global trade.

The group has seized new territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the strategic port city of Mocha, and expanded toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The waterway connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and carries a significant share of global maritime trade and energy shipments.

For the Trump administration, the Houthi advance is becoming as much a financial challenge as a military one. Washington is intensifying efforts to choke off the money sustaining Iran and its proxies, but the Houthis have built a sprawling sanctions-evasion network while controlling ports, trade routes and millions of Yemenis — raising a difficult question for Treasury: how do you cut off the cash fueling the group without cutting off food, fuel and other lifelines to civilians?
SAUDI ARABIA TELLS TRUMP NOW IS THE TIME FOR MILITARY ACTION AS IRAN-BACKED HOUTHIS ADVANCE

Yemen's Iran-backed armed Houthi group has warned they will move to shutter the Bab Al-Mandeb Strait through missile-drone attacks if Gulf nations join the U.S.-Israel war on Iran. (Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images)
The Houthis operate a financial network that extends far beyond Yemen, according to Adam Rousselle, founder of Between the Lines Research.
"We’re dealing with a very well-capitalized group," Rousselle told Fox News Digital.

In a 2025 investigation for the Global Network on Extremism and Technology, Rousselle traced a financing system spanning Houthi-controlled ports, tariffs, Iranian oil, informal hawala networks, cryptocurrency exchanges and foreign facilitators across Russia, Turkey and Southeast Asia.

Control of ports has historically been central to Houthi revenue because Yemen depends heavily on imports. Rousselle’s GNET report said the Houthis have imposed steep fees at ports they control and tariffs on goods brought into their territory from rival Yemeni ports.
HOUTHIS ENTER US 'KILL BOX' AFTER SEIZING RED SEA 'CORK,' FORMER PENTAGON OFFICIAL WARNS
Satellite imagery shows Bab el Mandeb Strait, a key shipping waterway and the gateway to the Red Sea, in this handout picture dated July 12, 2026. (Nasa Worldview/Handout via Reuters)
The group’s latest territorial gains could strengthen that economic base even further.

Nadwa Al-Dawsari, a Yemen expert and associate fellow at the Middle East Institute, told lawmakers in Sept. 1 testimony before the House Foreign Affairs Committee that territory is central to the Houthis’ ability to withstand outside pressure.

"The most important source of that leverage is territory," Al-Dawsari testified. "The Houthis have been able to consolidate their power and build increasingly sophisticated military capabilities because they control significant territory, a large population, ports, infrastructure, and resources."
"That territorial base allows them to recruit, generate revenue, manufacture and store weapons, control smuggling routes, and regenerate capabilities degraded by airstrikes and sanctions," she added.
IRAN LOSES KEY ECONOMIC LIFELINE IN MIDDLE EAST THAT TRUMP'S SANCTIONS COULDN'T REACH AS DEADLOCK PERSISTS
Houthi supporters chant slogans during an anti-U.S. and anti-Israel rally in Sanaa, Yemen, March 17, 2025. (AP Photo/Osamah Abdulrahman)
Rousselle said the Houthis’ finances should not be understood simply as Tehran handing cash to an Iranian proxy.
"It’s a bit of a misunderstanding that the Iranians just give them money," he said, describing the Houthis instead as embedded in a broader Iranian commercial ecosystem.

"The Houthis aren't sanctions-proof; they're sanctions-adapted," Miad Maleki, senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital. "Most of their money is made inside Yemen — customs and taxes at Hodeidah and Ras Isa, and fuel above all."

Treasury has estimated that the Houthis generate more than $2 billion a year from oil sales, while Iran provides the group with a free monthly oil shipment through Iranian-owned or affiliated companies based in Dubai. Treasury has also documented Houthi revenue from taxes imposed on petroleum imports.
CHINA ORDERS FIRMS TO IGNORE US IRAN SANCTIONS, DARING US TO ENFORCE CRACKDOWN
Scott Bessent, Treasury secretary, departs following a tariff announcement in the Rose Garden of the White House on April 2, 2025. (Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Sanctions can't reach domestic extraction," Maleki said. "What they can reach is the plumbing between Sana'a and the outside world; the exchange houses, the Dubai and Muscat correspondents, the tankers and the wallets."

At the center of that system is Sa’id al-Jamal, whom the Treasury Department has identified as an Iran-backed Houthi financial official operating an international network that sells Iranian commodities and channels proceeds toward the group.

Treasury said in April 2025 that al-Jamal’s network had procured tens of millions of dollars in weapons, sensitive goods and commodities from Russia and identified eight digital-asset wallets used by the Houthis. Blockchain analytics cited in Rousselle’s GNET research identified nearly $900 million in outflows across those addresses.
Rousselle cautioned against treating that figure as a complete picture of Houthi wealth.
"The system is more important than the number itself," he said, describing the network as fluid and difficult to quantify.
Russia, he argued, has become a particularly significant part of the network. "The Russians are definitely more hands-on in their support," Rousselle said.
TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA
Houthi supporters demonstrate in solidarity with Iran, in Sanaa, Yemen, April 10, 2026. (Khaled Abdullah/Reuters)

Al-Dawsari’s congressional testimony similarly highlighted the Houthis’ expanding relationships beyond Iran, saying the group is "deepening ties with other U.S. adversaries, particularly Russia and China."

She cited reports that Russia provided targeting data used to help the Houthis attack Western ships in the Red Sea and that Russian petroleum products were transferred ship-to-ship into a Houthi-controlled tanker before reaching the Houthi-controlled port of Ras Isa.

The China connection is more complicated. Rousselle said Chinese-linked private commercial actors appear in parts of the network but distinguished that activity from proven direct Chinese government involvement.
"The Chinese are kind of… turning a blind eye," he said.

His GNET report described Iranian oil flowing to privately owned Chinese "teapot" refineries and examined transactions linked to Southeast Asian financial networks, while cautioning that the available evidence did not establish direct Chinese government control of Houthi financing.

Al-Dawsari pointed to a broader Chinese role in Houthi supply chains. Citing U.S. officials, she said a Chinese satellite company with ties to the Chinese military provided satellite imagery supporting Houthi attacks against U.S. warships and international shipping. She also cited interdiction data showing that 60% of the components and materials used in the Houthi Qasef-2K drone came from China, compared with roughly 15% from Iran.
That sprawling network is now testing Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s broader effort to isolate Tehran economically and disrupt the financial channels sustaining Iran and its proxies.
Rousselle said decentralized illicit-finance networks present a fundamental challenge.
"You’re dealing with a ‘you shut down one, another pops up’ kind of situation," he said.
Maleki argued that Washington should concentrate on the points where Houthi money intersects with the formal financial system.
IRAN TAPS FINANCIAL LIFELINE, RUSSIAN ARMS AS TRUMP ESCALATES 'CRUSHING' ECONOMIC WARFARE
Houthi supporters show solidarity with Palestinians in the Gaza Strip and to condemn U.S. strikes in Yemen, in Sanaa, Yemen May 30, 2025. (Reuters/Adel Al Khader)

"The soft spots are wherever Houthi money touches the formal system," he said. "Treasury has named the Yemeni banks and the Sana'a exchange houses that pay for missile components; it should now name the foreign correspondents still clearing for them. That is the one tool that changes behavior overnight."
Oman represents another potential pressure point. "Oman is the Houthis' land bridge and their mailing address," Maleki said.

But squeezing Houthi finances presents another dilemma: Yemen remains one of the world’s most fragile humanitarian environments, and the Houthis control ports and infrastructure through which civilians receive food, fuel and other basic goods.
"I would be lying if I had a concrete answer to it," Rousselle said when asked how Washington could disrupt Houthi revenue without worsening the humanitarian crisis.
IRAN-BACKED HOUTHI THREAT IN RED SEA COULD LEAD TO MAJOR US POLICY SHIFT, ANALYSTS SAY

Members of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces react during clashes with Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis in a location given as near Al-Hazm, Yemen, in this screen grab obtained from a handout video released Sept. 9, 2026. (Media Centre Of The Yemeni Armed Forces/Handout via Reuters)
"The humanitarian argument is the Houthis' best shield, and it's backwards," Maleki said. "Food and medicine are licensed and should stay that way."
"Keep the goods flowing and take away the toll," he added, arguing that Washington should seek ways to prevent humanitarian trade from generating taxes and fees for Houthi authorities.
Rousselle warned that the challenge extends far beyond Yemen.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A map highlights the Yemeni port city of Hodeida on the Red Sea coast, where Israeli airstrikes targeted Houthi military infrastructure on Sept. 16, 2025. (Associated Press)
"This isn’t just about the Houthis," he said. "This is about any sanctioned actor worldwide capable of harnessing financial systems that are completely outside of regulatory control."
The Treasury Department did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Houthis enter US 'kill box' after seizing Red Sea 'cork,' former Pentagon official warns
summary: Houthi rebels seized Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, but a former Pentagon official warns they've entered a vulnerable U.S. Navy kill box.
story: Houthis seize Perim Island, exposing themselves to U.S. firepower, former Pentagon official says.

Iran-backed Houthi rebels captured Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait Sept. 11, opening a new front at a vital global shipping chokepoint as a former Pentagon official warned Sunday the militants had entered a "kill box."

The island's capture came after a month-long offensive along Yemen’s western coast that killed more than 1,500 soldiers and forced Yemen’s government to acknowledge a "painful" defeat, according to The Associated Press.
"With Perim, they have gained what we could call the cork in the Red Sea bottle," Morgan Murphy, a former Pentagon press secretary and Navy Reserve captain, told Fox News Digital.

"But they've put themselves into a kill box. They're nowhere near the capability of the United States and if the president so chooses, he can wipe them off the face of that rock pretty easily," Murphy warned.
SAUDI ARABIA TELLS TRUMP NOW IS THE TIME FOR MILITARY ACTION AS IRAN-BACKED HOUTHIS ADVANCE
The Houthis reached the strategic island of Perim in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on September 11 in a move to tighten their grip on a vital global shipping route. (Reuters)
Despite Perim sitting in the middle of the narrow maritime passage, Murphy detailed how the Houthis had effectively placed themselves in an area that is vulnerable to concentrated fire.
"Perim cuts that chokepoint right in half, and it's only 18 miles wide there," Murphy said.
He said the island has served as a pivotal maritime vantage point for hundreds of years, previously targeted for control by French forces and held by the British Empire for over a century.

Perim — a desolate volcanic island also known as Mayun — also sits roughly 20 miles off the Horn of Africa, placing it in proximity to Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, home to one of the largest U.S. military installations on the continent.
"We have incredible firepower in that region, and that's a little rock in the middle of that strait. It's a volcanic rock. It doesn't have any water. It's uninhabitable," Murphy warned.
"There's no vegetation to speak of. And the Houthis have just massed their troops on that rock. So what that is, what we would call that in the Navy, is a kill box."

Satellite imagery of the island shows a 1.85-kilometer (6,070-foot) runway alongside three military hangars, which regional intelligence reports attribute to past construction by the United Arab Emirates.
"There's a 6,000-foot airstrip on that island. I think that Emiratis built it," Murphy said.
‘GATE OF TEARS’ AT RISK: IRAN THREATENS MAJOR NEW GLOBAL CHOKEPOINT IF US MOVES ON HORMUZ

"It's nice to have an airstrip, and especially a long runway, but we don't know the condition of that runway. We don't know how they could possibly use that runway, and they certainly don't have the sophisticated air power that the United States and its allies have to project power from that runway."
He added that the U.S. military holds overwhelming force options if commanders elect to target the island.
"We could wipe that rock into glass, just blast it into a smooth glass surface, put skates back on our feet, and skate all over it," Murphy said.
"That's why the Houthis have kind of played coy with the president, and they know that even if they fortify that rock they're not going to be able to hold it in the face of the United States Navy."
The developments come amid diplomatic maneuvering between Washington, Riyadh and the Houthis in recent days.

Sources confirmed to Fox News Digital that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had called President Donald Trump twice Sept. 10 to urge him to authorize U.S. military strikes against Houthi positions.
Trump declined direct intervention, with U.S. officials noting the administration has no immediate plans for direct combat involvement but will continue offering intelligence assistance.
IRAN AND HOUTHI TERROR PROXY FACING RED SEA THREAT FROM PRO-US AFRICAN NATION

Satellite imagery shows Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping waterway and the gateway to the Red Sea, as Iran threatens using Yemen's Houthi allies to shut the Bab el-Mandeb gateway to the Red Sea, in this handout picture dated July 12, 2026. (Nasa Worldview/Handout via Reuters)
Speaking to reporters in Dublin on Sept. 12, Trump also indicated the Houthis had signaled a desire to avoid direct confrontation with American forces.
"The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us. They let us know, they don’t want to fight with us... they don’t want us to go after them," Trump said.
Murphy suggested, however, that Washington’s restraint should not be mistaken for inaction.
"I can't speak for the president. But this administration has not shown a lack of resolve to use force," Murphy said.
"I wouldn't doubt at all if the president took steps to pound some of these folks into the sand if they continue to really disrupt the global energy supply."

Yemeni government, regional and Iranian sources told Reuters the Houthi advance was sustained by Iranian weaponry and tactical direction from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC, with U.S. officials estimating hundreds of IRGC officers remain active in Yemen.
Murphy noted that Tehran's strategy appears designed to drive up global fuel prices by choking critical shipping lanes.
TRUMP THREATENS 'MAJOR MILITARY PUNISHMENT' FOR IRAN OVER FUTURE HOUTHI ATTACKS

Protesters who support Yemen's Houthi group brandish weapons and shout slogans as they celebrate the ban imposed against the maritime shipping of Saudi Arabia on July 20, 2026, in Sana'a, Yemen. (Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images)
Comparing the conflict to historical naval power struggles, Murphy emphasized the strategic mismatch.
"We're in a different era. They are nowhere near the sophistication of the world's major powers. The Houthis are using a 19th-century playbook. They are not using 21st-century warfare," he said.
"So, yes, they've caught a critical cork in the Red Sea bottle, but how they use it remains to be seen," Murphy concluded.

"This is an example of why great powers really have to have a strong Navy. This is why Great Britain had a strong navy. This is why the United States has a strong navy, because there's so many regional powers who want to try to bottle up shipping, whether it is in the Strait of Malacca, whether it is in the Strait of Hormuz, and here, in this case, in the Red Sea."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I think what we're going to see in the next several days and weeks is a coordinated effort by the Trump administration to make sure our allies are on board in helping us keep these critical waterways open, free, and clear for freedom of navigation," he said.

title: Could Africa be the next AI frontier as US and Europe hit limits?
summary: U.S. companies are winning massive data center and AI deals across Africa, including a $6.2 billion project in Lesotho for hydropower and computing.
story: China expert Gordon Chang discusses why he believes Beijing is looking to exploit U.S. opposition to new data centers as China works to narrow America’s lead in AI infrastructure.
FIRST ON FOX: Africa could become the next major frontier for data centers and artificial intelligence, experts say.
The Trump administration is backing and promoting American companies to make AI development, in their words, "the gold standard."
The U.S. is trying increasingly to grab business opportunities in Africa as backlash and environmental restrictions hit data center development in the U.S. and Africa.

"Africa is emerging as a significant potential location for building AI infrastructure, especially as many mature markets face increasing environmental and power constraints," Abhishek Goyal, consultant at specialist research group Arizton Advisory & Intelligence, told Fox News Digital.
US COMPANIES WIN BILLIONS IN AFRICAN DATA CENTER DEALS IN DIRECT COMPETITION WITH CHINA

A rendering of U.S. company Cybastion’s projected data center in the Ivory Coast, West Africa. The U.S. Embassy in Abidjan helped facilitate a $170 million contract with the government of the Ivory Coast, which includes the provision of the data center.  (Cybastion)

"The continent could become the next major frontier for AI infrastructure development. As the U.S. and Europe encounter challenges such as power scarcity, grid congestion, permitting issues and environmental regulations, Africa's underdeveloped infrastructure presents an opportunity rather than a disadvantage."

A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "We are committed to ensuring that American AI, including enabling infrastructure like data centers, continues to be the gold standard worldwide and that we remain the partner of choice for foreign governments and businesses who are seeking to upgrade their telecommunications networks and AI capabilities."
Amongst other deals, this year with U.S. help, an American company has won a $6.2 billion deal in Lesotho in Southern Africa for a data center and hydropower plant.

In the central African country of Gabon, the U.S. Embassy helped win $600 million in business for American companies in 2025. And this year, the embassy in this central African country has assisted in securing a $100 million contract to supply two data centers and a gas-to-power plant in the face of strong competition from China.
TRUMP GETS MAJOR WIN AGAINST CHINA IN AFRICAN RARE EARTH MINERALS RACE

A rendering of the Kobong, Lesotho, Pumped Hydro project, which is to be constructed in Lesotho by U.S. company Convalt Energy as part of a $6.2 billion deal with the government of Lesotho facilitated with the assistance of the U.S. government. (Convalt Energy)

Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Frank Garcia previously told Fox News Digital, "Under President Trump’s leadership, the United States is assisting U.S. companies to find new markets and flourish in Africa."

"Africa is experiencing a data center boom, but it begins from a very small base," Arthur Goldstuck told Fox News Digital. Goldstuck is CEO of South African technology research group World Wide Worx and author of "The Hitchhiker’s Guide to AI – The African Edge."
MASSIVE AI BOOM PUTS ONE OF AMERICA’S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS ON PATH TO DOUBLE IN SIZE, CEO SAYS

Goldstuck said that because of a lack of capacity, "Africa will not replace either market as any kind of center of global computing. Rather, its attraction lies in serving a rapidly growing African cloud market and processing African data closer to the people and businesses that generate it.

He continued, "Africa also gives U.S. companies access to a cloud and AI market that remains severely underserved. The opportunities extend from operating data centers to supplying AI chips, cooling systems, cybersecurity and power infrastructure.

"In some countries, a data center can also become the guaranteed customer that makes a new renewable energy project financially viable. American companies can therefore develop computing capacity and electricity generation together, in partnership with African companies and governments."

A recent site visit to the construction zone for a new data center in the Ivory Coast, which is part of a $170 million contract facilitated by the U.S. Embassy for development by the U.S. company Cybastion.  (Clement Djakey for Cybastion)
But Goldstuck said data center growth is fueled by local needs on the continent.

"It is a boom by African standards," he said. "Africa remains far behind the U.S. and Europe in installed capacity, and weak electricity grids make construction and operation more difficult. Demand is growing rapidly as governments, banks and other large companies seek local cloud and AI services. They increasingly want sensitive information stored within their own countries, which adds momentum to the expansion."
Arizton’s Goyal added that "countries such as South Africa, Kenya, Nigeria, Morocco and Egypt are attracting large-scale (AI) projects.

"The U.S. government aims to offer credible solutions that leverage public and private financing in priority areas, such as emerging technology, which demand that global telecoms networks remain secure for U.S. citizens and business," a State Department spokesperson said.
"For example, undersea cable networks are being constructed across the Atlantic, providing more opportunity and connectivity to Africa than ever before."
THE BIGGEST THREAT IN AMERICA'S RACE WITH CHINA ISN'T BEIJING, TECH EXECUTIVE WARNS

The Isando Campus, home to the Teraco Data Environments JB1 East & West, JB3 and JB5 data centers, in Johannesburg, South Africa, Sept. 28, 2025. Outside South Africa, computing resources on the continent are often expensive and scarce.  (Leon Sadiki/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
U.S. companies using undersea AI cables to connect with African data centers is a possibility, Goldstuck said, but there are limitations.

"Distance creates a slight delay, so African facilities would be less attractive for U.S. services requiring an instant response from American users" Goldstuck said. "They could work well for backups, disaster recovery and some intensive AI processing, provided that the cost, security and legal jurisdiction made sense."

Analysts say much of Africa lacks regulation and is creating the risk of a Wild West approach to business. The South African government recently claimed the country hosts 70% of the continent's total data center capacity.

But Pitso Tsibolane, senior lecturer in information systems at the University of Cape Town, told Fox News Digital that, in South Africa, "there is currently no public register of data center facilities, no requirement that operators disclose how much water, electricity and land they will use and no binding commitments against which performance can be measured.
The Isando Campus, home to the Teraco Data Environments JB1 East & West, JB3 and JB5 data centers, in Johannesburg, South Africa, Sept. 28, 2025.  ( Leon Sadiki/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"That gap serves nobody. Communities cannot see what is being traded on their behalf, and responsible operators cannot distinguish themselves from the rest because nobody’s numbers are on the table.

"South Africa hosts the majority of Africa’s data center capacity and has a real opportunity to become the jurisdiction that gets this right early: transparent disclosure, an independent factual baseline and predictable approvals. That combination is good for households, good for the grid and good for every investor who intends to be here for the long term."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Arizton’s Goyal says the future for Africa could be bright.

"Several African countries present a unique opportunity due to their abundant renewable energy potential — such as solar, wind, hydro and geothermal sources — as well as available land, lower development costs and fast-growing digital economies," Goyal said.
Paul Tilsley is a veteran correspondent who has reported from four continents for more than three decades. Based in Johannesburg, South Africa, he can be followed on X @paultilsley.

title: Sweden votes as migration, crime and economy dominate high-stakes election
summary: Gun violence, asylum policy and welfare reform dominate Sweden's election as Ulf Kristersson's coalition battles Magdalena Andersson's Social Democrats.
story: ‘Saturday in America’ host Kayleigh McEnany discusses President Donald Trump’s visit to Ireland, warnings to Europe over its immigration policies and more on ‘Fox & Friends Weekend.’

Swedes head to the polls Sunday with Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s center-right party slightly behind the center-left Social Democratic Party led by Sweden's former prime minister, Magdalena Andersson, and the election dominated by fears of mass migration, crime and the economy.

"Years of gang violence, Islamist extremism, persistent unemployment and pressure on public services have intensified the debate over whether integration has kept pace with immigration," foreign policy expert and author Daniel Schatz, told Fox News Digital.

Sweden Democrats party leader Jimmie Åkesson addresses an election campaign event at Sjodalsparken in Huddinge near Stockholm Aug. 18, 2026, as part of his party's national campaign tour ahead of Sweden's upcoming general election in September.  (Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via GettyImages)
After Germany's AfD victory in a state election last week, Sweden's hard-right Sweden Democrats are in a position to enter government if Kristersson's party wins again.
DENMARK'S LEFT-WING PM WARNS: 'BIG ENEMY HAS STARTED TO GROW FROM WITHIN' AS EUROPE FACES MIGRANT RECKONING

The Associated Press reported that the anti-immigration party has shifted toward the political mainstream and is likely to get cabinet posts. It has so far supported the Kristersson government from the outside.

The Associated Press reported that the Sweden Democrats were founded by activists in far-right-wing extremist groups, including neo-Nazis. But since then, under its leader, Jimmie Åkesson, it toned down that rhetoric and kicked out racist members. Åkesson, who has led them since 2005, is said to be responsible for the success of a once marginal party.
Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson trails in polls as Sweden holds its general election Sept. 13 to elect members of its parliament, the Riksdag. (Kristian Tuxen Ladegaard Berg/NurPhoto)
Sweden, once a model of the Western social welfare state, has been under economic strain as governments from both the left and the right were forced to restructure their welfare system.
While social benefits continue to be extensive, Sweden’s welfare state has changed amid rising crime rates, but the expectations for public benefits remain.

"Sweden went from being described as a ‘humanitarian superpower’ to a 'humanitarian basket case.’ Discontent with migration policies extends to both foreign-born and native-born residents. Shootings have declined sharply, but fewer shootings do not mean the integration problems are solved," Schatz, who is Swedish, added.
Gang violence has rocked parts of Sweden over the last few years. (Oscar Olsson/TT News Agency/AFP via Getty Images)

Prime Minister Kristersson’s government took power in 2022, when the nation was experiencing a dramatic rise in gun-related violence, with the country witnessing 391 shootings resulting in 62 deaths, according to The Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention, a government agency under the Ministry of Justice.
SWEDEN JAMS SUSPECTED RUSSIAN DRONE NEAR FRENCH CARRIER AS NATO WAR FEARS RISE
The homicide rate in Sweden has been on the rise since 2013, when gun homicides contributed to a general increase in Sweden’s total homicide rate.
The Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention notes that Sweden’s homicide rate ranks high compared with other European countries, at approximately four deaths per million inhabitants per year.
The average for Europe is approximately 1.6 deaths per million inhabitants.
Swedes go to the polls on Sunday in a closely watched election race. (Fredrik Sandberg/TT News Agency/AFP via Getty Images/Sweden OUT)

The issue of immigration is another major issue that dovetails with voters’ concerns over crime and gun violence. Like much of Europe, Sweden experienced a wave of immigration in 2015 coming from those fleeing the Syrian civil war as well as the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Sweden took in over 160,000 asylum seekers in 2015, or 12% of all those who sought protection in the EU, according to Sweden’s Migration Agency.

"After the 2015 influx of asylum seekers from Syria and other war-torn countries strained its reception system, Sweden began tightening its borders. The current government has taken that shift much further," Schatz said.
ANTI-MIGRANT AFD SEEKS TO BREAK GERMANY’S POLITICAL ‘FIREWALL’ IN HISTORIC STATE ELECTION

Election campaign posters featuring Swedish Prime Minister and Moderate Party leader Ulf Kristersson are displayed in central Stockholm, Sweden, on Sept. 7, 2026. (Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via Getty Images)
Prime Minister Kristersson’s parliamentary ally, the right-wing Sweden Democrats, filled the void in the anti-immigration position in parliament.

Nicholas Aylott, professor of political science at Södertörn University in Stockholm, told Fox News Digital the link between the increase in immigration and the rise in crime changed Swedish politics.
Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats leads the polls against the incumbent Prime Minister, Ulf Kristersson. (Anders Wiklund/various sources/AFP via Getty Images/Sweden OUT)
"Migration and law and order became much higher electoral priorities," Aylott said.

"The Sweden Democrats based their pitch on them. The other parties, rather belatedly, adapted their positions. The Sweden Democrats had at first been completely ostracized by the other parties, but they were gradually accepted as a legitimate partner by three of the other parties of the right between 2018 and 2022," he said.
As anti-immigration backlash rose and the Sweden Democrats were more included in the policymaking process, Sweden cracked down on immigration and made it harder to seek asylum.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

While asylum claims dropped and gun violence was dramatically reduced as well, with only 158 shootings and 44 fatalities to date, the government still might suffer a defeat at the hands of Andersson’s center-left coalition.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Indonesian passenger ship carrying 240 people loses contact in Java Sea, search underway
summary: The Virgo Transport 8 vanished crossing the Java Sea with 240 people aboard en route from Surabaya to Banjarmasin, triggering an urgent search.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A passenger ship carrying 240 people vanished from contact in the Java Sea on Sunday, triggering an urgent search as Indonesian crews raced to locate the vessel.

The Virgo Transport 8 was traveling from Surabaya, East Java, to Banjarmasin on the island of Borneo when communications with the ship were lost, The Associated Press reported, citing Indonesia’s Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office.
Authorities said the vessel was last tracked roughly 92 miles from a pier in Banjarmasin, the capital of South Kalimantan province.
MOM LOSES GRIP ON DAUGHTER AS PASSENGER FERRY CAPSIZES WITH 20 PEOPLE STILL MISSING
Authorities are searching for the Virgo Transport 8 after the passenger ship lost contact while traveling from East Java to South Kalimantan. (EyesWideOpen/Getty Images)
Search-and-rescue teams launched an operation after receiving a report that the ship had lost communications capability during the voyage, according to the AP.
Officials had not reported any deaths or injuries as of Sunday, and it was not immediately clear what caused the vessel to lose contact or whether weather conditions were affecting the search.
MULTIPLE RESCUED FROM PONTOON BOAT NEAR ALCATRAZ AS SEARCH CONTINUES FOR MISSING PERSONS
The Virgo Transport 8 lost contact while traveling from Surabaya to Banjarmasin, according to officials. (EyesWideOpen/Getty Images)
The Virgo Transport 8 departed Surabaya, Indonesia’s second-largest city, before losing contact while crossing the Java Sea toward South Kalimantan.
The search remains underway.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Trump says he’s banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House
summary: President Donald Trump said Friday that he had banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House over what he called their “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.”
story: President Donald Trump said Friday that he had banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House over what he called their “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.”
In a Truth Social post Friday afternoon, Trump said media outlets “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.”
As of Friday afternoon, reporters from those three outlets were still at the White House.
Trump also warned “other outlets” would “follow” but did not specify which.
CNN, MS Now and Politico did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The First Amendment guarantees freedom of the press, and the outlets are likely to challenge any ban in court.
CNN reported that its team remained at the White House as of Friday afternoon.

“CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting,” the network said. “We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right.”
Politico Press, the publication’s communications team, said in a post on X that Trump’s claims that Politico “received government subsidies are false and have been thoroughly debunked.”
“POLITICO will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them,” the post said.

In his post announcing the bans, Trump claimed that the U.S. government paid “an illegal and ridiculous $8 Million Dollar subscription” to Politico. The claims stem from the Trump administration’s assertion in early 2025 that DOGE had found the subscriptions.

Trump, responding to a reporter in the Oval Office shortly after announcing the ban, said the new policy was the result of “cumulative stories over the last few years.” He did not specify a particular news report, and a White House spokesperson referred NBC News to the president’s spoken comments.

The move is the latest in Trump’s ongoing efforts to punish news organizations and broadcasters for their coverage. Shortly after taking office, Trump banned The Associated Press from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some events after it declined to acknowledge his call to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.
The AP filed suit, and the case is ongoing.

Trump has also taken legal action against outlets including the BBC, The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal after they published unfavorable reports. The suits against the Times and the Journal were subsequently dismissed. The BBC has filed to get Trump’s suit against it tossed.
Democrats denounced Friday’s move.

“This is yet another attack on the First Amendment from a president who knows he and his party of bootlickers are deeply unpopular,” Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker wrote on X. “Donald Trump can’t hide from his failing record, so he’s banning journalists he doesn’t like to keep you from hearing about it.”
Donald Trump just did what dictators throughout history have done. @realDonaldTrump - this is a democracy. You will not be able to manipulate the news or hide the truth. https://t.co/IVr3K1CRd8
The Freedom of the Press Foundation, a nonprofit founded in the wake of the WikiLeaks scandal in 2012, also criticized Trump’s announcement.

“It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the People’s House for criticizing the government,” a spokesperson said. “It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move. The historically unpopular president has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn’t helped him.”
Legal scholar Jonathan Turley, who argued against Trump’s impeachments during his first presidential term, called Trump’s announcement “an assault on long-honored principles of a free press.”
“I have often joined in the criticism over the bias of these outlets, but barring disfavored media from the White House is a terrible precedent and practice,” he wrote on X.
In a statement, Reporters Without Borders said Trump was “once again spewing lies about ‘fake news’ to try to control who covers him and where.”

During his first administration, Trump banned CNN’s then-chief White House correspondent Jim Acosta from the executive mansion. CNN sued, and the White House subsequently restored Acosta’s credentials.

Friday’s bans come as Trump’s approval ratings have sagged and with Democrats gaining a polling edge in many pivotal midterm races that could see Republicans lose control of Congress. He has at times taken particular issue with reporting on the Iran war, writing on Truth Social earlier in September that coverage of ammunition shortages was “actually treasonous.”

title: Singer-songwriter and Broadway composer Duncan Sheik dies at 56
summary: Singer-songwriter and Broadway composer Duncan Sheik has died, according to a post on his Instagram account.
story: Singer-songwriter and Broadway composer Duncan Sheik has died, according to a post on his Instagram account. He was 56.
His mother, Suzanne Sheik, told The New York Times that his cause of death Thursday night was cardiac arrest.

“The world has a lost a singular talent, and deeply influential voice in music and theater. From his Grammy-nominated hit ‘Barely Breathing’ to his groundbreaking, Tony and Grammy Award-winning work on Spring Awakening, Duncan’s artistry touched many and leaves an indelible mark on the cultural landscape,” the Instagram statement said.
2001: Duncan Sheik performs and previews ‘Spring Awakening’

“Duncan was a father, husband, son, brother, and friend. He will be remembered for his sensitivity, wit, inteligence [sic], and depth of spirit he brought to those who knew and loved him,” it continued.

“We are deeply grateful for the outpouring of love from his fans, friends, collaborators, and the artistic community,” the statement said. “His musical legacy will continue to inspire generations to come.”
“Duncan passed away last night surrounded by love,” the statement added.

Sheik had recently been receiving medical care, with his family saying in a statement on Wednesday that he was in “critical but stable condition.” At the time, it was not immediately clear what he was being treated for or where.
Sheik shared a daughter with his longtime girlfriend, Nora Ariffin, and was a practicing Buddhist.
Sheik exploded onto the pop music scene in 1996 with the hit single “Barely Breathing.” The song earned him a Grammy nomination for best male pop vocal performance.
He went on to release nine studio albums over his career, but “Barely Breathing” remains at the top of Sheik’s Spotify page. His most recent album was released in 2022.

In 2020, he told HuffPost that he used to resent performing “Barely Breathing” because “it lived on the radio far longer than it should have,” he said. “And then other things that I was hoping would make it onto the radio never got a chance to, so I was being cock-blocked by my own song at the time.”
Breaking out on Broadway
Sheik also found his footing composing for the theater. His first gig for the stage came in 2002, when he composed the music for the New York Shakespeare Festival production of “Twelfth Night.”
Sheik saw his biggest theater break in 2006, when he and Steven Sater wrote the music for the breakout Broadway musical “Spring Awakening,” an adaptation of a German play from the 1800s.
The show proved to be a big break for many: Actors Lea Michele and Jonathan Groff got their first major Broadway jobs playing the starring roles.
Sheik went on to win two Tony Awards for the “Spring Awakening” music, including best orchestrations and best original score, which he shared with Sater.
“Spring Awakening” also won best musical that year at the Tony Awards and earned a Grammy Award for best musical show album.

title: Kim Kardashian’s new health scare: What is esophagitis?
summary: Kim Kardashian revealed in the trailer for Season 8 of “The Kardashians” that she’s facing a new health condition.
story: Kim Kardashian revealed in the trailer for Season 8 of “The Kardashians” that she’s facing a new health condition.
“I have something called esophagitis,” Kardashian says in one clip from the trailer, released Thursday. In another clip, Kris Jenner, Kardashian’s mother, says the diagnosis “makes me want to cry.”
According to the Mayo Clinic, esophagitis is inflammation of the tissue lining the esophagus, the muscular tube that carries food and drink from the mouth to the stomach.

Later in the trailer, Kardashian is shown lying in a hospital bed, hooked up to machines, while someone off camera asks whether that is what her father, Robert Kardashian, died of. Robert Kardashian died of esophageal cancer in 2003, at age 59.

Dr. Stuart Spechler, a gastroenterologist at Baylor University Medical Center and a member of the American Gastroenterological Association, said that there are many types of esophagitis and that Kardashian did not specify which type she has.
“Far and away the most common form is reflux esophagitis, which is a complication of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD),” he said.

In those patients, Spechler explained, the mechanisms that normally keep stomach acid from moving back up the esophagus are defective, allowing refluxed acid to irritate and damage the esophagus. Common symptoms include heartburn and regurgitation.

Some patients with reflux esophagitis go on to develop Barrett’s esophagus, a condition in which chronic acid exposure damages the esophagus’s normal lining and causes it to be replaced by cells resembling those found in the intestine and stomach, Spechler said.
“It is a risk factor for developing a type of esophageal cancer called esophageal adenocarcinoma,” he said of Barrett’s esophagus.
Still, Spechler noted that esophagitis is only a small risk factor for esophageal cancer and that women are less likely than men to develop both Barrett’s esophagus and esophageal cancer.
“Most patients who have GERD and reflux esophagitis do not have Barrett’s esophagus, and most patients with Barrett’s esophagus do not develop cancer,” Spechler said.

Both conditions are diagnosed using endoscopy, a procedure that lets doctors examine the esophagus and take biopsies to check for abnormalities. Patients with Barrett’s esophagus typically undergo regular endoscopies, Spechler said, “to identify early changes that indicate higher risk for developing cancer.”

In 2019, the Kardashian family helped open the Robert G. Kardashian Center for Esophageal Health at UCLA, established as “a center for holistic, patient-centered treatment, research and education related to disorders of the esophagus,” according to a news release. The family said at the time that it planned to launch fundraising efforts to support the center’s key initiatives.

“Our family is proud to pay tribute to our father by partnering with UCLA Health to establish the Robert G. Kardashian Center for Esophageal Health,” Kardashian said, according to the 2019 release. “We look forward to working with our longtime family friend, Dr. Eric Esrailian, the Melvin and Bren Simon Digestive Diseases Center, and the UCLA Vatche and Tamar Manoukian Division of Digestive Diseases to build the best program of its kind in the country.”
She added: “We hope to save lives and help the community for many years to come in honor of our father.”

title: The AI debate takes the political spotlight: From the Politics Desk
summary: In today’s edition, Kristen Welker takes stock of how the AI debate quickly exploded in Washington and beyond.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Kristen Welker takes stock of how the AI debate quickly exploded in Washington and beyond. Plus, Ryan J. Reilly and Kelly O’Donnell dig into the attorney general’s unusual political appearances.
— Adam Wollner
The AI debate takes the political spotlight

The debate over the future of artificial intelligence is intensifying ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington next week, emerging as a major flashpoint on the campaign trail and Capitol Hill.

While the House passed a bill to shield consumers from higher energy costs that result from new data centers, members left Washington this week without deciding whether to take any action on the broader issue of regulating AI development.

I pressed House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., on “Meet the Press” last Sunday on whether Congress would act on AI before November. He called AI regulation “a very important issue” but said “it’s not one that we can rush into.”

“We have to put up some guardrails,” Johnson told me. “But at the same time, we’ve got to make sure that we don’t lose our edge in the global competition on this with China. Because that would be a national security threat.”

But some Democrats are calling for more immediate action. This Sunday, I’ll speak exclusively with Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., who wants President Donald Trump to call on Congress to convene for a special session focused on AI.
“Congress will soon leave Washington for two months,” Booker said in a Senate floor speech this week. “Artificial intelligence will not recess.”

For his part, Trump has called fears about AI taking over the world a “hoax” and wrote this week on Truth Social: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”

The issue is also shaping the early contours of the nascent 2028 presidential race. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro echoed concerns about competition with China at an AI summit in Pittsburgh this week, while also calling for new safeguards.

“Real leadership means keeping America ahead of China in AI innovation, pushing Beijing on practical guardrails to reduce risks to the American people, and putting effective safety measures in place here at home,” Shapiro said.
Meanwhile, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, another Democrat seen as a potential White House contender, signed an executive order today designed to boost AI oversight “before it’s too late.”

It all comes as AI industry leaders are increasingly sounding the alarm over the rapidly advancing technology. The “Godfather of AI,” Geoffrey Hinton, warned lawmakers this week that they have about a year to regulate the technology before AI systems could begin operating beyond human control. And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has also urged policymakers to take a closer look at guardrails for advanced AI.

AI is sure to be a major topic at the state dinner Trump is hosting for Xi next week. NBC News reported today that former White House AI czar David Sacks will attend, and that tech leaders including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Apple’s Tim Cook and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have accepted invitations.

The debate is also reaching kitchen tables around the country, as Americans wonder whether this technology will help society or will rip it apart. It’s reaching their backyards, too, as state and local officials decide whether to invest in more data centers.

A recent NBC News Decision Desk Poll found that 70% of adults were more worried about AI than excited by it, with majorities opposing the construction of a new data center in their local area. They also raised concerns that AI will do more harm than good across important sectors like elections, national security and how we digest news and information.

I’ll talk about all of this and more this Sunday on “Meet the Press” with Booker and Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo. Steve Kornacki will also join us with the results of a new national NBC News poll.
🤖Related: From drafting bills to writing birthday songs: How Congress is using AI, by Scott Wong, Kyle Stewart, Zara Morris and Allan Smith
Todd Blanche’s political appearances shatter another DOJ norm
Last month, politicos at the Iowa State Fair saw an unusual sight: Attorney General Todd Blanche.

A few days earlier, he had spoken at a rally at the Nassau County Police Academy, praising the Republican nominee for New York governor. He then addressed the GOP’s midterm election convention in Dallas to tout the administration’s law-and-order record and President Donald Trump for “making America safe again.” And on Wednesday, Blanche was at a campaign rally with Trump in Gastonia, North Carolina.

The sitting attorney general is blurring politics and policy at a time when he is also claiming Democratic administrations politicized the Justice Department and as other top Trump administration officials serving in positions that traditionally remain apolitical are attending political events.

“It’s safe to say that none of the 14 AGs who served in the position since 1981 would have considered appearing at political events or rallies,” said Michael Bromwich, a former DOJ inspector general who started in the department during the Reagan administration.
“It would never have occurred to them — 10 Republicans, four Democrats — so firmly was it established that such appearances were inappropriate for a person holding that office,” he added.
A spokesperson for the Justice Department said in a statement that “Blanche’s appearances at political events are made in his personal capacity.”

“His appearances are reviewed and cleared by the department’s ethics officials,” the spokesperson said. “Travel expenses are reimbursed by the Attorney General in accordance with federal law, regulations, and policies.”

At the Republican midterm convention, Blanche was described as a “former federal prosecutor” when he took the stage. Two sources familiar with the planning for his appearance said he did not use Justice Department statistics or verbiage in his remarks and did not engage in any political fundraising. They said he also did not discuss Justice Department policies or official business, just the administration’s broader record.
