title: The first mRNA flu shot is now available. Here’s who can get it.
summary: People looking to get their annual flu shot this fall may find a new option alongside the usual vaccines: an mRNA flu shot. Not everyone is eligible, however.
story: The first mRNA flu shot is now available, but not everyone is eligible.

Moderna’s mFlusiva is the first flu vaccine in the United States to use messenger RNA technology, the same platform used in Pfizer and Moderna’s Covid shots. Scientists have long been interested in using mRNA against the flu because the vaccines can be made faster, potentially making it easier to keep up with changing flu strains.

It’s too early to predict how severe the upcoming flu season will be and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention hasn’t started tracking cases yet. The CDC recommends getting vaccinated by the end of October.

In a late-stage clinical trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in May, mFlusiva was found to be about 27% more effective than a standard flu shot. The Food and Drug Administration approved mFlusiva in August for people 50 and older, clearing the way for the shot to reach pharmacies in time for this year’s flu season.
Pharmacies, however, say the new vaccine is already causing confusion among some patients about who can get it, how it compares with traditional flu shots and where people will be able to find it.
Here’s what you need to know:
Who can get the new mRNA flu shot?
The mRNA vaccine is available only for people 50 and older.
“If you have not celebrated your 50th birthday, this vaccine should be of no interest to you,” said Emlah Tubuo, an independent pharmacist in Ohio.

The FDA granted traditional approval for adults 50 to 64 and accelerated approval for people 65 and older, with Moderna required to conduct another trial in that age group. People who do not want the mRNA vaccine can still get a traditional flu shot.
The additional trial in adults 65 and older stems from a controversy that nearly derailed the vaccine’s approval.
In a large clinical trial, Moderna compared mFlusiva with a standard-dose flu shot in people 65 and older, even though the CDC recommends a high-dose flu shot for that age group.

The FDA initially refused to review Moderna’s application over that issue before reversing course and agreeing to a post-approval clinical trial. In June, the FDA’s independent vaccine advisory panel unanimously recommended the approval of the vaccine for older adults.
People younger than 50 won’t be able to get mFlusiva this flu season. Instead, they can get one of the other flu vaccines approved for their age group.
How is the mRNA shot different from a traditional flu shot?
The biggest difference is how the vaccines teach the immune system to recognize influenza.
Most traditional flu shots use a deactivated version of the virus — often grown in eggs — to teach the immune system how to fight it.
MFlusiva uses a small snippet of genetic code to train the body to recognize and fight the flu virus. The mRNA from the vaccine is then broken down and does not remain in the body.
“It’s like a temporary instruction to your immune system to alert your body’s natural defense to recognize influenza,” Tubuo said. It takes about two weeks after vaccination to build protection.

One point of confusion among patients, according to Brigid Groves, a pharmacist with the American Pharmacists Association, is whether mFlusiva also protects against Covid. It doesn’t. The vaccine only targets the flu and is separate from Moderna’s combination Covid and flu vaccine, which was approved by the European Union in April.
Like the traditional seasonal flu vaccines this year, Moderna’s shot is a trivalent vaccine, targeting two influenza A strains and one influenza B strain.
Another difference is that Moderna’s vaccine can be made faster, said Dr. William Schaffner, an infectious disease specialist at Vanderbilt University Medical Center.

Scientists typically have to choose which flu strains to target months before flu season begins, leaving time to manufacture millions of doses. Traditional flu vaccines can take about six months to produce, while Moderna says mFlusiva can be made in two to three months. That shorter timeline, Schaffner said, allows them to wait longer before choosing which strains to target, giving them a better idea of which ones are likely to circulate.
Is the mRNA shot safe and effective?

Published data from a Phase 3 clinical trial suggests mFlusiva should work better than a standard-dose flu shot.More than 40,000 adults 50 and older across 11 countries, including the United States, participated in the trial. The trial found mFlusiva was about 27% more effective than the standard-dose vaccine at preventing laboratory-confirmed illness.
FDA reviewers did not identify any serious safety problems with the vaccine.
Rates of side effects — such as injection-site pain, fatigue and headaches — were more common in the mFlusiva group but still mild to moderate.
Schaffner said the higher rate of side effects may be “a reflection of the vigor with which the immune system responds to the vaccine.”
Will insurance cover mFlusiva?
MFlusiva is reaching pharmacies without a formal recommendation from the CDC or its vaccine advisory committee, a step typically needed to require insurers to cover vaccines for free.
A spokesperson for AHIP, a trade group for health insurers, said it expects most private insurers will cover the vaccine.
Dorit Reiss, a vaccine policy expert at University of California Law San Francisco, said Medicare is required to fully cover the cost of FDA-approved seasonal flu shots.
Reiss said it remains unclear, however, how widely Medicaid will cover the new shot this season, as the program typically requires a formal recommendation from the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee.

According to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, mFlusiva has a price tag of around $171 per dose without insurance. Depending on the pharmacy, the cost could be as low as $154, according to GoodRx.
Where can people get it?
As with any vaccines, whether you can get the shot right away will depend on your local pharmacy’s current stock and delivery schedule.
In a statement, a Moderna spokesperson said the company has begun shipping doses of mFlusiva across the U.S.

Amy Thibault, a CVS Health spokesperson, said mFlusiva is available at its U.S. pharmacies. A Walgreens spokesperson said it expects to begin receiving shipments of the vaccine any day now, although it’ll be available to patients in “limited quantities” this season.
Tubuo, the Ohio pharmacist, said that demand for mFlusiva is currently low, noting that it is still early in the season and most people do not seek vaccination until October.

title: Authorities search for glider after it collided with another above Saratoga County, New York
summary: Authorities on Friday were searching for a glider involved in a midair collision with another in the sky over the Edinburg, New York, area.
story: Authorities on Friday were searching for a glider involved in a midair collision with another in the sky over the Edinburg, New York, area.
New York State Police said one glider landed safely at nearby Plateau Sky Ranch Airport, where its pilot emerged uninjured. The whereabouts of the other glider were unknown, it said.
“The investigation and search are ongoing,” Trooper Stephanie O’Neil said in a statement. “The public is asked to avoid the area to prevent interfering with the search.”
State police responded to a report of a collision just before 2:30 p.m. on Friday, she said.
The crash prompted a sizable response from area first responders, according to Broadcastify radio traffic from the Saratoga County Fire and EMS.
Another glider in the area reported seeing the collision.
New York State Police said the collision took place above Wheeler Road.
Edinburg, a town of a little more than 1,300, is located in Saratoga County and is about 54 miles northwest of Albany.

title: Ponzi schemer who defrauded Travis Kelce tried to marry U.S. citizen to avoid deportation, prosecutors say
summary: The undocumented Indian immigrant behind a multi-million dollar Ponzi scheme tried to marry an American citizen before he was sentenced to 11 years in prison, court records show.
story: The undocumented Indian immigrant behind a multi-million dollar Ponzi scheme that defrauded Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce and other investors tried to marry an American citizen before he was sentenced this week to 11 years in prison, court records show.

Federal prosecutors opposed Siddharth Jawahar’s request to marry Caroline Tredway, saying he may be an attempting “to obtain immigration status in the United States,” according to a Sept. 4 filing in the U.S. District Court for Eastern District of Missouri.

Jawahar’s lawyer, however, insisted his client was not engaging in “marriage fraud” and said Tredway was willing to buy a $25 wedding ring and spend another $75 on an “officiant” to perform the ceremony.

“The truth is, Mr. Jawahar very much hopes to stay here after his sentence and build a life with Caroline, and he plans to pursue any legal avenues to do so,” attorney Doug Passon stated his Sept. 13 response.
Passon also acknowledged both Jawahar and Tredway are aware that “given this case and his current immigration status, his ability to remain here is highly unlikely.”

The revelations came two days after the 38-year-old Indian national, who pleaded guilty to three counts of wire fraud in January, was sentenced to prison and ordered to repay $31 million in restitution to victims he defrauded from 2016 to 2023.

It was during this proceeding at the U.S. District Court in St. Louis that a prosecutor briefly mentioned that Kelce was one of Jawahar’s many high-profile victims. Kelce has not addressed the report publicly.
NBC reached out to Tredway, who lives near Cleveland, to find out if she and Jawahar are still intending to marry. She has not responded.
“I don’t have any comment on that, and find it wholly irrelevant to the issues at hand,” Passon said in an emailed response to NBC News.
But in a June 30, 2026 phone call that was monitored by the authorities, Jawahar and Tredway discussed the implications of them getting married, court records revealed.
“What if you get deported?” Tredway asked.
“If you don’t marry me, I guess that might happen,” Jawahar replied.
During that same conversation, the records showed,  Jawahar also told Tredway that “the chance of me getting deported goes down dramatically” if they tied the knot.
Tredway, in an August letter to the court, said they met in 2021 and “officially became romantic” in February 2023.

“That night, Sid voiced his interest in me and asked me out on a date for the next evening,” she wrote. “That date turned out to be the best date of both of our lives. Because we already had such a strong foundation of trust and friendship, we fell deeply in love very quickly.”
Tredway, in her letter, insisted that “legitimizing our marriage before he enters a federal facility is vital for our family.”
“I enter into this marriage with my eyes completely open to Sid’s legal situation,” Tredway wrote.

In subsequent conversations with Tredway’s relatives, Jawahar also said he expected be sentenced to “close to time served” and that he would then “focus on getting a pardon because there were a lot of gross violations of the law.”
“But my move after that is — I’d most likely be teaching a class in business ethics at Fordham University,” he was recorded as saying.
Marrying a U.S. citizen was apparently not the only gambit by Jawahar to avoid a lengthy prison sentence.

Jawahar in August, according to prosecutors, paid a prominent Missouri political consulting firm called Axiom $10,000 to try and sway the judge presiding over the case by getting U.S. Rep. Sam Graves, a Missouri Republican, to write a letter of support on his behalf.

Axiom also engineered the publication of a favorable article about Jawahar in a local newspaper that did not mention he was awaiting sentencing for a scheme that resulted in what U.S. District Judge Zachary Bluestone called “enormous losses” for investors.
Jawahar also tried to coach a victim to give a favorable statement to authorities and sought to have his sister wipe his iPhone, prosecutors said.
Much of Jawahar’s past remains murky, but records show that he arrived in the U.S. from India around the time he began studying at the University of Texas in fall 2005.
Jawahar was a government and philosophy major and took classes as recently as spring 2012 but did not graduate with a degree, a spokesperson at the school said.

The U.S. attorney’s office, however, says Jawahar ran a Texas-based investment company called Swiftarc Capital LLC and carried out a classic Ponzi scheme, using money from new investors to repay older investors and to fuel an extravagant lifestyle.
Jawahar traveled on private jets, stayed at luxury hotels, went on spending sprees and had memberships at private clubs across the U.S.
From July 2016 to December 2023, Jawahar’s company took in more than $35 million but invested roughly $10 million, the prosecutor’s office said.
In addition to Kelce, Jawahar was reportedly able to lure other top athletes to invest in his venture capital fund.
That group, according to a Forbes article published Jun 14, 2021, included NBA players Gary Harris, Tim Hardaway Jr. and Mason Plumlee.
“I’m thankful for Sid bringing me in, taking me under his wing and believing in me,” Harris was quoted as saying of Jawahar.

NBC News reached out to their agents asking whether the NBA players lost any money as a result of their investing with Jawahar and whether they cooperated with the federal investigation. There was no response from their agents.

title: Trump says he’s banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House
summary: President Donald Trump said Friday that he had banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House over what he called their “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.”
story: President Donald Trump said Friday that he had banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House over what he called their “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.”
In a Truth Social post Friday afternoon, Trump said media outlets “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.”
As of Friday afternoon, reporters from those three outlets were still at the White House.
Trump also warned “other outlets” would “follow” but did not specify which.
CNN, MS Now and Politico did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The First Amendment guarantees freedom of the press, and the outlets are likely to challenge any ban in court.
CNN reported that its team remained at the White House as of Friday afternoon.

“CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting,” the network said. “We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right.”
Politico Press, the publication’s communications team, said in a post on X that Trump’s claims that Politico “received government subsidies are false and have been thoroughly debunked.”
“POLITICO will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them,” the post said.

In his post announcing the bans, Trump claimed that the U.S. government paid “an illegal and ridiculous $8 Million Dollar subscription” to Politico. The claims stem from the Trump administration’s assertion in early 2025 that DOGE had found the subscriptions.

Trump, responding to a reporter in the Oval Office shortly after announcing the ban, said the new policy was the result of “cumulative stories over the last few years.” He did not specify a particular news report, and a White House spokesperson referred NBC News to the president’s spoken comments.

The move is the latest in Trump’s ongoing efforts to punish news organizations and broadcasters for their coverage. Shortly after taking office, Trump banned The Associated Press from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some events after it declined to acknowledge his call to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.
The AP filed suit, and the case is ongoing.

Trump has also taken legal action against outlets including the BBC, The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal after they published unfavorable reports. The suits against the Times and the Journal were subsequently dismissed. The BBC has filed to get Trump’s suit against it tossed.
Democrats denounced Friday’s move.

“This is yet another attack on the First Amendment from a president who knows he and his party of bootlickers are deeply unpopular,” Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker wrote on X. “Donald Trump can’t hide from his failing record, so he’s banning journalists he doesn’t like to keep you from hearing about it.”
Donald Trump just did what dictators throughout history have done. @realDonaldTrump - this is a democracy. You will not be able to manipulate the news or hide the truth. https://t.co/IVr3K1CRd8
The Freedom of the Press Foundation, a nonprofit founded in the wake of the WikiLeaks scandal in 2012, also criticized Trump’s announcement.

“It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the People’s House for criticizing the government,” a spokesperson said. “It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move. The historically unpopular president has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn’t helped him.”
Legal scholar Jonathan Turley, who argued against Trump’s impeachments during his first presidential term, called Trump’s announcement “an assault on long-honored principles of a free press.”
“I have often joined in the criticism over the bias of these outlets, but barring disfavored media from the White House is a terrible precedent and practice,” he wrote on X.
In a statement, Reporters Without Borders said Trump was “once again spewing lies about ‘fake news’ to try to control who covers him and where.”

During his first administration, Trump banned CNN’s then-chief White House correspondent Jim Acosta from the executive mansion. CNN sued, and the White House subsequently restored Acosta’s credentials.

Friday’s bans come as Trump’s approval ratings have sagged and with Democrats gaining a polling edge in many pivotal midterm races that could see Republicans lose control of Congress. He has at times taken particular issue with reporting on the Iran war, writing on Truth Social earlier in September that coverage of ammunition shortages was “actually treasonous.”

title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom inks AI oversight executive order to improve safety ‘before it’s too late’
summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday signed an executive order intended to increase oversight of and safety measures regarding artifical intelligence “before it’s too late.”
story: California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday signed an executive order intended to increase oversight of and safety measures regarding AI “before it’s too late.”

Newsom, widely seen as a 2028 presidential hopeful, is the latest of a growing number of Democrats and potential White House contenders to call for stronger regulation of AI amid increasing concern nationally over how rapidly the technology is advancing.
Newsom’s order calls for a group of AI experts to meet and then, within two months, develop a plan for the state to strengthen its laws on AI safety and security.

Specifically, Newsom’s order urges the expert group to consider among new regulations the creation of a “kill switch” —  an emergency shutoff system — that would shut down any AI system in the event of a major problem. It also urged the group of experts to come up with bolstered laws that would require independent third-party organizations to develop comprehensive safety plans for AI companies and that AI companies embed those independent organizations on-site to conduct safety audits.
In a statement released alongside the order Friday, Newsom said state action was crucial due to the federal government having ignored the issue.

“The federal government’s abject failure to create any form of meaningful AI oversight or accountability should alarm every American, especially when AI CEOs themselves are begging for regulation,” Newsom said in a statement. “We’re not waiting to act — we’re going to speed up our work on substantial and responsible AI oversight before it’s too late. We’re going to do this thoughtfully but with urgent velocity; the stakes are too high to wait or delay action.”
Newsom has also raised the possibility of calling a special legislative session specifically to address AI concerns.
President Donald Trump has called recent AI safety warnings a “hoax.”
Newsom’s order comes amid rapid advances in the AI industry — including some that many experts in the field have said are alarming.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Industry researchers and leaders, at AI companies including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, have loudly sounded the alarm about their concerns surrounding advanced AI systems. Notably, AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Claude-maker Anthropic, warning on social media “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

A report released over the summer revealed that in July, a swarm of hundreds of AI agents created by OpenAI carried out a July hack of an open-source platform — and in some cases attempted to cover its own tracks. Meanwhile, early Friday, AI company Anthropic said that its Claude system was helping to build the next version of itself.

Newsom’s order came as several other governors — and a raft of potential 2028 Democratic presidential contenders — have rushed to develop policies intended to address AI and the growing concerns around its evolution.

Earlier Friday, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, signed an executive order that launched an AI task force, as well as a data center accountability plan, both intended to address, her office said, “growing concerns and risks posed by the rapid development of artificial intelligence — including workforce displacement, data privacy, and cybersecurity.”

Also on Friday, Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo, a Republican, signed an executive order that barred data centers from receiving a tax break on a particular school tax. His order also required data centers receiving other tax incentives from the state to cover their own power costs.

Less than 24 hours earlier, Pennsylvania Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro, in an interview with NBC News,  called on the federal government to quickly pass regulations that would help rein in the AI industry — but also said he opposed pausing development on advanced AI models until those regulations were enacted.

“We’ve got to regulate this. We have to have real guardrails. We have to understand this technology better,” Shapiro told NBC News. “You’ve got to have third parties be in the rooms with these companies, understanding what they’re doing. When the CEO says, ‘I can’t control what I’ve built, and what I’m building could destroy humanity,’ that’s not time to kick the can down the road.”

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker — who, like Shapiro, are also thought to be mulling 2028 runs — have also called for action. Former President Barack Obama has also offered a warning, too, telling Democrats at a congressional campaign arm fundraiser that the party must have “a very clear plan” on AI policy and that he’d make it a central issue if he were running for president in 2028.

title: Hackers breached OpenAI, adding to fever pitch of security and safety concerns
summary: A small group of cybersecurity researchers said Sunday that they broke into OpenAI earlier this year, an announcement that has added a new element of alarm around AI security and safety.
story: A small group of cybersecurity researchers said Sunday that they broke into OpenAI earlier this year, an announcement that has added a new element of alarm around AI security and safety.

The researchers, from a small company called Hacktron, found that by chaining together two unknown vulnerabilities, one in a third-party company called Discourse and one in how OpenAI validates its employees, they could access employees’ ChatGPT accounts. As is customary for researchers — sometimes called “white-hat hackers” — they caused no harm to the company’s systems.
Hacktron conducted the entire operation within 72 hours in late July, soon after some of OpenAI’s agents broke containment and hacked the AI platform Hugging Face.
An OpenAI spokesperson confirmed Hacktron’s report and said the vulnerabilities have since been patched.
“We thank the researchers for contacting us and sharing their findings,” the spokesperson said.

The news comes as concerns about AI safety have exploded into public view in recent weeks. Safety researchers have resigned from major companies and issued stern warnings that the advanced technology could pose a risk to the human race, and politicians from across the political spectrum have called for action.

While most of those concerns have centered on the capabilities of advanced AI models, the security of the companies themselves is also a significant issue. AI development is extremely competitive, and concerns of theft — primarily through a process known as distillation — abound.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Like many companies, OpenAI maintains a “bug bounty” program, which offers to pay cybersecurity researchers who find novel ways to hack it instead of selling them to malicious hackers who would do the company harm. Hacktron’s researchers wrote in their blog post that OpenAI paid them $6,500 for the discovery.

There is no evidence that any other hackers exploited the same vulnerabilities that Hacktron did. But American countries have for years accused Chinese intelligence of economic espionage, saying China’s elite government hackers routinely share stolen trade secrets with Chinese companies. China broadly rejects the accusations.
More recently, the U.S. formally accused the Chinese AI industry of systematically distilling against American AI companies.

Greg Linares, a cybersecurity researcher at Persona, a company that helps authenticate users, said that Hacktron’s finding would have given China or other countries’ elite hackers the ability to break into OpenAI systems.

“What they chained together was not untypical from what very high-level real-world attackers, such as APTs or nation-state-backed hackers, would use to compromise targets,” Linares told NBC News, using the abbreviation for “advanced persistent threats,” meaning hacker groups that operate in perpetuity and are usually state-backed or state-adjacent.

“The hack conducted demonstrates the need for constant vigilance in these environments and when there’s so many moving parts and the pressure to constantly develop and be delivering; patches get neglected, configurations get missed and cracks in layers of security get exposed,” he said.

title: Kim Kardashian’s new health scare: What is esophagitis?
summary: Kim Kardashian revealed in the trailer for Season 8 of “The Kardashians” that she’s facing a new health condition.
story: Kim Kardashian revealed in the trailer for Season 8 of “The Kardashians” that she’s facing a new health condition.
“I have something called esophagitis,” Kardashian says in one clip from the trailer, released Thursday. In another clip, Kris Jenner, Kardashian’s mother, says the diagnosis “makes me want to cry.”
According to the Mayo Clinic, esophagitis is inflammation of the tissue lining the esophagus, the muscular tube that carries food and drink from the mouth to the stomach.

Later in the trailer, Kardashian is shown lying in a hospital bed, hooked up to machines, while someone off camera asks whether that is what her father, Robert Kardashian, died of. Robert Kardashian died of esophageal cancer in 2003, at age 59.

Dr. Stuart Spechler, a gastroenterologist at Baylor University Medical Center and a member of the American Gastroenterological Association, said that there are many types of esophagitis and that Kardashian did not specify which type she has.
“Far and away the most common form is reflux esophagitis, which is a complication of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD),” he said.

In those patients, Spechler explained, the mechanisms that normally keep stomach acid from moving back up the esophagus are defective, allowing refluxed acid to irritate and damage the esophagus. Common symptoms include heartburn and regurgitation.

Some patients with reflux esophagitis go on to develop Barrett’s esophagus, a condition in which chronic acid exposure damages the esophagus’s normal lining and causes it to be replaced by cells resembling those found in the intestine and stomach, Spechler said.
“It is a risk factor for developing a type of esophageal cancer called esophageal adenocarcinoma,” he said of Barrett’s esophagus.
Still, Spechler noted that esophagitis is only a small risk factor for esophageal cancer and that women are less likely than men to develop both Barrett’s esophagus and esophageal cancer.
“Most patients who have GERD and reflux esophagitis do not have Barrett’s esophagus, and most patients with Barrett’s esophagus do not develop cancer,” Spechler said.

Both conditions are diagnosed using endoscopy, a procedure that lets doctors examine the esophagus and take biopsies to check for abnormalities. Patients with Barrett’s esophagus typically undergo regular endoscopies, Spechler said, “to identify early changes that indicate higher risk for developing cancer.”

In 2019, the Kardashian family helped open the Robert G. Kardashian Center for Esophageal Health at UCLA, established as “a center for holistic, patient-centered treatment, research and education related to disorders of the esophagus,” according to a news release. The family said at the time that it planned to launch fundraising efforts to support the center’s key initiatives.

“Our family is proud to pay tribute to our father by partnering with UCLA Health to establish the Robert G. Kardashian Center for Esophageal Health,” Kardashian said, according to the 2019 release. “We look forward to working with our longtime family friend, Dr. Eric Esrailian, the Melvin and Bren Simon Digestive Diseases Center, and the UCLA Vatche and Tamar Manoukian Division of Digestive Diseases to build the best program of its kind in the country.”
She added: “We hope to save lives and help the community for many years to come in honor of our father.”

title: U.S. clears potential $24.3B F-35 sale to Saudi Arabia despite security concerns
summary: The State Department just approved a potential $24.3 billion sale of advanced F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia. But some lawmakers are sounding the alarm that the deal could put America’s top military secrets within reach of China.
story: The State Department has approved a potential $24.3 billion sale to Saudi Arabia for 48 F-35 Lightning II Joint Strike Fighter jet and related equipment, the agency said in a news release, as the critical U.S. ally confronts a new front in the war with Iran.

Saudi Arabia has long pursued the F-35’s but to date Israel has been the only country in the Middle East to secure access to Lockheed Martin’s fighter jet considered the most lethal, stealthy and survivable aircraft in the world.
“The proposed sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military balance in the region,” the State Department said in a news release.
Saudi Arabia accuses Houthis of targeting Mecca

Congress was officially notified Thursday of the possible transfer of the advanced military aircraft to Saudi Arabia and some lawmakers have already raised concerns that the technology behind it could be acquired or stolen by China, which has a military partnership with the kingdom.

“The Trump Administration should not move forward with its proposed sale of F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia when our own intelligence community is warning that it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party,” Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., said in a social media post. “Beijing has spent decades stealing American intellectual property and technology to close the gap with the United States, and we must not help them do it. We must not sell our most advanced fighter jet anywhere the CCP may be able to get its hands on the technology inside it.”

On Wednesday, The New York Times cited U.S. officials as saying that intelligence analysts had raised the possibility that China could get F-35 technology by spying in Saudi Arabia or through its partnership with the kingdom.

Previous arms sales to Saudi Arabia, including one for $110 billion proposed by the Trump administration during President Donald Trump’s first term, also faced scrutiny by Congress after the 2018 murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, a columnist for the Washington Post.

In his second term, the Trump administration prioritized weapons sales to the Kingdom as the largest recipient of U.S. arms. The approval of F-35 shipment follows Saudi Arabia’s agreement to purchase $142 billion in military equipment and services from the U.S. during Trump’s May 2025 trip to Riyadh — the largest defense sales package in history.

“President Trump has made clear that Saudi Arabia is an anchor for regional security, and increased capabilities for the Saudi armed forces benefits the security of the United States and the wider region,” a State Department spokesperson said. “The sale strengthens the U.S. defense industrial base and ensures Saudi Arabia continues to buy American.”

Saudi Arabia has been fighting to turn back the advancements of the Iran backed Yemen rebel group the Houthis who have been launching drone and missile strikes into the Kingdom as they work to secure a critical shipping route in the Red Sea.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has urged Trump to take military action against the Houthis, NBC News previously reported, but so far, the U.S. has declined to join in military strikes.

The State Department declined to provide a timeline for a possible shipment of the military aircraft but a spokesperson said the U.S. is committed to “further strengthening the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia’s capabilities to deter regional threats, protect its borders, and contribute to regional stability.”

“The proposed F-35 sale reflects the strength and enduring nature of the Saudi-U.S. strategic partnership and the continued advancement of our defense cooperation,” the Saudi Embassy in Washington said in a social media post. “For decades, Saudi-U.S. security cooperation has contributed to regional stability, strengthened our collective defense capabilities, and advanced our shared security interests.”

title: Gas prices approach highest level this year with just weeks to go before midterms
summary: U.S. gas prices approached their highest level of the year Friday, after the national average rose another 3 cents overnight.
story: U.S. gas prices approached their highest level of the year Friday, after the national average rose another 3 cents overnight.
The nationwide average price is $4.46 per gallon. Friday’s price sits just 10 cents below the highest level hit earlier this year, on May 21, when the national average was $4.56 per gallon.
Gas prices are also once again within striking distance of their all-time highest level of $5.01, which was hit in June 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine.

Already, at least six states have average gas prices above $5. California has the highest in the nation, at $6.11 per gallon. A handful of other states, such as Michigan, Utah and Illinois, were on the cusp of hitting $5 Friday.
Gas prices overall have risen 50% nationwide since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.
At the same time, the price of diesel has been registering new daily all-time highs since it first breached $6 per gallon Sept. 11.
The national average diesel price was $6.44 on Friday, after rising 5 cents overnight. The price per gallon of the commercial fuel has risen 71% since the start of the Iran war.

title: How long does your food last in the fridge during a power outage? Experts explain
summary: Two food safety experts explain how long your fridge and freezer will keep food safe during a power outage, the warning signs it’s time to toss it, and how to prep before the next outage hits.
story: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends on our timelines, like how often you should watch your jeans.

When the power goes out, the clock starts ticking on everything in your fridge and freezer. A fall storm, a downed line, a grid emergency — however the outage happens, you’re often left guessing: Is this still good? Do I need to toss it? And no, a simple sniff test does not tell you what you need to know.

I spoke with two food safety experts about how long your food actually stays safe once the power fails, the signs it’s time to throw something out, and the simple steps that can help save your perishables the next time your power goes down.
How long does food stay safe in the fridge and freezer after a power outage?

First, to state the obvious, you don’t have to worry about non-perishable food in your pantry. When the power goes out, you really only need to think about perishable stuff in your fridge and freezer. The good news: “A refrigerator will keep food cold for about four hours if it is unopened,” says Dr. Vanessa Coffman, alliance director for Stop Foodborne Illness. “A full freezer will keep the temperature for approximately 48 hours, or 24 hours if it is half full, but only if the door remains closed.”

In other words, a well-stocked freezer buys you significantly more time than a fridge — but only if you can hold off on opening it. Both experts I spoke with agreed that this tactic of keeping your fridge and freezer shut is key.

“The most important thing you can do is keep your refrigerator and freezer doors closed as much as possible,” says Melissa Vaccaro, senior food safety program specialist at the National Environmental Health Association. “Every time you open the door, cold air escapes and the temperature inside rises more quickly.” That means you should resist the urge to peek inside and check on things — each open door lets precious cold air out and speeds up the clock on your food’s expiration.
How can you tell if food should be thrown out after a power outage?

It’s tempting to trust your senses — for example, sniffing for a bad odor or examining food to see if it “looks bad” — but experts say that’s the wrong approach. “One of the most important things for consumers to understand is that you cannot reliably determine whether food is safe by looking at it, smelling it, or tasting it,” Vaccaro says. “Food can contain disease-causing microorganisms without looking or smelling spoiled. And never taste questionable food to decide whether it is safe.”

Food that looks, smells, and even tastes normal can still make you sick, so don’t let your gut be the judge. Think about it, do you really want to be dealing with food poisoning during a power outage?

Instead, the only tried-and-true test is time. “Again, an unopened refrigerator will generally keep food cold for about four hours,” Coffman says. But once your fridge climbs back up to room temperature, the countdown gets much shorter. “Perishable foods such as milk, cheese, meat, poultry, seafood, and leftovers should not be left at room temperature for more than two hours,” Coffman says. “If they have been at room temperature for longer than two hours, they should be discarded.”

When the power comes back on, your freezer requires its own check. “Use time and temperature. After power is restored, check the temperatures in the refrigerator and freezer,” Vaccaro says. “If an appliance thermometer in the freezer reads 40 degrees Fahrenheit or below, the food may be refrozen. If no thermometer was present, check individual frozen packages. Food that still contains ice crystals or is 40 degrees Fahrenheit or below can generally be refrozen or cooked.”

No thermometer, no ice crystals, and a temperature above 40 degrees Fahrenheit, though, means it’s better to toss it than risk it. Keeping appliance thermometers in your fridge and freezer can be a helpful way to monitor whether food is safe or not (more on that below).
Which products help you keep your food fresh during a power outage?

Based on what food safety experts recommend having on hand, I rounded up products designed to help keep your fridge and freezer contents cold during an outage — from appliance thermometers to coolers and ice packs. Every item below has a 4-star average rating or higher from 1,000 or more shoppers.
Pecula 2-Pack Refrigerator and Freezer Thermometer

Both experts recommend keeping an appliance thermometer in your fridge and freezer at all times, so you can accurately monitor temperatures if the power goes out. This set comes with two thermometers that cover a range of -20 degrees Fahrenheit to 80 degrees Fahrenheit, with an easy-to-read safety indicator, making it simple to check whether your food is still within a safe temperature zone.
Coleman Classic Series Portable Rolling Cooler

During an extended outage, a rolling cooler can double as a practical “access cooler” for the items you reach for most, says Vaccaro. The Coleman Classic Series Portable Rolling Cooler has a sturdy, insulated design with wheels and a retractable handle, making it easy to move and keep near your kitchen.

“Move items such as milk, lunch meat, yogurt, and other perishable foods that require refrigeration for safety into a cooler with enough ice or frozen gel packs to keep them at 40 degrees Fahrenheit or below,” says Vaccaro. “This allows you to use those foods without repeatedly opening the refrigerator and losing cold air.”
Cooler Shock Reusable Ice Packs

These reusable ice packs lay relatively flat and can be tucked into a cooler alongside perishables like milk or deli meat to keep items at a safe temperature during an outage, or store them in your freezer year-round, nestled between frozen foods, so they’re ready to help maintain a safe temperature the moment the power goes out.
Satisure Power Failure Alarm

Say the power goes out in the middle of the night. You may not notice and then could wake to a fridge full of potentially spoiled food. This device plugs directly into an outlet and monitors your refrigerator, freezer, or other essential appliances. If the power goes out, it alerts you with a loud sound and flashing LED light, then continues alerting for up to 12 hours — giving you a chance to act before your food goes bad.
Anker Solix S2000 Portable Power Station

The Anker Solix S2000 is pricey, but it could save your groceries and charge devices and other appliances when the power goes out. It can run a standard refrigerator for more than 30 hours on a full charge, and it recharges from a wall outlet or solar panels, according to Anker. If you live in an area (like a hurricane zone) that gets hit with a lot of power outages, it may be worth the investment.
Is there anything you can do before a power outage to keep food from spoiling?

“If you know in advance that severe weather or another event may cause a power outage, prepare before the power goes out,” Vaccaro says. “Keep appliance thermometers in both the refrigerator and freezer and freeze containers of water or gel packs so you can move stuff to a cooler if needed.” The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) also recommends freezing refrigerated foods you may not need immediately, such as leftovers, milk, and fresh meat or poultry, and grouping frozen foods together so they stay cold longer.

If you know the outage is going to stretch on, it may be worth investing in extra cold power. “If you know the power will be out for a prolonged period of time, buy dry or block ice to keep the refrigerator as cold as possible,” Coffman says. “Fifty pounds of dry ice should keep an 18 cubic foot, fully stocked freezer cold for two days.” That kind of buffer can be the difference between saving a freezer full of groceries and losing everything in it.

Still, even with the best preparation, some judgment calls are unavoidable — and experts say it’s always better to be cautious. “When in doubt, throw it out,” Coffman says. “Eating food that has been held at unsafe temperatures can increase the risk of foodborne illness.” No amount of prep work is worth the risk of getting sick, so when you’re not sure, the safest move is always to let it go.

title: Apple just launched its newest iPhone, AirPods and smartwatch — these are the actual upgrades you should know
summary: Apple released its iPhone 18, Apple Watch Series 12 and AirPods 5. Here’s everything you need to know about the new products.
story: Apple’s iPhone 18, AirPods 5 and Apple Watch Series 12 officially hit shelves today, and if you’re trying to decide whether it’s time to upgrade — or which items actually make sense for you — I’ve got you covered. I’m breaking down everything you need to know about this newest lineup, from what’s actually different to pricing and availability.
Apple’s latest launches
AirPods 5

The AirPods 5 deliver up to 1.5 times more active noise cancellation than the previous generation and are powered by a new H2 chip. They also have dynamic head tracking, adaptive audio to switch between noise cancelling and transparency mode, depending on your environment. Similar to other AirPod models, they also have IP57 rating for dust, sweat, and water resistance.

On the software side, they offer hands-free access to the new Siri AI and real-time Live Translation. Battery life is up to four hours with ANC with the base model, or five hours (22 total with the case) with the USB-C Wireless Charging Case option, which also supports Qi and Apple Watch charging.

NBC Selected senior editor Shalwah Evans tried out the AirPods 5 after receiving a pair from the brand and immediately noticed that the open earbuds fit more comfortably than previous models. “I was pleasantly surprised that these pods with no rubber tip didn’t budge,” she says. “I also love how crisp the ambient sound is when ANC is turned off, which is a huge plus for when I’m walking my dog and need to be aware of my surroundings crossing busy streets.”
The new AirPods 5 start at $129 and are available now.
iPhone 18 Pro

The new iPhone 18 Pro holds onto its familiar silhouette, but the real story is underneath. Both the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max (also available today) now run on Apple’s new A20 Pro chip paired with a redesigned vapor chamber that Apple says delivers up to 40 percent better sustained performance than last year’s model. The camera system gets a meaningful bump too, with a 48-megapixel main camera that now features variable aperture, letting the lens physically adjust for sharper low-light shots and more control over depth. This marks the first time that technology has appeared on an iPhone.

The biggest difference between the two models is screen size — 6.3 inches on the Pro versus 6.9 inches on the Max — and battery life, which Apple is calling the largest leap in iPhone history. Under Apple’s “typical use” metric, the Pro is rated for up to 24 hours per charge, while the Max stretches to 30 hours. Both phones also charge faster than before, reaching 50 percent in about 15 minutes with a compatible adapter.
In terms of pricing, the iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, a $100 increase from the previous model, while the Pro Max starts at $1,299. Both phones are available for purchase now.
Apple Watch Series 12

The Apple Watch Series 12 centers on a completely reworked Health Sensing System, powered by the new S11 chip. Larger, more power-efficient green LEDs let the optical and electrical sensors work harder in the background — taking heart rate readings every five seconds and measuring heart rate variability up to 24 times more often than the Series 11, according to Apple. That stream of data feeds directly into a new Readiness score: a single number, calculated each morning from your recent activity, vitals and sleep, meant to tell you at a glance how much you can take on that day.

The design has gotten an upgrade too. It’s available in eight finishes, including two ceramic options in Pearl White and Night Blue, and the aluminum models now use Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple says is 60 percent tougher than the previous Ion-X glass.

Beyond health tracking, Series 12 leans into AI with new Siri-powered features, including Live Rewind, which lets you replay the last 15 seconds of audio you just missed, and Siri Recap, which generates quick summaries of conversations picked up by the watch’s microphone (a feature you program and can customize). It keeps the familiar 42mm and 46mm case sizes, along with standard safety staples like Fall Detection and Emergency SOS, and is rated WR50 and IP6X for water and dust resistance.
It starts at $399 — the same price as the Series 11 — and is available now.
Apple Watch Ultra 4

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is built around the same S11 chip and redesigned Health Sensing System as the Series 12, but tuned for endurance athletes and outdoor use. Battery life gets a major boost too: Apple rates it for up to 50 hours of everyday use, up to 18 hours of standard workout tracking with full GPS and heart rate monitoring, and up to 45 hours in a new Max Extended Workout mode — enough to cover a 100-mile race. It’s available in two titanium finishes, natural and black, and retains the built-in satellite communications that let wearers stay connected off the grid.

Like the Series 12, the Ultra 4 also has Siri AI and Audio Intelligence features powered by the S11 chip, plus the ability to start a request on iPhone and pick it up seamlessly on the watch. It keeps the rugged design and precision dual-frequency GPS that have defined the Ultra line. Pricing holds steady at $799, the same as the Ultra 3, and it can be purchased now.
